subtopic: CONSULTATIVE COMMITTEE TO MEET IN OTTAWA OCTOBER 4 TO OCTOBER 9

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONSULTATIVE COMMITTEE TO MEET IN OTTAWA OCTOBER 4 TO OCTOBER 9
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the house at this time that the annual meeting of the Colombo plan consultative committee will be held in Ottawa from October 4 to October 9. Previous meetings have been held in Sydney, London, Colombo, Karachi and New Delhi.
The countries participating in or associated with the Colombo plan now include Australia, Burma, Cambodia, Ceylon, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, New Zealand, Pakistan, the United Kingdom, the United States and Viet
Nam. Dependent territories of the United Kingdom in southeast Asia-the Federation of Malaya, Singapore, Brunei, North Borneo and Sarawak-also fall within the scope of the plan. Thailand and the Philippines have sent observers to some previous meetings of the consultative committee and have been invited to send representatives to the Ottawa meetings.
I am sure hon. members will be glad to know that it is intended that the meetings should be held in this building, with the consent of the Speakers of both houses. It is expected that the opening session, which will be held in this chamber, will be addressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and by leaders of some of the visiting delegations.
The Colombo plan, which was framed to cover the six-year period from June 1951 to June 1957, is now in its third year. The consultative committee meets annually to discuss common problems, to review the progress of economic development and basic economic trends in countries of the Colombo plan area, and to survey the contributions which member countries are making to economic development in this region. A progress report by the consultative committee is published at the conclusion of the meetings. I am confident that the Ottawa meeting, like previous meetings, will be of real value to all the Colombo plan countries, and I know that I speak for all members of the house when I say that we are very glad that we shall have the privilege of receiving the members of the committee in Ottawa next fall.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could hardly let the feast of St. Jean Baptiste go by without extending my best wishes to all my French-speaking compatriots in this house. On the occasion of this, their national holiday, I would like to say to all my French-speaking fellow citizens, first how sorry we are to be unable to take part in the celebrations which are now taking place in the province of Quebec and throughout the country, next that we who are at this time sitting in this parliament have now and always have had the greatest

Questions
regard for them, a regard which is inspired by the best traditions of this country and which is such that we never fail to put their interest above everything.
In conclusion I wish to say that this feast is of very great importance for our compatriots. I should therefore like to pray our blessed patron saint to keep them in this confederation of ours, a durable institution which they could not do without.

There are one or two
questions I should like to ask on this item. In the first place I notice that the department has increased staff by the addition of 5 mail transportation officers. I should like the minister to tell us just what the duties of these officers are. It looks like the creation of a new position. There is another item to which I desire to refer. I believe I mentioned it on the first item of the estimates. I refer to what are now called senior transcribers. It would appear that this is a new classification. They are probably the same employees transferred from the classification formerly described as stenographers grade 2B and grade 2A and now to be known as senior transcribers, grade 2 and grade 1. If the minister would explain these changes in staff, I am sure the committee would be interested.

The employees of the department doing typing and stenographic work are reclassified on the basis of their competence and general efficiency over a six-month period. This classification scheme has worked exceptionally well and has permitted a reduction in the total number of stenographic positions. Hon. members will notice a reduction from 146 to 139 in the number of positions. At the same time it permits the better workers to receive some adjustment in their salaries based on their competence and efficiency. As far as the transportation officers are concerned, they are engaged in the implementation of the Woods-Gordon report.
I presume the position of senior transcriber is a new classification-
A new classification.
-which has been introduced because these people have reached the last bracket in the stenographic classification. Is that correct?
Not exactly. It is a reclassification by the civil service commission based on the efficiency of the employees.

I am sure I know what the minister means by that, but there is one other item about which I should like to speak. I notice that the boot allowance is $222,000 and was the same last year. Will the minister tell us how much each man receives in boot allowance, whether the amount has been increased and when, and how much of the $222,000 was expended last year?

Supply-Post Office
The boot allowance is $15.60 twice yearly, and the last one was paid in May, 1954.
How much of the total of $222,000 was expended? What was the actual amount paid to all employees as boot allowance?

Perhaps the minister will tell me whether the amount of $15.60 twice yearly is the same amount that has been paid for years and years or if there has been an adjustment in the amount in the last few years when the price of all clothing has gone up considerably. I should also like to know if the boot allowance is supposed to cover the entire cost of the shoes, boots, rubber footwear and so on that the postal carriers are required to purchase for their use in the course of their duties.
To answer the first part of the question, it has varied from year to year and it is only for boots. The amount is fixed after inquiry as to the purchase price for similar articles.
When was it last raised?
It has been practically the same for the last two years. I am sorry I have not got the figures for the previous year.

The last item in the list of details on page 416 is uniforms and letter carrier satchels, and the amount is reduced from $697,000 to $263,000. I understand that is because uniforms are supplied every second year. I have had some little experience with the Post Office Department and its employees and I have some knowledge of the uniforms that have been supplied. This leads me to ask the minister a question which he may think is facetious, but I assure him it is not intended as such. In view of the classification here, I wonder whether the uniforms are made by the same people who make the letter carrier satchels. If so, are they primarily makers of uniforms or makers of letter carrier satchels?

The uniforms are made by a firm which specializes in that sort of work. It is done after an inquiry has been made and an understanding reached. A meeting is held at which the employees are represented.

If the minister will
inquire into the matter a little bit he will find that the measurements are taken in a very offhand manner. I think about thirty seconds per employee is the time spent on that, and the uniforms really would fit better if they were just made in small, medium and

large sizes. In fact, I suspect that is about how they are made and that the manner of taking measurements is a camouflage. I would advise the minister to inquire into that matter and to actually talk to some of the postal carriers. I know that much of the information that reaches him reaches him through the usual channels, and probably by the time it gets to him it is slightly coloured. I am often interested to hear the minister say that such and such took place after consultation with the employees. Then I get an entirely opposite story from some of the employees, and I have had sufficient experience with employee relations to realize that when a story goes through several hands it may have a slightly different complexion by the time it reaches the head than .it had where it started. But quite apart from the abominable fit of these uniforms, does the minister not think that it might be well to separate these two articles? It seems to me it might be better to put uniforms and boot allowance together. I cannot see that uniforms and letter carrier satchels have any relation to each other.

I understand the natural taste for fashion of my hon. friend. I think she will understand that it is very hard to have employees all over the country of the same stature. But we are doing our best to make the uniforms suitable. There is a special board on which the employees have their representatives, and it is through consultation with these representatives that we come to a decision as to the types of uniform. If there are some who are not satisfied they have every right to complain to this board. If my hon. friend has some special names in mind, I will be glad to receive them personally, and if there is really something that can be corrected we will be pleased to investigate and make the correction.

Mr. Chairman, I think that is a rather poor excuse because the transportation companies, the fire departments and police departments of the various cities manage to take measurements of their employees and supply them with uniforms which look neat. If I might say one last word on this subject, I think the letter carriers' satchels fit better than the uniforms in most cases.
I wonder whether the Postmaster General has any information as yet as a result of his check-up on working conditions in the Fleet street post office in Toronto which he undertook some weeks ago.
The committee is still working on this question and they have not yet filed their final report.

I have just one other question. I wonder whether the minister could enlighten us on the mysteries of the classifications of employees in the post office? I note, for instance, the postal staff ranges all the way from grade 1 to grade 14. Is that general in other departments or is it applicable only to the post office? I further note that a grade 14 postal employee gets about the same salary as grade 7 in other departments. Now, it is a great mystery to me. I do not know whether it is to the Postmaster General, but perhaps he can enlighten us on that.
The technical classifications are made by the civil service commission and relate only to the Post Office Department, but the clerical classifications relate to all departments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Following upon the question of the hon. member for St. Paul's, I should like the minister to tell us how he chooses the media through which he does the advertising concerning changes in rates or notices about Christmas mailing. For instance, I have in mind that on or about April 1 there were several advertisements appearing in various newspapers in the county in which I live, but I observed there was no advertising in the local paper in Georgetown which serves a community of from 3,500 to 4,000. If we are to advertise efficiently, it seems to me the department should be advertising in all the local papers. Would the minister tell me how this choice is made?

It is done through the A.B.C. circulation by an advertising company. We do the advertising through the Walsh advertising company in Montreal and Toronto. They have to establish certain lines of demarcation. As an example, if a newspaper has no bona fide subscribers it is not considered, because that is one of the conditions necessary to be classified by A.B.C. We are not doing it ourselves; we are doing it through an advertising agency which considers all the qualifications of the respective newspapers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that is a very arbitrary and unfair way of choosing a method of advertising, that is through the audit bureau. I take it that is what the minister indicates. The newspapers are not necessarily all members of this audit bureau, and does that mean those newspapers that do not happen to be members of the bureau get no advertising?

We have only a small amount of money to cover this advertising. I appreciate that there
should be economy in the department, and particularly in the spending of the public's

money, but I am not sure we are getting the most efficient service when we observe Post Office Department notices can appear in papers serving perhaps from 1,500 to 2,000, while a newspaper serving a community of from 3,500 to 4,000 gets no advertising at all. I think that does not work toward efficiency in the department. These advertisements mean a great deal to the local weekly papers and, if possible, some fair way of allotting advertising should be undertaken by the minister. I say that just by way of suggestion to him, because it means a great deal to these local weekly papers. They give a very fine service in getting information out to the public, and keeping the public informed. I suggest that the minister and those in his department should look into the possibility of placing in the hands of those weekly newspapers any business that could be given to them, keeping in mind always the principles of sound business practice.
May I say that the minister has always been most kind to me in any communications f have had with him, and I would appreciate his giving this matter his consideration on behalf of all the weekly newspapers throughout the country. I suggest to him that it is an important matter.

I wish I could fulfil the hon. member's suggestion, for which I thank her. However, as a department we are not experts in advertising, and that is why we rely upon agencies. If there is anything that can be done along the lines suggested by the hon. member, we will look into it.

Mr. Chairman, the second item to which I wish to refer is one which has been raised by the Auditor General, and to which I referred earlier in the session. At page 38 of the Auditor General's report a suggestion is made to the Post Office Department which it seems to me has considerable merit as a means of effecting economy.
As hon. members know, the department had to come to parliament asking for an increase in rates to offset the heavier expenditures as a result of which, it was indicated, the department would have operated at a loss. So that every economy I suggest is worthy of careful attention.
The one I have in mind is related to the post office savings bank which has been carrying on for a great many years and in many communities and local areas and has fulfilled a useful service. This is particularly true where there are no branches of chartered banks readily available. I am not suggesting therefore that the service be discontinued. The point to which the Auditor General calls attention is that out of 278,000 accounts,

150,000	are inactive, the money involved having remained in that status for years.
He gives an illustration of an account opened in 1878 with a deposit of $700, in which there have been no transactions since that time. I would suppose that after this interval of time the depositor is dead. After some decades of bookkeeping, the adding of interest and the occupying of the time of employees in the post office bank to no good purpose, the balance in that account now stands at $5,448.
Hon. members will have in mind the fact that the Bank Act provides a scheme for dealing with unclaimed deposits held in the chartered banks. Interest is added for ten years, and then the account is transferrred to the Bank of Canada. The Auditor General suggests that the same procedure could be applied to the post office savings bank, with substantial reductions in the unnecessary carrying of small accounts which are dead.
This might give rise to a review of the postal savings offices now maintained, because where there are adequate banking facilities it is difficult to see how the post office savings bank is required. Certainly there is no advantage in the interest rate allowed, because I believe it stands at 2 per cent, just as it is in the savings accounts in the chartered banks. If there are chartered banks and trust companies operating savings accounts readily available in a community, it seems to me that this duplication of banking facilities might very well be avoided by having many of these offices closed, thus leaving the business to the chartered banks-keeping in mind always the fact that communities in which banking facilities are not available should not be deprived of those facilities.
I rise at this point because I notice the business of the postal savings offices has dropped off very substantially. In fact, looking over the report of the Post Office Department-I do not have it before me this morning-it becomes apparent that there is no great demand for this type of savings office. Withdrawals in the last ten years have almost equalled deposits, and it does not look as though the public requires this service that is now being maintained. Certainly it does not require the maintenance of accounts which long since have ceased to be active. I do recommend this to the minister for his consideration as a very direct way of effecting an economy in the department.
If the minister has no comment I have one further point.

I am glad the hon. member has brought this matter to my attention. He may rest assured that all the points he has raised,

as set out in the Woods-Gordon report, have been considered, and are continually under consideration by the department.
When parliament meets again we will look forward to some action having been taken.

If the hon. member wishes, I could give an explanation right now, although I would not want to lengthen debate unnecessarily. It can be pointed out however that the Woods-Gordon report indicated that the cost of operation of the savings bank has been estimated by the cost ascertainment division of the department to amount to $377,000 annually. It has been repeated several times and quoted as the amount which would be saved if the bank were discontinued. Such is not the case.
The $377,000 mentioned covers not only the employees actually engaged full time on savings bank work at headquarters of the department but also employees in post offices, who spend a small portion of their time on savings bank work. It also covers a proportion of the salaries of administrative officers at headquarters and at various district offices and post offices in the field.
If the bank were discontinued it would not be possible to make a saving of $377,000. It would not be possible to make an immediate saving of the total expenditures at headquarters.
It should also be taken into consideration that the money now on deposit is obtained at a cost of 2 per cent for interest, plus less than 1 per cent for all administration costs. This should be compared with the higher administration costs and possibly higher rates for funds borrowed by the government from other sources.
The savings bank is utilized a great deal by a certain sector of the Canadian public who have always been accustomed to a government savings bank. Furthermore, at points where we have military camps the savings bank is unquestionably a desirable and well utilized service.
This is why at the present time we have decided not to discontinue the savings banks. The hon. member has brought up the question of "closed" accounts, and we are actually investigating each case. We are constantly considering the whole question so that, if it is necessary to make a change, we shall have all the information.

I am not advocating the discontinuance of the post office savings bank because, as I said in opening my remarks,
I believe it performs a necessary service in some communities. But it seems to me that 83276-418
Supply-Post Office
150.000	inactive accounts out of a total of
278.000	leaves a good deal of room for economy such as the Auditor General has recommended. The service is already being given by the chartered banks.
The cases to which the hon. member has referred are gradually being investigated.

This involves a change in the law for which a pattern has already been set. Those of us who served on the banking and commerce committee were told what the chartered banks do with their accounts after they have become inactive for a period of ten years. It is a matter of bringing the post office savings department under that.

Is there any special
expense incurred by the Post Office Department in looking after these inactive accounts, or any disadvantage in the government having these deposits?
Very little.
I can see no reason wny that money should not lie in a government account as well as in a private-bank account.

To keep the record straight, I am not suggesting that it lie in a private-bank account. If an account in a private bank is inactive for ten years it is transferred to the Bank of Canada and becomes a government account. I am suggesting it could be transferred from one government account to another government account where, as an inactive account, it could be handled more cheaply.

Item agreed to.
343.	Transportation-movement of mail by land, air and water, including administration, $48,524,258.

This item covers transportation of mail by land, air and water, and also administration. There is one matter to which I should like to draw the attention of the minister in this connection. It is a matter within my personal experience, which happened during the past few weeks. In May of this year it was necessary for me to send some passports down to Montreal to a friend of mine who was leaving for Europe. I did not have time to send the passports to Wolfville and I arranged to send them to my friend in Montreal and have him pick them up there prior to his sailing for Great Britain.
On Thursday evening, May 27, at ten o'clock, I mailed in the post office here in this building a special delivery registered letter addressed to my friend in Montreal at Notre Dame de Grace. The letter arrived

Supply-Post Office
in Montreal at 1.40 a.m. on Friday, the 28th.
I heard no more about the matter until, on the following Wednesday, my friend phoned me from Montreal. He was not in hysterics, but under a reasonable degree of excitement, in view of the fact that he was sailing that night and there were no passports. I got in touch with the assistant postmaster here who was most co-operative. He got Mr. Dempsey of the investigation branch of the Post Office Department, who was certainly very co-operative and very efficient. To make a long story short, Mr. Chairman, at two o'clock on Wednesday afternoon Mr. Dempsey located this letter lying in the Notre Dame de Grace post office. It had been there from Friday night until Wednesday. I could have walked to Montreal in that time. It was raining, and I would have had to walk rather slowly, but I could have walked to Montreal in a rainstorm, delivered the letter and been back here and had a good night's sleep in that time. As a matter of fact, probably I could have made two journeys. There is something radically wrong with a special delivery system that works in that way. It is true the mail courier called at this home and there was nobody there. I am not in a position to comment on that. The people who were in the home say that there was always someone there.
I wonder just what the regulations are. I understood that if somebody called with a special delivery letter and made some memo it should have been left. I understood that they were required to call at least twice. This envelope has marked on it "one call" and somebody initialed it. I hardly think that is the worst of it. Mr. Dempsey was able to locate this letter shortly before two o'clock on Wednesday afternoon. My friend was sailing that night. Mr. Dempsey told me himself that the postmaster in Notre Dame de Grace said it was impossible to deliver the letter until the next morning. That would be on Thursday. I want to be fair. He said: "If you want to have that done now I will issue special instructions to have that done." Why in the name of common sense would it be necessary to have to get special instructions issued to deliver something which has already been lying around there for five days? I have heard a lot about the forty-hour week, the five-day week and the eight-hour day, but I wonder what hours are in force when at two o'clock in the afternoon a letter which has been missing for five days is discovered and they say: "Well, we are sorry we cannot deliver this until the next morning", despite the fact that I spent about $20 in telephone calls getting in touch with various parties and telling my

friend to sit there in Montreal, and also to the postmaster, inquiring as to why it was not delivered. In the end I telephoned the man to whom this letter was addressed and said: "Don't take any more chances in this thing. We have found the letter." He hired a taxi and drove out to the post office and got the letter and came back with it; otherwise it would not have been delivered yet. I know the Postmaster General is not responsible himself for this situation. I do not expect him to deliver the mail. I know he will understand that this is not uttered in any way against himself; but when you pay money for a special delivery letter, I think you assume, and the public assumes, that you are going to get efficient and speedy service. As a matter of fact, you get a poor quality service. I do think the Postmaster General or the department should warn the people particularly not to pay for special delivery letters, and if they do they are just taking a chance. They will deliver the letter only in certain hours, and it is much more difficult to get it than it would be if it was sent by ordinary post. I would suggest that special delivery be refused by the Post Office Department in any case where there are no couriers who will make special delivery of them. If there is to be no special delivery why call it "special delivery"? You pay 20 cents for a special delivery stamp and I presume the department takes in quite a lot of money out of that. There must be hundreds of thousands of them throughout the country. The public expect a little bit better service than we got in this case. Why a letter should lie around in the post office from Saturday morning until the following Wednesday I cannot understand. I can understand that with the five-day week no one works on Saturday and you would not expect anyone to work on Sunday. Even so, there was still Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. The letter was growing moss by the time it was discovered. Had it not been for Mr. Dempsey we would not have found it yet; the passport would have been of no use on this occasion.
I draw it to the attention of the minister. I think it is indicative of a situation which occurs very often, and something which should be investigated by the department.

This is a case where I think I should first remind my hon. friend that we deliver twice, and if the person to whom the letter is addressed is not there, then we leave a notice. This is exactly what happened in this case.
If it happened in this case why put "one call" on the letter?
I will come to that.
And nothing left.

There might be some contradiction, but here is the information I have:
Re: Registered special delivery letter
No. 647, addressed to Dr. Konstanty
Rayski-Kietlicz, 4069 Northcliffe,
Notre Dame de Grace, Montreal.
Was received in Montreal on the 28th May at 3.52 a.m. via flight 240 from Ottawa.
It was given to the special delivery contractor at 8.10 a.m. on the same morning. He called at the above address but received no answer.
That was the first delivery. I continue:
Therefore, he brought it back to the general post office registration branch at 1.30 p.m.
On the 29th May, 5.20 a.m. the letter was sent out to Notre Dame de Grace postal station for delivery by letter carrier. It was taken out by the letter carrier, but still there was no answer to the call-
That was the second delivery. I continue: -so he left a card indicating that it was to be called for at Notre Dame de Grace postal station.
The letter in question was placed in the general delivery, Notre Dame de Grace postal station on the 31st May, where it remained until called for on June 2.
There might be a difference in the appreciation of the facts, I do not know; but these are the facts I have. My hon. friend might have been informed that the letter was delivered only once. We have information based on facts. That does not mean that this or any other system is perfect. Incidentally, my hon. friend called my attention to the fact that the postmaster there refused to allow the letter to be delivered. I do not know about that but I will have inquiries made. However, in the main the rules and regulations have been applied in this case as in other cases. We made two deliveries and on both occasions there was no one there and, as the regulations require, we left a note. We know these facts to be accurate and I believe they are as have been reported to us. I believe that in the circumstances we did what the postal regulations require us to do.

I can only say, Mr. Chairman, that if the minister did not make a mistake in the information he gave me then there must be something wrong, in view of the fact that he states it left the office for delivery at 5.20 a.m.-

No, that is not exact. On the 29th of May it was sent from the office at 5.20 for delivery to the postal station and it would then be taken by the letter carrier. But when he called there was no one there and he left a card. It was sent to the postal station and then given to the letter carrier to deliver and he attempted to deliver it but without success.

Well, the envelope I have here has only one call marked on it. I would 83276-418J
Supply-Post Office
imagine that a proper carrier who had instructions to deliver this letter according to the regulations would make more than one call, but this has only one call marked with some initials after it. As I said, I am not going to debate the facts. The minister has given some of the facts according to his report-
We have a full report here.

Well, I have the facts from people who are thoroughly reliable and they say there was always someone in the house and that no card was ever left there. They even took up the carpet and moved the bookcase to see whether the card may somehow have slipped under them but they were unable to find any card. I think this is a situation which indicates that the system might be reviewed, because after a survey of the facts in this case it seems rather strange that the letter should have lain there without being delivered. It might even lie there for a year. Would you allow that to happen, or what would you do in a case like this?

After two deliveries without success we leave a card requesting the people to call for the letter. That is exactly what was done in this case. We have the names of all the employees who tried to deliver the letter. I do not say the system we have is perfect but we are trying to improve not only this part but other parts of the service. As far as the regulations are concerned I believe, and I think the hon. member will agree, that we have followed the regulations and attempted a delivery on two occasions without success. We then left the card. As it may be of some interest to my hon. friend, I might inform him that according to regulations special deliveries are made from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. every day including Sunday.

Mr. Chairman, on this item I wonder if the minister would make a brief statement for the information of the public on a matter about which there is some confusion, namely just when and where letters can be carried by air with an ordinary five-cent stamp, and when anyone wanting special air delivery has to affix a special stamp.
All first-class mail is taken by air up to eight ounces when it will speed the delivery of such mail.

speechtext: Is it not the case that this applies only to mail delivered in Canada?
Yes.

speechtext: It does not apply to letters sent to the United States, for example?

No, for domestic delivery only.

Before this item is carried,
Mr. Chairman, I would like to draw the attention of the minister to one matter which I believe has already been brought to his attention on various occasions. This item covers postage stamps and I know the minister has adopted the principle that stamps cannot be issued in commemoration of the founding of any particular city or town. I do not think anyone can quarrel with him on that because, if the department issued special stamps commemorating the establishment of one city, naturally the people in another city would feel they would have to receive the same consideration, and special-issue postage stamps would have to be issued for every town and city in the Dominion of Canada. And we know that could not be done.
But the minister has already been approached by one historical organization requesting that next year a special stamp be

issued in commemoration of the founding of the first settlement of white persons north of the gulf of Mexico. It is to this that I wish to draw the minister's attention. I believe when the minister received the application he assumed that it was a stamp to commemorate the founding of the town of Port Royal. Incidentally, the town of Port Royal grew out of that settlement. Champlain established the first permanent white settlement north of the gulf of Mexico at Port Royal, and the 350th anniversary of that occasion will be celebrated next year.
I think it is an historical event of profound significance and one in the celebration of which I think the national film board and other federal organizations have been requested to co-operate. I believe they will.
I am going to take the liberty of urging this historical society to resubmit its application to the minister and I hope he will reconsider it and give the matter favourable consideration, not because it is a town or community but because this was one of the great historical events which went to the making of this nation. If that event had happened in the country to the south of us, I am sure that they would have several issues of stamps, several flags, several anthems; they would have many things done. Our government has rebuilt Port Royal in order to show the historical significance of it. As the parliamentary assistant well knows, the government spent $100,000, $200,000 or more-I do not know exactly how much-in order to rebuild, in its original shape, the habitation of Champlain, the old wooden log building which I am sure many hon. members have seen, with its wooden pegs and hand-drawn nails. It was rebuilt because it was realized that this was an historical shrine. Because of the 350th anniversary of the founding of this settlement, I am making this suggestion. I am not going to take up any more time of the committee now, but I urge the minister to reconsider this matter. It has the support of the historical societies throughout the whole dominion. It has the support of the government of Nova Scotia. I think it has a broad appeal to each and every one of us in this country.

In connection with what the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has just been saying, I should like to point out that, if I recall rightly-and I am just speaking from memory-I believe I have seen a special stamp which was issued in 1908 to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Champlain's founding of the city of Quebec. I think perhaps there is a precedent there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
In line with what has just been suggested by the hon. member for

Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the hon. member for Queens, I should like to express once again the hope that consideration might be given to the recognition of the 100th anniversary of the opening of the first post office in western Canada. I agree with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings that there is no point in having too many of these stamps. Their value would be cheapened if that course were followed. However, I suggest that we do not have too many events of this kind yet, particularly in western Canada, that can be celebrated.
Surely the 100th anniversary of the opening of the first post office in western Canada is an event that should be recognized. I believe that anniversary will occur at the end of February next year. If the Postmaster General still finds it impossible to recognize the event by the issuing of a commemorative stamp, perhaps I should invite him to come out with me next February when the event is recognized. As he knows, that first post office in western Canada is located in the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre and is an old building which has been put into shape and is being cared for by the historical society of Manitoba.

The matter I wish to deal with is something which I have had brought to my attention by several people. It is the fact that some of our postage stamps, even of the new issue, are pale and anaemic. Also, for those people who probably have not 100 per cent eyesight, the figures designating the value could be improved on. I just bring these matters to the minister's attention so that when any changes are being considered-
Make them so people can see the figures.
Yes; they might be made so that people can see the figures.

There is a question I should like to ask the minister. A couple of months ago an announcement was made that a new machine for sorting the mail had been developed by the engineers in the department and that it would possibly be installed in Toronto, Hamilton or some of the larger cities. It was to be a rather expensive machine. At the time the increased postal rates debate was going on we were searching to find economies in the department. This would have been a good proposition to have been introduced then. The expense is so great that it is out of the question at the present time. However, I understand it is going to be of such benefit that it would take care of all the Post Office Department requirements in connection with sorting letters. Can the minister
Supply-Post Office
give us any information on that development or as to the possibility of its introduction in the future?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No. Can the minister give us any information as to this new machine or its introduction?

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to elaborate on this matter at this time because I did so previously. It will take a few years before we are in a position to operate the machine. We are working on it now. The national research council has helped in telling us that it would work. Our experts and technical engineers have made progress. I hope it will be possible to make use of it sooner rather than later, but it will take a few years before we are actually able to operate the machine. Once it is in operation it will represent a fantastic advance in the sortation of mail; it will be unique in the world.
I thank the minister for his statement. I think that is information the committee should have.

I just want to refer to the matter of commemorative stamps which was raised by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and supported by the hon. member for Queens and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I think it would be helpful if the minister would make a statement on this subject which is of intense interest to everybody in the country, and would let us know what is the general policy of his department with regard to it. It would also be helpful if he could give us a list of the commemorative stamps that have been published recently.
As has been pointed out, if too many of these stamps are put out, the whole idea is cheapened. That is why I suggest that perhaps there must be some well-outlined policy that the department has adopted. If not, it is for us to discuss now what it should be. The commemorative stamp serves a useful purpose. I grant that the minister might be inundated with requests for them unless it was made clear what should be done with regard to that type of issue. If the minister would give us an explanation now, perhaps the matter would be cleared up.

I do not want to elaborate again at length on that subject but I may say this. The basic principle with regard to the issuing of these stamps is, first, that the subject must be of national interest. The suggestions which have already been made today, just within five minutes, show that, if it were

Supply-Post Office
possible, not only every member of the committee but every person in the country would like to have a commemorative stamp of his own. Therefore each case must be studied on its merits. The event must be one of national interest. On the other hand, I may say that Canada has an extremely high reputation. We do not issue stamps every day of the week, every week of the month and every month of the year. We have regard to the timing and we try to issue the stamp when we deem it necessary. Because of that fact, our issues of stamps are well received in all parts of the world. I do not want to make comparisons with any other country but I may say this. Those countries which have made a business of frequently issuing stamps find that the stamps have no value, philatelically speaking. To come back to the basic principle, I say again that the subject must be of national interest. Otherwise there is no line of demarcation. If that were not the principle followed, we would be swamped-as we are-with all sorts of suggestions. They are good suggestions in themselves. But if we were issuing a commemorative stamp for my home town anniversary or for the home town of anybody else, in which there might be some minor feature of national interest but more local interest, there would be no limit or no end to the requests. In those circumstances, we would not be able to respond to all the demands we have and would have.

Mr. Chairman, I am not advocating the issue of large numbers of commemorative stamps. What I am really interested in is a declaration of policy. The minister has pointed out that national interest is the most important factor. Would he tell us then who makes the decision and would he strengthen his position by giving us a list of commemorative stamps that have recently been published? It would then be open to us to determine whether national interest has been the overriding factor.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Mr. Chairman, I am waiting for a reply.

I might refer my hon. friend to the Postmaster General's report for 1953, page 12. I will not impose the reading of all this on my hon. friend, but I might read the second paragraph. It reads as follows:
On July 26, 1952, a 4 cent postage stamp was issued to commemorate the 18th international Red Cross conference which was held in Toronto. Additional commemorative postage stamps were issued on November 3, 3 cent and 4 cent denominations,
fMr. Cote.]
displaying portraits of the two former prime ministers, Hon. Sir John J. C. Abbott and Hon. Alexander Mackenzie. This stamp was issued to replace the 7 cent commemorative postage stamp that was first issued on September 24, 1951.
I am informed that we do that each year, and I will be glad to give my hon. friend more information if he wishes to have it. We will send him a complete list if he wants to have it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I am glad to have had a statement of policy by the minister in connection with this matter, but I must confess that I still think the opening of the first post office in western Canada 100 years ago is an event of national interest. I think it is of just as much national interest as what is on this 4 cent stamp that I hold in my hand. I see the minister straining his eyes to see what it is. It is a walrus. At least, I think it is. I am not too familiar with the animal. But I ask the question, of what greater national interest is a walrus than an event in the history of Canada such as that to which I have referred?
Having mentioned this first post office in western Canada, and having done so on a number of occasions, I hope I may be permitted to take a moment to tell you, Mr. Chairman, since as a British Columbia member you frequently have occasion to go through Winnipeg, and also to tell all members of the house where this post office is located. When you travel through Winnipeg by Canadian Pacific Railway, if you will just step out the front door of the station during the hour stopover that usually takes place there and look across the street you will see this log structure to which I have had occasion to make reference quite a number of times. It is that log structure which was the house of the late Mr. Ross in which the first post office in western Canada was opened in February, 1855.

In order to add to the information given by my hon. friend, the stamp he showed was one of an issue of 4 cent and 5 cent wildlife design stamps issued in April, 1953. The series of wildlife stamps was introduced for annual issue to support Canada's national wildlife week and the preservation of wild life. The grey coloured 4 cent stamp depicts a walrus and the blue coloured 5 cent stamp depicts a beaver. These two stamps will be short-term commemorative issues. The stamps were designed by Emanuel Hahn of Toronto.
What is the quantity of commemorative stamps issued? Is there some policy with regard to that? How great or how small is the issue?

I will give the postage stamp impressions purchased. In 1951-52 there were
1,863,845,000	stamps and in 1952-53 there were 1,870,075,000 stamps.
How many were commemorative?
I have not got that breakdown, but those are the total impressions purchased in 1951-52 and 1952-53.

What the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just said reminded me that perhaps the time has come, as the walrus said, to speak of many things. Therefore I should like to ask the minister if he can indicate to the committee what series of stamps, if any, have been approved for issue in the near future that have not yet appeared. Perhaps he might give that for the year ahead. I am thinking particularly of any commemorative stamps that may have been approved but have not yet been issued in connection with such events as the British Empire games.

It is not news to the committee that we have issued a new set of stamps depicting the Queen to replace the not so successful stamp on the coronation. We must admit that the new one is far better. I am sorry that I cannot answer the second part of the question as to commemorative stamps for the coming year.
I was not referring to the present general issue with the new likeness of the Queen. I was thinking of any special stamps which have already been approved but have not yet appeared.
There are none so far.

If I may be
permitted to revert to item 343 for a moment, I should like to ask the minister what percentage of first class mail is actually transported by air?
What percentage?

Yes, what
percentage of first class mail is actually airborne?
The closest I can come to it now is between 30 and 40 per cent.

This supplementary item is a companion item to one we had in the main

estimates a few moments ago. In other words, it has to do with the same question of operations. I should like to say a few words concerning a matter which comes under the operations branch. In 1953 he came over to Winnipeg North Centre and gave me the benefit of his candidacy as the Liberal candidate and once again enjoyed defeat. Mr. W. A. Molloy was

the Liberal candidate in Winnipeg North Centre in 1949. As I pointed out there is also a good deal of correspondence in this file, as in the other one, between the operations branch and the secretary of the Minister of Justice. There seem to be no letters addressed directly to the Minister of Justice and no letters written by the Minister of Justice. Rather the letters are to the minister's secretary and she is asked to forward the minister's recommendation. She replies stating that her minister recommends such and such and then another letter goes back to the secretary of the Minister of Justice advising that her minister's recommendation has been accepted.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, it would be an imposition on my part were I to regale the house with the same kind of outline as was given by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North. But I do feel I should draw attention to one or two aspects of this file which are a little different. I have referred to the fact there are letters here addressed to the same Alderman Peter Taraska, who had a good deal to do with appointments in Winnipeg North and he has had something to do with appointments in Winnipeg North Centre as well. This seems to have begun about the time he moved over and became a candidate in Winnipeg North Centre.
The case of Mr. Molloy is extremely interesting. I find that there has been correspondence, according to this file, with him with respect to five different small post office appointments in the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre. In only one of those five cases, so far as I can ascertain from going through this file, did Mr. Molloy make a recommendation; that was back in 1949. I do not know why, but apparently Mr. Molloy does not seem to be too interested in this matter of post office patronage. I say that to his credit, and I repeat that he was my Liberal opponent in 1949. Indeed, I ask hon. members to note this with regard to the other four cases. They are found on pages 18 to 23; 26 to 31; 49 to 55; and 80 to 85 of this sessional paper that I hold in my hand. Those page numbers are inclusive in all cases. Strangely enough in each of those cases hon. members will notice that I have referred to six pages in the file-six letters-and the pattern is the same in all four instances.
First of all, there is a letter-let me take the first one I gave as an example, pages 18 to 23 of this file. As hon. members know, these files are built up from the bottom, sc we start on page 23. Starting with that page, we note that on May 29, 1950, a letter went to Mr. Molloy from the director of
IMr. Knowles.]
operations, advising him of a certain vacancy and asking him for his recommendation. There was no answer immediately, so on June 19, 1950 a second letter went to Mr. Molloy with respect to the same vacancy. Mr. Molloy answered that letter on June 23, 1950. His letter, addressed to the director of operations reads as follows:
I acknowledge your request for recommendation of a suitable person for permanent appointment as postmaster at the above-mentioned post office.
I thank you for referring this matter to me, and I wish to advise that I am not in a position to make any recommendations.
That is the third letter on the file. First, there are two letters to Mr. Molloy advising him of the vacancy and asking him for his recommendation. Then, Mr. Molloy writes back and says he is not in a position to make any recommendation. Following that, there are three more letters addressed to Mr. Molloy still telling him about this vacancy and eventually telling him what has happened in the matter.
Three more?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Three more letters after Mr. Molloy had indicated in a rather tactful manner his disinterest in this question. I am not going to read all of these letters. I have indicated by giving the page numbers that there are four instances exactly the same, where two letters are written to Mr. Molloy telling him of a vacancy and inviting him to make recommendations. He writes back and says, I have none to make, but the department goes on writing him three more times after that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Molloy must be a good man.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Molloy is a very fine man. As I pointed out a while ago, he was the Liberal candidate in 1949 and joined a long succession of Liberal candidates who have stood in Winnipeg North Centre, but that is as far as they got.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: They still have hopes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Molloy has since transferred his political interest to other parts of the city of Winnipeg. The point of this is obvious. Even when you have a political person out in the field who is obviously disinterested in post office patronage, the operations branch keeps fostering it. I submit that is very clear evidence that this business of patronage in the post office is fostered and pursued by the Post Office Department here at Ottawa. I think it is fair to say that Liberal members themselves, and even defeated candidates, would be quite glad if this whole business of patronage in the Post Office Department were discontinued. And in view of this evidence that

it is being foisted upon them by the operations branch, I feel very strongly that serious consideration should be given by the department to discontinuing this patronage in the matter of making these post office appointments.
Perhaps I should go a little further with regard to this one case. I can give it as a sample, because the pattern is practically the same throughout the whole file. With respect to this Winnipeg sub-post office No. 15, situated in the heart of my constituency, not only was Mr. Molloy written to, but the provincial secretary of the Canadian Legion was advised. Oddly enough, or perhaps significantly, the letter to the provincial secretary of the Canadian Legion is a form letter, a mimeographed letter, with the secretary's name put in. In the case of the letters to Mr. Molloy, four out of five of them were original letters. The provincial secretary of the Canadian Legion was written to, but there is no reply on the file.
Then, D. W. W. Revie, 803 Charles building-I am sure that should read Childs building-was also written to about it. He made no reply so far as the file is concerned. But this is not so in the case of the correspondence addressed to the secretary of the Minister of Justice. First there is a letter to her asking for her minister's recommendation. There is a reply from her indicating whom the minister recommends. And then there is a reply back to her stating that the appointment has been made in keeping with the recommendation of that secretary's minister. I do not think it is very fair to a secretary to a minister to put her in the position of having to carry on this correspondence in her name. If the Minister of Justice is going to be the dispenser of patronage in respect of these matters in Manitoba-and I would point out that his constituency is that of Marquette, which is up on the Saskatchewan boundary, and this matter has to do with a constituency in the city of Winnipeg-if he is going to do it, then I suggest he should do it over his own signature.
As I say, the hon. member for Winnipeg North has made very clear what is going on with respect to the matter, and I do not need to go further with it. But so far as this aspect of the matter is concerned I do wish to point out what struck me when I got this file, namely that even when a man like Mr. Molloy is not very interested in the patronage aspect of the matter, it is continued by these letters from the operations branch, which he does not bother to answer.
Supply-Post Office
Of course that is not so in connection with Mr. Taraska. There is no letter to him that is not answered. He seems to be active in these matters.
Then, there is one other point. I am now looking at page 22 in the file which happens to be a letter addressed to Mr. Molloy; but there are quite a few letters in the file which are like this one. It reads in part as follows:
The order of preference which, according to law, is observed in making such appointment is as follows:-
(a)	patron of the office entitled to disability preference;
(b)	patron of the office entitled to overseas preference;
(c)	patrons not entitled to preference under either
(a) or (b);
(d)	non-patron entitled to disability preference;
(e)	non-patron entitled to overseas preference;
(f)	non-patron not entitled to preference under either (d) or (e).
Now, as I say, these people who are asked for their recommendations are informed that according to law this is the order of preference. The question I would like to put is this-
It is strictly followed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What happens if a person like Mr. Taraska or Mr. Molloy or Mr. Revie or the secretary to the Minister of Justice, or anybody else, recommends anyone who does not come under these categories? What happens in that event?

I am glad my hon. friend has asked that question, because we should not dramatize it too much. This was done after a committee of the house decided to do so, following recommendations and information. And it is done to avoid the great expense that would be involved if we had to send an inspector perhaps 100 or 200 miles. It would cost more than the annual revenue of these little post offices.
And that is exactly why in 1932 a committee decided to follow this procedure-that is, to ask for information and recommendations from the member or the defeated candidate, because the committee felt they were the persons in the best position to give this information.
And now, to come to the question asked by the hon. member. Let me say that the order of preference is strictly followed. And when A, B or C recommends somebody who does not fall within the order of preference the recommendation is not followed. We receive this information or these recommendations in respect of the appointments to be made, but those recommendations are

Supply-Post Office
not appointments by any means. And it is going a little too far when an attempt is made to dramatize this matter.
I am glad my hon. friend adopted the tone he did this morning, because there was considerable difference between the tone he used and that used by his colleague from Winnipeg North. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has brought forward some factual reports.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: So did the member for Winnipeg North.

Yes; but within the meaning of that word, they are not patronage. This is just a useful proceeding to get information. Appointments are made in the order of preference mentioned by my hon. friend, and not because the information is given by A, B or C.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What happens if one of these unofficial people makes a recommendation of a person who does not fit into the order of preference?
He is not appointed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Such a person does not get the appointment?
No. If a man who is recommended or suggested does not fit within the order of preference, then he is not appointed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that. Now, just a word or two further. The Postmaster General seems to be satisfied that it is perfectly all right to follow this system of getting these items of information from these unofficial people. It has never been my view that in any business concern it is a matter of economy to have people do things for nothing. In the end they can turn out to be very costly.
I would point out that Mr. Taraska, Mr. Molloy and Mr. Revie, who figure in this correspondence, have no official standing so far as the Post Office Department is concerned, or so far as the government of Canada is concerned.
And they make no appointments, either.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No, but their advice is sought, and their recommendations are sought.
They are asked for information because they are in a position to give information. But giving information does not mean that they make appointments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: I am satisfied with your tone.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But this point is strong. Let me make it clear-
Crystal.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Somebody used the word "crystal".
Crystal clear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let me make it crystal clear that I do not think we people here should be involved in this kind of business at all. I do not want the minister to ask me for my recommendations with regard to these appointments. I want him to do this work in and through his department. But I do want him to clarify what he said a moment ago when he referred to the practice of writing to defeated candidates and members of parliament. He means defeated Liberal candidates and Liberal members of parliament.
Why not?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I take it from that question that the Postmaster General thinks that the patronage system is all right. I may tell him it went out a long time ago in any democracy worthy of the name.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been attempting to make something significant out of a couple of returns that have been brought down in connection with post office matters in the two constituencies in Winnipeg, and from his observations one would think that the people whose names have been referred to have done something wrong, when they have intervened in a matter which is not their business. Well, I think it is regrettable that he took occasion to dig these people's names out in the manner in which he has. They are all good, responsible, reputable citizens. If they happen to be Liberals, they are that much better.

I come back to the practice that has been in effect in this country for a long period of time in so far as post office appointments are concerned. I do not think there is very much wrong with it. If, as he apparently would suggest, we should turn the selection of postmasters in the smaller postal stations over to the civil service commission or to some other branch, I am sure it would add greatly to the expense and it would not bring about greater efficiency or greater satisfaction to the public.
I am sure that in these cases-I will not say so much for the city constituencies, but I will so far as the country post offices are concerned-apart from elected members or people who have been candidates no one is in a position to give the same type of satisfactory recommendations that these people can. It is often not easy to get people to take certain post offices in certain outlying areas. The point I make is that any elected person, if you like, or any defeated candidate, is going to attempt to secure the person who will do the job efficiently and well and who is acceptable to the community.
My hon. friend the Postmaster General referred to the conditions of appointment and I am sure that no one is going to step very far afield in making recommendations to the Postmaster General for the selection of postmasters that do not conform to those conditions. I am sure that if anyone were to recommend a civilian ahead of a pensioner who was equally qualified and equally entitled, he would hear from the community in no uncertain manner. Therefore one is governed by his conscience in matters of this kind. I cannot for the life of me see how you are going to devise a system that works any better than this, unless you are going to bring the whole thing under the civil service commission, which I am sure would add greatly to its cost.
Let me say this to my hon. friend. As he knows, I have been here some little time, and I presume he will ask for files on the constituency of Portage-Neepawa, and I hope he does.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You are putting ideas in my head.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I will tell him this. In all the experience I have had, I have had more trouble and more irritation over appointments made by the civil service commission than anything that I ever had to do with. So it works both ways. I do not think I would have done any better had I tried to inject myself into the larger post offices in the appointments made by the civil service commission; but I do know that my own 83276-419J
Supply-Post Office
experience is that there has been more fuss made over appointments made by the civil service commission than over any other types of appointments that have been made. Let me give you one illustration which I find very curious. Take a civil service appointment, where one man in a competition is rated for the appointment by the commission and he gets the position. Within months, not years, another office comes open, and this man, as he is entitled to do, applies in the second competition. In the one competition he is placed at the top of the list and gets the appointment. In the other competition, with the same competitors, he is placed fourth or fifth on the list and somebody else gets the appointment. How are you going to explain that? It happened to be out of my category. I was not interested in it, and I was glad to be out of it, but these things can work both ways, even in so far as appointments by the civil service commission are concerned.
I am going to say nothing more about this except this. If these are the greatest mistakes that have been made by the Postmaster General, or if these are the biggest complaints that my hon. friends can dig up about the administration of the Post Office Department even in the province of Manitoba, I am afraid that we shall have to say that our Postmaster General and those associated with him are pretty pure in the administration of that department.

I have one word on this, and it is in regard to the opinions of the member of parliament vis-a-vis the opinions of defeated candidates. That is the one thing that I cannot get straight. I am interested to hear the hon. Postmaster General and the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa defend the patronage system. If that is their opinion they are entitled to it, and they are on record in regard to it. I have no quarrel with that expression of opinion, but I do not believe in that system. I do not believe it is worth anything to anybody.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: May I just submit one question to my hon. friend? This system is in vogue at the present time. Do I take it that my hon. friend would rather have the officials of the Post Office Department go out and take recommendations from the drugstore operator, the storekeeper, the bank manager or somebody else instead of from a duly elected person or one who has offered himself for public service?

My answer to that question is largely yes. If the administrators of the Post Office Department are efficient, and if the appointments are made on the basis of efficiency and convenience, I suggest then

Supply-Post Office
they should do it and that members of parliament or defeated candidates should have nothing to do with it. But I do want to say just one thing. The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa has said that somebody may be appointed who is suitable to the community, and from that angle I was interested in it. He wants someone suitable to the community, and he goes out to get the advice of somebody who has proven himself to be unsuitable to the community as far as being elected as a member of parliament is concerned. They go to that man to find out who is suitable to the community. I imagine a great many people in Saskatoon-I will flatter myself and say there are not too many; there are some-think I am not suitable for that constituency.
Agreed.

The hon. member sitting on the other side of the house can make that statement and I love him for it. He is just like a lot of the people in my constituency who happen to belong to the unfortunate political designation of my hon. friend. The point I want to make is that it is a ridiculous thing to me as a member of parliament for Saskatoon. I do not want to be bothered with anything like that. I want you people over there to put into these jobs people who are supposed to be qualified to carry on their work efficiently; make your appointments and you will never hear a growl from me in that department; but I do say this in respect to consulting the defeated candidate to find a man suitable to the community. In doing that you are consulting a man who will recommend a man who in the opinion of the defeated candidate would be suitable to that community, but he himself who is advising the department on this man is a man who has proven to be unacceptable and unsuitable to his community.
Rejected.

Rejected by his community, and this is the man to whom my hon. friend goes for advice. They consult the defeated candidates. The question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was fair and it was not answered.
What question?
The question is, in the case of a defeated candidate belonging to another party but the Liberal party, does the Postmaster General write to him?
We receive recommendations and information from members of every party and we even receive recommendations from many of my hon. friends opposite.

The minister can wriggle and he is in a good place in which to learn how to do that, but I am asking the minister this question. And let me put it in this specific manner. If we had an election tomorrow and if I were defeated for the constituency of Saskatoon, during the following three or four years would I be receiving letters from the Postmaster General asking for recommendations, or, as he puts it, for information?
I can answer that question in two ways.
There are two ways-yes and no.

The hon. member has asked a question and he should at least permit me to answer. He told me a few moments ago he did not want to be bothered so I do not think we should bother him. Secondly, he has asked me what I would do tomorrow. Well, I will tell him tomorrow.

The minister has simply
wriggled around the question and refused to answer it. I can only accept that as his answer. It is on the record.
One o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, before we carry this item I want to support the case made by my colleagues. I might say that I have a great deal of confidence in the officials of his department. But the interjection made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle prompts me to say that in the last copy of the Saskatchewan Gazette there was an item stating that Mr. G. M. Ferrie of Invermay had been made commissioner of oaths by the C.C.F. government. I was not consulted about that appointment and I offer no objection because I do not want to be consulted by this government or the government of Saskatchewan as to who should or should not be appointed to government positions, but I hope the Postmaster General will have another look at this patronage question.

Mr. Chairman, I want to be fair to everyone but the hon. member who has just spoken wrote an article in his local newspaper telling the people there that he was the one who obtained certain concessions by means of pressure on this government. I think if that is the way in which my hon. friend-

Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, I would ask the Postmaster General to quote from the article he mentions. I deny the charge he has made and I suggest

he put the article in question on the record. If he cannot do so I suggest he withdraw his remarks.

Mr. Chairman, I am ready to be corrected if correction is needed, but I am referring to the erection of a public building in my hon. friend's riding about which he wrote that he had obtained it because he forced the government to do so.
Mr. Chairman, I must ask the Postmaster General to withdraw his remarks or substantiate his statement by putting the article in question on the record.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I remind the committee that we are not debating the erection of a public building. I have followed very closely what has been said by the Postmaster General. The minister suggested that the hon. member for Mackenzie had written certain things in a newspaper article and the hon. member for Mackenzie said, "I deny that", and the Postmaster General said, "I am willing to be corrected if correction is needed." I take it from the Postmaster General's remarks that he has accepted the denial of the hon. member for Mackenzie, as he is bound to do.
But, Mr. Chairman, I would like the Postmaster General to put on record that he withdraws the remarks he has made. He is nodding his head but I would like him to withdraw his statement.

Mr. Chairman, I am willing to withdraw that remark, but may I just point out to the committee that I was informed that an article was written by my hon. friend in a local newspaper in his own constituency. He did not deny he wrote the article. If what I said is incorrect, then I am willing to withdraw my remarks.
I write a weekly letter for the newspapers in my constituency and I am quite prepared to have the minister quote from anything I have written at any time to show-
