speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Hon. members will find the vote on page 28 of the blue book and the details commencing on page 229.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at various times during the session I have had the feeling that I should like to give the members of the committee of the whole a good deal of information with regard to the activities listed in pages 28, 29 and 30, but at this late date I must confess that I shall curtail my remarks. If I leave out some of these activities, I hope hon. members will not think that I do not consider them to be important, because I do. However, the things that I shall refer to are perhaps those which, in my opinion, require a little bit of explanation.
The estimates represent an increase over last year of $4,044,957 due, in large measure, to the general salary revision for civil servants announced last December and the normal increase in the contribution to the unemployment insurance fund. That $4 million approximately is an increase for both agencies, the department proper and the unemployment insurance commission. Staff strength remains virtually the same as last year, with no change with regard to the unemployment insurance commission and an increase of one in the Department of Labour. The members of both these staffs have continued to render excellent service during the year. The consistently high quality of their work is, I think, a credit to the public administration in Canada.
The industrial relations branch is provided for in votes 180, 181 and 182. The last fiscal year was a period of good industrial relations in the industries within federal jurisdiction. Out of 184,000 workers involved in 78 disputes dealt with during the fiscal year by our conciliation officers and boards, less than 1,600 workers were involved in a total of two strikes. Of the 78 disputes, 59 were settled, and 16 were still being dealt with at the end of the year, by conciliation officers and boards. In one case, conciliation proceedings lapsed without a settlement but also without a strike, and strike action occurred in two cases. I think this is a good record. Let me 'interject the pious prayer that we may have as satisfactory a record during the oncoming months. This branch is also responsible for the administration of legislation governing wages and working conditions on government contracts, for the promotion of

Supply-Labour
productivity to the benefit of both workers and employers through the medium of labour-management production committees, and for the administration of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act.
The Canada Fair Employment Practices Act is, as the committee knows, new legislation and the experience so far gained under it has been encouraging. When the act came into effect at the beginning of last July, steps were taken to make its provisions known to the public, and particularly to the employers and trade unions whose operations fall within federal jurisdiction.
I believe that educational activity is an essential element in the administration of this legislation, and a broader program of educational publicity is planned for the present fiscal year.
No serious enforcement problems have been met in the administration of the legislation thus far. Up until the end of last May only three official complaints of alleged violations of the act had been received, and all three had been quickly settled either by correspondence or by direct investigation and conciliation.
One of the most encouraging features of the experience we have had in administering this legislation has been the willingness of employers and trade unions generally to co-operate in the work of establishing employment practices that may truly be called "fair".
Amendments to the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act have been the subject of debate at this session of the house and, for that reason, I intend to limit my remarks to the activities under votes 189 and 190. In vote 189 there is an increase over last year of $84,200. This additional sum is necessary mainly because of an expansion in our apprenticeship training program. This program, in co-operation with the provinces, is one of the most important training projects in which the department participates. As its name suggests, it is designed to stimulate apprenticeship and, in doing this, to ensure that this country will have an adequate supply of the tradesmen whose skills play such an important role in maintaining and developing the productive power of our economy.
Earlier this session I promised to say a word on my estimates about the retraining of unemployed persons. I might refer, if I may, to item 189 in the main estimates and item 669 in the supplementary estimates. Heretofore, trainees in these classes have been referred for training individually by the local offices of our national employment

service. The nature and extent of the training in each case has been determined by the availability of definite jobs on completion of training and the capacity and previous experience of the trainee. Recently serious unemployment situations have developed in a number of localities. In some cases displaced workers have been absorbed in other plants or industries, but in other cases workers possessing specialized skills have found it impossible to find suitable employment in other fields. The provisions and conditions of schedule M are being reviewed with a view to facilitating the establishment of special training programs to provide such workers with new skills which will fit them for employment in other industries or occupations. In addition, a special committee of the advisory council on vocational training has been named to study this program and officials of the Department of Labour and of the unemployment insurance commission have been designated to co-operate with the provinces in dealing with specific situations.
In vote 190 of the main estimates, which provides for payments to the provinces for capital expenditures in connection with vocational schools, a decrease of $100,000 is shown. This reduction is because the obligations of the federal government under the vocational schools assistance agreement have been met in all areas of Canada except Newfoundland and the Northwest Territories. During the past ten years a total of $30 million has been made available under this agreement for sharing with the provincial governments the cost of building, equipping and operating vocational and technical schools of less than university grade.
Provision is again made, in vote 185, for the farm labour program which has been carried on ever since world war II. During the past year, farm labour agreements were concluded with all provinces except Newfoundland and, under these agreements, organized movements of farm workers were carried out to meet seasonal demands in different areas. The program is a co-operative venture and is characterized by the excellent teamwork of provincial officials and officers of the Department of Labour and the national employment service. It has served, in large measure, as a means of overcoming the shortage of farm labour which we in Canada have experienced for over a decade, and it will continue to operate during the present fiscal year. As a matter of fact, it is operating now. Farm workers are being recruited for certain crops at the present time.
It has been necessary not only to carry on a farm labour program aimed at the most

effective utilization of the farm labour force, but also to supplement that force from time to time by bringing immigrant farm workers to Canada in organized groups. These group movements have been used to meet unsatisfied demands for labour in several basic industries and there are indications that some such movements will have to be organized this year. On the whole, however, this is likely to be on a smaller scale and, consequently, the provision made for it in vote 194 represents a reduction of $115,574.
I want to make special mention of item No. 186 initiated in my estimates for the first time last year for a women's bureau. During the year the civil service commission undertook a survey and competition for the purpose of finding a suitable head for this bureau. I did not think, I can tell the committee frankly, that it would take so long to bring this task to a conclusion, but I am glad to say now that it is expected that an announcement will be made very shortly as to the person selected for this post by the commission.
During the past year the economic and research branch continued its important work of research and analysis, providing to both the government and the public accurate information on vital subjects such as manpower, factors affecting levels of employment and unemployment, trade union organization, collective bargaining trends and the incidence of work stoppages resulting from industrial disputes. Much of this research material has been printed in the Labour Gazette, a publication which needs no introduction to hon. members.
I should like to say something about the help being given by my department to establish a comprehensive plan for the rehabilitation of Canada's disabled. This work is being done in close co-operation with the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Veterans Affairs. It has been greatly aided by suggestions made by the national advisory committee on rehabilitation. The government has offered to make to each province, on a matching basis, a maximum contribution of $15,000 a year through my department towards the salaries and expenses of a provincial rehabilitation co-ordinator and his staff, and towards the cost of supplying certain rehabilitation services not otherwise provided for.
Last year the national co-ordinator, Mr. Ian Campbell, accompanied by the senior medical officer of the Department of National Health and Welfare, discussed this offer with the appropriate government officials in each of the provinces, and these discussions have produced encouraging results. To date, eight

provinces-Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Newfoundland, Alberta, Prince Edward Island, British Columbia and Nova Scotia-have signed the co-ordination agreement, and it is now being studied in all the remaining provinces. This rehabilitation effort is of course closely co-ordinated with the federal-provincial pension plan for the permanently disabled initiated this year by my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
And now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to turn to the estimates of the unemployment insurance commission. There are three votes, one for the administration of the act, one for the contribution of the government to the fund, and one for the transfer of unemployed workers to areas where jobs are available. The vote for administration shows an increase over last year of $2,227,753. Most of this is to be used to meet increases in salary requirements resulting from the general salary revision, normal statutory increments and casual assistance to handle an enlarged load of claims for unemployment insurance benefit. The number of claims received in the fiscal year 1952-53 was 17 per cent greater than in the fiscal year 1951-52, and the number received in the twelve months to the end of March, 1954, was about 25 per estit greater than in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year.
In spite of this increasing claim load, the payment of unemployment insurance benefit has been speeded up appreciably by the judicious use of casual help during the midwinter period of seasonal unemployment, and, I may add again, without any addition whatsoever to permanent full-time staff. During the fiscal year 1953-54 a total of $186,850,766 was paid out in benefit, and the number of beneficiaries was 950,000. Total contributions were $190,409,070, with the government contributing $31,735,794 of this amount. At the close of the last fiscal year the balance in the unemployment insurance fund was $881,278,689, an increase of $29,693,525 over the balance on March 31, 1953.
The most important function of the commission of course is the operation of the employment service. The value of this work cannot be overemphasized. The fact that both employers and workers have at their disposal, without direct charge to them, a national organization manned by men and women experienced in the field of employment is of great value in a country such as ours where mobility of workers is so very important. During the last fiscal year 966,880 placements were made by the national employment service.

Under the provisions of the act the Minister of Finance from time to time credits the fund, out of moneys provided by parliament, with an amount equal to one-fifth of the aggregate contributions made to the fund by employers and employees. Over the years good employment conditions and annual increases in the working force have increased the total contribution of employers and employees and the government contribution has risen accordingly.
The item for the transfer of labour, vote 197, remains unchanged from the previous year in the main estimates but an increase has been recommended in the supplementary estimates now before the house, and is found in vote 671. This item is designed, and the reason for the increase is, to assist in the transfer of unemployed Canadian workers to places where employment is available. Expenditures are made when they can be recovered from employers who are willing to pay the transportation costs of these transfers and, to that extent, provide a revolving fund of working capital to aid in the movement of workers to jobs. Where such a refund cannot be assured and where the minister finds that conditions in an area are such as to warrant such action, he may use this vote to assist unemployed workers in meeting the cost of moving to a job elsewhere. That concludes what I want to say on the opening of my estimates.

Mr. Chairman, any approach to the estimates of the labour department at this time must take cognizance of the present unhappy employment situation. Despite the optimism expressed by the minister and his officials in announcements which have been forthcoming within the last couple of days, there are still many distressing conditions and the clouds are far from having been dissipated. However, before going into the matter of the unemployment problem as such, there are a few other matters of departmental jurisdiction and labour matters in general on which I should like to make a few remarks. I preface those remarks with the observation that I believe, as I stated a moment ago, that the most important problem is now the pressing one of how we shall find jobs for those workers who are now unemployed.
But there are these administrative matters that should be referred to at this time, and I shall take a few minutes to speak of several matters which have claimed my attention recently. First of all I should like to say something about apprenticeship. The minister made some remarks about it in his statement, and I am pleased to see that the government has recognized the importance

of this phase of employment by the increase of $84,000 odd under item 189, which the minister mentioned, and the $125,000 in the supplementary estimates.
It is a fact that there is a grave need for skilled workers in Canada today, and it is a peculiar thing that, in a time when employment generally is at its lowest ebb for many years, there is still this grave need for skilled workers. We are still importing into this country people with peculiar skills to fill positions which otherwise might be taken by Canadian workmen or by those who are already here. I believe everyone who is experienced in labour matters will agree that it is desirable that the learning of skills should be at the practical level.
I am one of those people who believe probably we have a tendency to depend too much upon the teaching of skills in our various academic institutions. We leave too little to the actual practical application of those skills. If then, as has been shown to be the case, there happens to be a lack of incentive on the part of young people to apprentice themselves to a given trade, we might well ask ourselves just whose fault it is. Certainly, it is not entirely the fault of the employer, nor is it entirely the fault of the trade unions, most of whom have apprenticeship schemes of their own and definite rules whereby these people acquire the training they need.
But I suggest to the minister that even the increased amounts to which he has already drawn attention will not entice young people into the learning of specific trade skills unless some other incentive is given to them. While I realize that the minister has had committees working on this very point, I suggest to him that money alone is not going to bring these people into the skilled trades. About six months ago in the Financial Post I noticed a summary of apprenticeship matters. There is a table there indicating that training is falling off, and it gives the ratio of allowed apprentices to journeymen. The interesting thing is, for instance, that for bricklayers and masons, while the number of apprentices allowed is 426, the actual number of apprentices employed is only 178. An even worse picture is given with regard to carpenters, where carpenters were allowed 2,475 apprentices and only 333 were actually employed; plasterers and lathers were allowed 242, and only 103 were employed; painters were allowed 1,984 and only 39 were employed. There is a similar picture for plumbers and steamfitters, with 1,514 allowed and 765 employed; electricians, 2,580 allowed and 637 employed.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that is not only a most interesting picture but also a most

deplorable one. Here, in no case have we even 50 per cent of the allowable apprentices employed-oh, yes, plumbers and steamfit-ters just manage to come up to the 50 per cent mark. In all other cases the ratio is extremely low and in some, notably in the case of painters, it is quite deplorable. This table only shows the picture in a few of these skilled trades, but I would think it would be similar in others. I would suggest the department should concern itself with a scheme for educating the young people of this country to the importance of these skilled trades and to the opportunities which are open to them in these fields. I believe it is very important to Canada that our young people should be learning these skills and that they should learn them at the most practical level, right in the employment of those industries that will ultimately need them when they have attained journeyman's status.
Along this line of employment at various levels, I should like to speak for a few minutes about the older workers. While workers generally are concerned over employment these days, it is nevertheless a fact the older worker has a general concern of a very different order. Attention has been drawn by many persons in editorials, and in discussion groups on the radio, to the increasing life expectancy of the people of this nation. It is a fact we are living longer these days. We are living longer, and we can expect to live longer still because we have learned how to take care of ourselves. For this we can thank our scientists whose research along medical and scientific lines has produced knowledge that has resulted in the defeat of disease in some cases, in its alleviation in others, and the general enrichment of health in the life of the average person.
It is true that there is a changing age pattern, and it is not yet static. We hope it never will be. We hope that the pattern will continue to change and enlarge. If this is true, then the present retirement pattern is scarcely realistic, taking into consideration the life expectancy of most persons today. The question has been asked before, and it will be asked again, should a longer span of life mean a longer span of work? Of course, this is a question which each individual must ask for himself because many people retire voluntarily at an even younger age than that usually dictated by industry and by the professions.
If it is conceded then that the span of work should bear some relationship to the span of life, then the whole pattern of employment and the age of retirement, which of course is optional, as I said, might well undergo radical changes. With retirement pensions
Supply-Labour
based on the longer work expectancy, it might well be that those over 40 years of age, and who have been experiencing difficulty in finding employment once they have been severed from employment, would not be in such an undesirable position with respect to industry as in the past.
The other day I noticed a United Nations report on work opportunities for older women, and an interesting comment which came by way of a memorandum from the British ministry of labour and national service. Their remarks were these:
For compelling social and economic reasons the door must be open widely to the employment of men and women able and willing to work, irrespective of age. These social and economic reasons are not remote and abstract. This is essentially a human problem of providing a proper place in our society for the ever growing proportion of elderly persons. The solution to this problem requires a radically changed outlook on the part of employers, workers and the general public. Age 65 for men and 60 for women ought no longer to be regarded as normal retiring age.
The remarks I have just read, Mr. Chairman, from the British ministry's memorandum will find an echo, I am sure, in the hearts of many people today who are at or approaching retirement age and who feel that they still have a great contribution to make to the life of this country. Certain it is that we are even now faced with a fantastic waste of skills and experience, which is sure to be more pronounced as time goes on. I think we must ask ourselves, and the Department of Labour must consider, whether or not we can afford this waste in an expanding economy. And if the answer is that we cannot afford it, then we should make a definite study of this particular problem, with a view to finding its solution.
I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to the Government Employees Compensation Act, because I notice in the April issue of the Labour Gazette, to which he has referred, there appears an item in which an official of the compensation branch is quoted as saying the following:
Some important changes in the Government Employees Compensation Act have been recommended by an interdepartmental committee and are being incorporated in a bill that it is hoped will be submitted to parliament at the current session.
Well, we have seen nothing of that bill, and I am wondering what progress, if any, has been made, or whether the government has thought better of the proposal. Or, if not either of these, is the bill just shelved for this session?
Of course we realize that the matter of federal government compensation is administered by the provinces. Just last year seven of those provinces made rather drastic

Supply-Labour
changes in their amounts of payment, as well as changes in their regulations. As I understand it, all these changes become applicable automatically to federal employees who suffer injury, and who come under government compensation regulations. I feel however it would be interesting for the house to know just what progress has been made in the study which, apparently, is currently under way.
I should like also to make some observations in respect of the anti-discrimination legislation passed by the last parliament, and in which all of us concurred. I am pleased to hear the minister's remarks with reference to the educational aspect of the work of his department; and I noticed only recently in a news release coming from his department, and also in one of the labour publications, that there is to be a series of eight radio broadcasts commencing next week. It is pointed out that they are to have wide coverage, right across Canada.
No doubt this is part of the educational program the department has undertaken. However, I should like to draw attention to the fact that, while apparently the government is making an effort to bring this legislation to the attention of as many people as possible, the scope of the program could be widened very materially, and greater realism could be given to the whole picture if the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act were amended so as to include within its provisions certain provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. Along with the representations which have been made to the minister by different organizations, I urge that consideration be given to the inclusion of those provisions in the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act.
It is nearly two years since the minister first told us that the department was undertaking a complete revision of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Last year when the committee on industrial relations met, and was considering the matters referred to it by the house, once again the minister stated the act was being revised, and that the revisions would be placed before the House of Commons for ratification. I realize he did not set a time limit, and I also understand that no doubt it is quite a job. But it seems to me we should be making greater progress. After all, two years is a reasonable length of time in which to expect some sort of report, even if only an interim report. I should like very much to see something done to bring the act up to date and to remove from it that peculiar patchwork-quilt pattern it presents at the present time.

Certainly it is true that conditions have changed greatly even within the last ten years; and I think it is about time the minister made some announcement as to when we may expect a revision of this act.
A matter which has claimed a considerable amount of my attention in the last year is the establishment of the women's bureau. Or perhaps I should have said the "non-establishment", because I find that while a year ago we budgeted for $21,560, the estimates indicate that only about $2,560 was spent. I suspect most of that amount was spent in advertising for a director, because that is about the only bit of activity discernible at this distance from the department.
I would ask the minister whether anyone is actually working in this branch. Has it been set up? Is there anyone there? A year ago provision was made for three or four employees. Provision is made again this year, the only difference being that there is to be an increase in salaries-an increase which, I must say, applies to people who were never employed.
Apparently the minister has had some difficulty in securing someone to fill the post of director. I recognize that in the establishment of a new branch it is always difficult to decide upon the qualifications required to produce the desired results. But, in line with my remarks in the house in connection with the civil service estimates, I would say to the minister that if more women-or even some women-were included in courses such as the administration course just completed at Kemptville, there might not be the same difficulty in determining the qualifications of civil servants who would be encouraged to apply for positions like this.
I cannot understand why it has been so very difficult to secure a director. The minister now says he expects one will be appointed soon. Despite that statement however I notice that while the vote is now increased by $2,530 over last year, the amount asked for stationery and office supplies is down by $500 as compared with last year, and that the amount for publications and reports is down to the extent of $1,000. On the other hand salaries have been increased to the extent of $4,030. I am interested in learning the reasoning which would prompt that kind of budgeting. It would look as though the operations of the office are predicated upon an assumption of inactivity for at least another six months. And yet salaries have been increased to take care of a full year's operation.
It is most important that this bureau get under way as soon as possible. Frequently we hear remarks in the house and elsewhere

to the effect that the number of women employees is likely to diminish as circumstances change, and that there are certain classifications of employment not open to women and certain other classifications for which they are not suited. Yet we find in a return from the Department of Labour that 1-8 per cent of the 116,432 women now employed in Canada are employed as labourers, or positions which would indicate fairly heavy work. Some are in transportation, others in farming, and even some in construction work. Certainly these are occupations in which one would not expect to find great numbers of women.
Quite apart from the type of work they are doing, it is a fact that the numbers of women employed and seeking employment increase every day. I was interested in an article written not so long ago by Mr. James Barrie, who writes an excellent column on labour matters for the Hamilton Spectator. It is a most interesting daily column and I recommend it to hon. members. He brought out the point that one out of every seven women employed is the sole support of her family. Probably this picture has not presented itself to many people heretofore. They might very' well consider that one in seven of all the women employed are employed because they must support dependents. He goes on to say that the reasons that motivate the woman worker today are exactly those that motivated the woman of pioneer days who, because of her position, had to work at home weaving, making clothing and producing many of the household goods. He says it just seems to be that the circumstances differ. In the old days the woman made these things with her own hands, so that the family could enjoy them. Today she goes out to work in plant and factory so that the money she earns may buy them. That is a point we might well consider. We should realize that women in employment are not going to decrease in number but are going to increase, and consequently the problems which they will encounter in employment will increase with the numbers of employees, and the federal Department of Labour should get a move on and get this women's bureau operating, and not finally jump in when the problems have become so numerous that they will not be able to cope with them.
I had intended to say a few words on unemployment insurance, but time is slipping away and I have some other remarks to make. Therefore I shall content myself with just two requests, which I have made before, and which I could not overlook when speaking on the labour estimates. My first request is that the minister abolish regulation
Supply-Labour
5A (1). It has been a thorn in the flesh for some time now. It has been changed a couple of times. The fact that it has been changed would indicate that the department itself is not too sure of it. I urge the minister to see that this clause is taken right out of the regulations. It permits a discrimination against women that does not exist against any other types of employees. I can see no reason for having this discriminatory clause in the regulations. It just offends one section of worker. I urge him to take it right out of the regulations and be done with it.
The other matter on which I wish to speak is the appointment of a woman to the unemployment insurance commission. I have made this request every year and I make it again. I have an idea that the minister's reply will have something to say about the way in which the commission is set up and as to how the appointments are made. I am quite well aware of that, but there is nothing in the regulations that would prohibit the enlargement of the commission by one member, and I urge the minister to take this strongly under advisement, because I am sure the women workers of this country need and deserve representation on that commission. I am sure of one thing. If there was a woman on that commission clause 5A (1) would not be written into the regulations.
There is another major problem which has been in existence for a long time. I refer to the responsibility for unemployed employables. I have spoken on this matter in the house on a good many occasions, and not only on the labour estimates. It is a problem that is assuming considerable importance in the life of the present-day unemployment picture. A short time ago a pamphlet was published by the Canadian Welfare Council which is entitled "Public Assistance and the Unemployed". I am sure the minister is familiar with its contents. If any hon. members are not I would suggest that they get this pamphlet and study it. In the introduction it points out the various committees which have been set up and the reports that have been made from 1938 on. It makes this statement:
No action has been taken on the recommendations in any of these for public assistance to the employable unemployed.
The recommendations have been gone over in this house on numerous occasions. Probably the best known are those which are made in the dominion-provincial conference report and which were set out as government recommendations. And yet nothing has been done to implement them.
To come back to this pamphlet of the Canadian Welfare Council, may I say that a

Supply-Labour
number of suggestions and recommendations are made. I shall not attempt to name them all, but the ones that immediately attract my attention are these. The first one I should like to refer to is No. 2 in the recommendations. It states that the Unemployment Insurance Act should be kept under constant review. I am sure we all agree with that, Mr. Chairman, because this act has been in operation for some twelve or thirteen years. I believe the minister tabled the thirteenth report this morning. Basically there has been very little change in it.
Under the heading, "Review of the Unemployment Insurance Act", the report cites various points which should be kept constantly in mind. The report claims that the duration of supplementary benefits should be extended and the amount increased in keeping with increasing costs of living. It mentions also that the greatest possible flexibility in procedures should be permitted in order to meet needs quickly and with the minimum of administrative difficulty. One of the other recommendations, which is important, is one which has been made in this house on two or three occasions in the last couple of years. It reads:
The needs of the unemployed In periods of "abnormal" unemployment, national or regional, should be planned for in advance, by the legislative provision of extended benefits for persons who have exhausted their insurance rights-
It goes on to state a point that was brought out in the dominion-provincial report, not in quite these words, that the federal government should assume most of the financial responsibility for the residual assistance required by all employable unemployed persons not provided for adequately by unemployment insurance or extended benefits. It proceeds to set out ways and means for doing just that.
I cannot see how the federal government can escape responsibility when, by its own admission, by its own statistics, it is proved that there is still a large percentage, almost one-half of the labour force in Canada, which is not insured or insurable under the act. There are several other comments in this pamphlet which are worthy of consideration, but once again I find time getting away from me. I should like to say this. The matter of responsibility for unemployed employables, and those who have exhausted benefits, or for one reason or another are unable to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits, is of very grave concern to everyone in this country. The mayors and reeves association made their own particular contribution to the consideration of

this problem. I hold in my hand press reports which quote various mayors and reeves and their comments on what is to them a very grievous problem.
It is true that social service and welfare workers across the country have also made representations to the government. The real estate taxpayers of the municipalities know full well who is going to pay the shot for increased welfare costs in times of serious unemployment. We could very well ask ourselves just how bad it must be before the federal government will take the matter into consideration. If, as has been claimed on several occasions, the provinces should enter into the matter, then let us get together with the provinces and find out wherein lies the solution to this problem. Let us take the load off the backs of the home owners in Canada who are otherwise forced to carry the entire load of unemployment relief for these people who should be covered by the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to come to the most important problem which we have to face today, and that is this matter of serious unemployment into which we have fallen this year, and from which it looks as though we will not easily recover. If the employment situation is a cause of concern in the month of June at the time when the difficulties of seasonal employment would, we are told, have been overcome, what can we expect for next autumn and winter? Has the government an answer to that question? If so, this house and the worried people of this nation should hear about it. Has the minister taken any steps to inaugurate a program of training for unemployed persons in parts of Canada other than at Marysville? Has the program undertaken there been as successful as the minister had hoped that it would be?
I notice that as late as about three weeks ago the publicity director for the textile workers union reported that the Minister of Labour told a recent textile delegation to Ottawa that he is considering initiating a scheme of vocational training for unemployed textile workers. I would like to hear about that and to know just what is being done.
On May 13 in a news release from the minister's own department reference was made to ways and means of extending training for unemployed persons, a matter which the minister apparently had urged upon the delegates to the Canadian vocational training advisory council. But, whatever the picture is at the present time, we would like to know just what is being done.
The minister referred to an amount in the estimates for moving jobless persons from

one part of the country to another. But how many of these people can be moved? I would venture to say that only those who are single and have no domestic responsibilities can really be moved to another part of the country, because it is an almost impossible task to uproot a man and his family from one municipality to another even if it is only a matter of a few miles away. These are matters which we have to consider.
It is all very well to say quite blithely, "We will move some of the jobless from one district and put them down in another district." But if the minister tries to put such a scheme in operation he will find it is an entirely different matter.
There have been a number of reports issued, so many in fact that it is almost impossible to keep track of them, in which there have been assertions by various members of the government and by some of the leaders in industry that the present labour situation is largely due to seasonal fluctuation. But I contend, Mr. Chairman, that this is a totally false viewpoint and I should like to spend a few minutes on this matter of seasonal unemployment.
Personally I am sick and tired of the phrase. I think it has been overworked. I think it is becoming an excuse for anything and everything regardless of whether seasonal or not.
The other day the monthly report from the minister's department was issued and it stated that the spring pick-up is now in full swing. But I contend that any pick-up, spring pick-up or otherwise, which leaves over 358,000 people out of work is not swinging very freely and, in fact, despite that pick-up, 7 per cent of our labour force remains idle. In view of that, does the minister think that 7 per cent of the labour force is a negligible amount, particularly in the month of May, which is the month in which these figures were issued?
Every month since the first of the year little squibs have appeared in the newspapers carrying optimistic headings, but the figures are dreadful. For example, one reads, "Unemployment rise is halted on the first day of June." Yet the figures show that in the city of Hamilton there were 10,220 people seeking work and the week before there had been 10,178. In other words, there were 42 more people seeking work on a day on which the "unemployment rise was halted". Another one reads "fewer males seeking jobs than a week ago." But it fails to show that there were a lot more women seeking work than the week before. Here is another, "Number seeking work declines," and there again the
Supply-Labour
figures show that the number of males seeking work had declined by about 100 and the number of women seeking work had increased by 200. Yet another, "Jobless figures show increase", and that is the only pessimistic headline among all of these. But then it seeks to alibi the matter of increase in unemployment as of June 12 by starting out in this fashion: "The temporary closing down of the Ford plant at Oakville made a considerable difference." Well, of course, that is what causes unemployment, namely, a shutdown or lay-off. But why alibi that? Why not say the jobless figures show an increase? It might be said, "Oh, yes, but this is only because the plant has had a lay-off or a shutdown." But that is what causes unemployment, and it is still unemployment no matter what the reason for it may be. It does not help anyone to say, "Well, this is only a temporary condition and you will all be back at work in a month or so." If there is no pay envelope coming in it is still tough to take for all these workmen and their families.
Even in the trade papers issued by the banks the story is much the same and we find an apology for the current conditions, though it is a rather watered-down apology, for it says, referring to the increase in number of unemployed: An increase of 36,000 relative to mid-March is below the seasonal increase reported in 1953.
All the way through these various press reports there have been apologies or half apologies for conditions, but in every case it says, "Well, true enough, conditions are bad but 'not as bad as they might be." Or, "Everything is going along fine, true enough at a somewhat slower pace than last year."
But even after saying that employment increased seasonally but at a slower pace, the report from the minister's department states that the unemployment level was about twice as high as for the same period a year earlier. In other words, it is increasing but not fast enough, and it is still twice as bad as it was a year ago. So the picture goes on all the way down the line, and while the minister has had a committee working on the problem of seasonal unemployment the number of industries which claim to suffer from seasonal unemployment have increased. Perhaps what the minister should do is to throw out the committee. Perhaps seasonal unemployment might not then be so bad if the committee did not function. Possibly it should be the other way around, and perhaps the committee in its deliberations has found more industries are affected by seasonal unemployment than the minister has been

Supply-Labour
aware of previously. But whatever the case is, it is still true that the number of industries which are now deemed to be suffering from seasonal unemployment is greater than it was. Yet at the same time the work of this committee was supposed to be to find ways and means of relieving that situation.
In the April issue of the Labour Gazette I find a complete report of this committee. I read the thing through. It makes some recommendations. This report came down on February 17. I wonder what the minister's department has done to implement any of the provisions of that report? Four months have elapsed and in those four months we have gone through some fairly rugged times; and it looks to me as though we shall go through more of them.' I should like to know what the minister proposes to do with regard to the recommendations of that committee. Will the recommendations be left as were the recommendations of other committees which I cited in connection with the responsibility for unemployed employables, or will the department really get down to work and try to do something about them?
After all, Mr. Chairman, the outlook is far from bright. It is only about a month ago that the minister at a meeting in Montreal was bragging that we had passed the unemployment peak for this year. I use the word "bragging" advisedly because I do not blame him for that. I am sure that any little break in the clouds must have looked particularly bright to him. But an article which appeared in the Belleville Intelligencer points out that the effect of unemployment is cumulative, and it goes on to say this:
Many of those who were unemployed during the past winter exhausted their benefits. Getting jobs this spring, they will easily qualify for more benefits next winter, should they again become unemployed-but the periods for which they will be entitled to draw these benefits are likely to be shorter. If seasonal unemployment were to continue, even the man who, through years of steady employment, had built up a right to receive benefits for the maximum period of one year would eventually find his "savings" had dwindled away.
It then goes on to say this:
That is why, just because the employment situation improves with the coming of spring, we cannot afford to be complacent about the factors which left men without work during the winter.
Unemployment insurance, like a savings account, is a great friend in need, but it is no adequate substitute for steady employment.
Mr. Chairman, the time which is at my disposal has expired but I should just like to say a few more words. No nation is greater than its people, and no economy is stronger than the degree of employment it provides. What makes prosperity? Jobs make prosperity. The labour income of this

country has been cited as being 62-3 per cent of the total personal income. What happens to our economy when more and more people are unemployed? What happens to us when pay envelopes are cut off from those workers? It is not the millions of dollars which are poured into oil fields or mining operations that make prosperity, lucrative though the returns from those operations may be. It is jobs for Canadian workers. They and they alone are the backbone of this economy.
When a government becomes so shortsighted that it seeks to tax commodities right out of a competitive position; when the members of that government blithely refuse to regard the danger signals; and when complacency permits unemployment to mount without any attempt being made to correct the situation, save where it happens to hit the constituency represented by a cabinet minister, then the danger to the economy is grave indeed. It is grave not alone because of what has already happened but because of the indifference of those who should be planning for the months ahead when, following a historical pattern of employment, we may expect less employment than in these summer months. If the government is misjudged-if it has been making plans-then let us know what those plans are. Let the minister tell the House of Commons what he intends to do and thus take the load of anxiety off the shoulders of all those people in this country who have been worrying themselves sick over the situation.

Mr. Chairman, it is always a pleasure to discuss the minister's estimates; there is a great deal of meat in them. I am going to be as brief and as realistic as I possibly can. I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Hamilton West and during the course of her remarks I was wondering about certain things. She made a good deal of valid criticism on many matters, but in the final analysis, when it comes to a matter of regulating the economy of this country to cure the problems that she complained of, I think she forgot that both she and the minister play on the same team.
Be careful.
That is only the hon. member's conception of it.

All right. Before I am through I hope I shall be able to convince the hon. member. I have been sitting here and looking at the minister, whom I have known for a long time. I am sure that the next four or five years in the field about which we are talking today are going to be some of the toughest years this country will ever have

gone through and that it is going to take a great deal of serious thinking and co-operation on the part of all of us if we are to avoid the greatest possible dislocation and discontent among our people.
I appreciate the fact that the minister is obliged to play according to the rules of the game. That is what I meant when I said that the hon. member for Hamilton West and the minister, when it comes to the mechanics of society, are playing on the same team. They both believe in a system of free enterprise. The minister is doing the best he can to make a very bad state of mechanics work. The old 1903 model Ford car cannot compete with the Cadillac of today. That is exactly the position that the system is in.
A socialist Cadillac?

The hon. member has not the slightest idea what he means when he says "socialism". I would suggest that some time during this debate he define socialism for us. He is just frightened of that word because the manufacturers association and the bankers association and those who are responsible for unemployment in this country have told him that there is something bad about socialism and he continues to throw that bogeyman around. Let him tell us something about it during this debate.
I shall be very glad to do so. I believe what I say.

All right. I should like to hear his definition. I have heard that crack made so often that I am getting fed up with it.
To return to this matter of unemployment, may I say this. Unemployment is merely the symptom of a disease in the body politic. That is all it is. Why have we unemployment in this country today? That is the first question. If you get a disease, you call in a doctor and put yourself in his hands for examination and diagnosis. Then when he tells you what is wrong with the body, he will generally recommend something to cure it. The reason we have unemployment today in Canada is international cutthroat competition. There is not anyone who can dispute that statement. Why has our textile industry gone practically out of business? Simply because they cannot compete with the textile industry in the United States and with textiles coming in from Britain. The basic philosophy of both the Liberal and Conservative parties is to maintain the status quo, the system of free enterprise, and the basis of that is competition. Textile workers are unemployed in Canada because international competition is preventing the selling of Canadian textiles
Supply-Labour
and the maintenance of the standards that have been built up. That is why textile workers are unemployed.
The same thing is true of the electrical appliance industry. That industry is making the same complaint. They are laying off men. They cannot compete with the products of other countries. It is competition again that is responsible for unemployment in that industry. The same thing is true of the automobile industry. There is competition between Ford, Chrysler, General Motors, the little English cars, and to some extent today cars coming in from Europe in the cheaper price field. Again it is competition.
We are only starting to get into this situation. We would have had it for a long time if it had not been for Korea. Prior to the outbreak of hostilities in Korea we were pretty much in the same position with respect to employment as we are today. But we diverted a lot of money to the manufacture of armaments, threw them away and still maintained full employment and prosperity. We have got to examine that question if we are going to get any sanity in our economic set-up.
I do not expect the Minister of Labour to cure unemployment as long as the country has to function in the way it is functioning today. Drastic changes will have to be made not only in Canada but elsewhere because today the problem is world-wide. In my judgment the final answer to unemployment in the world rests with the United Nations. We set up the United Nations Organization in the first place to maintain peace and negotiate international difficulties in the only way that befits this day and age, that of sensible people sitting around a table and working out their problems in a sensible way. But in addition to giving it the responsibility of policing the peace of the world we set up other organizations in conjunction with the United Nations that were designed to iron out the kinks in other fields. We set up the world bank to deal with the question of international finance and the world food organization that was going to distribute the surplus foods of the world to people without food.
In the final analysis that is where the answer to this whole problem will be found, and it will not be found by fighting among ourselves either in Canada or in the United States. All of the mechanics are there but they are not permitted to work because of this other idea of competition. We have had two or three hundred years of competition. We have had two wars and a partial war with depressions between wars. Surely it is time that we smartened up and began to realize

Supply-Labour
that the mechanics that have pretty well destroyed us over the last two or three generations cannot work. Some serious thinking has to be done about the problem, and we must realize that about 75 per cent of the people of the world are starving to death.
The answer to unemployment in Canada and the United States lies in international trade, and unless we can free the channels of trade and get our goods moving to places where they are needed we are not going to cure unemployment. Do not forget that countries are going to have to give up some of their sovereignty if they are going to take part in a world government. They are going to have to try to do something for the world and not stick to the old outmoded machinery just because it was good for their grandfathers. The difficulty in the world today is to get people to let go of anything that they think belongs to them. You do not have to leave this chamber to see that. When you suggest changing the hours and cutting speeches from forty minutes to thirty minutes everybody gets on their high horse and says that ten minutes belongs to them and they are going to hang on to it.
It is a difficult thing to get individuals, sections of a nation or a nation to let go of things that they consider are their right, but before an answer is found to the problem of distribution throughout the world some concessions will have to be made. It is a question of distribution. Unemployment is a misnomer. We have got an abundance, and every time we have an abundance we get in trouble. We have learned how to build atomic bombs and all that kind of thing but we have never learned how to distribute food. Getting that food into somebody else's hands is a terribly difficult problem.
I have no intention of delivering a lecture on socialism. I hope my friend will give us one when he gets a chance to talk. I want to make certain suggestions as to things we can do that might relieve the spots where there is trouble. I leave the thought with the Minister of Labour that at this time in 1954 unemployment is 90 per cent worse than at the same time in 1953. That is not good, but as I said before you cannot solve the problem alone. You have got to get co-operation. You have got to get the surpluses of the country moving. No matter whether we sell them or give them away, we have got to get them moving. Otherwise we will have more unemployment.
But there is something that can be done. The minister will remember that he has had some correspondence on the question of the

relationship of section 108 of the Unemployment Insurance Act and subsection 1(f) of section 31 of the same act. I sound like a lawyer, but this is what I mean. In July, 1953, about 1,600 men were laid off at colliery IB of the Dominion Coal Company. At the time they were laid off they were paid their vacation pay covering two weeks coming to them in 1953 and a week coming to them in 1954. That was in July, 1953. The unemployment insurance commission, applying subsection 1(f) of section 31, decided that they were not entitled to unemployment insurance because they had received that vacation pay.
In my opinion a section in the act that permits a ruling of that kind is wrong. These men paid their unemployment insurance dues in order to protect them during a period of unemployment. When these 1,600 men were laid off en bloc they were unemployed. They were not on vacation. They paid for that insurance in order to get certain benefits as laid down by the act if they were unemployed, and they were unemployed. The three weeks' pay they received was received as the result of the trade union agreement between the employer and the employees. It was a gratuity which they were paid for services rendered. I want to leave this thought with the minister.
When an industry shuts down for vacation purposes it is not compulsory to go on vacation. If it had been the case of an ordinary vacation and these men had wanted to remain at their employment they would have got their vacation pay and wages for the period that they worked. In my judgment that should influence the people who made the decision in that case to either change that regulation so that the situation can be treated as straight unemployment or the regulation as it stands should be interpreted to mean that these men were unemployed, which they were. They were laid off. Let me deal with how section 108 comes into the picture. These men went back to work a month or two ago, although some are not back yet. If their employment had been continuous, in August of this year, they would have been getting their ordinary two weeks' vacation. There is no vacation coming to them, because they have not been working a year.
These mines will close down at that time for the two-week vacation period, because that is part of the agreement between the men and the company. These men will find themselves laid off for two weeks, and they will not be able to draw any unemployment insurance because they will not have worked

a sufficient time to make the necessary number of contributions that would entitle them to draw unemployment insurance. They were laid off, and they will be laid off again for vacation purposes, and they will be penalized again so far as unemployment insurance is concerned.
There are about 1,600 men affected, and in my judgment the unemployment insurance commission owes that group of men three weeks' unemployment insurance. I would suggest that the minister and some of his officials take a look at the section of the act I have mentioned and at least determine the status of those men when they start their vacation period. They will not have any vacation pay. If they were not entitled to it when they were laid off first, then they should certainly be entitled to it when they are idle in August for vacation purposes and have not any vacation pay coming to them. They should not lose it at both ends; they should get the protection for which they paid. The minister and his department can do something about that, and I hope they will.
The second matter to which I should like to draw his attention is also a matter about which he can do something. At Moncton, New Brunswick, there is an agency known as the Drake-Merritt employment agency which selects personnel in Canada for contracts that are in the hands of the United States government in Labrador and Newfoundland. This Drake-Merritt agency has recruiters, people who go around and pick up men for these jobs. They are not taking their men through the national employment office. I want to stress again that the employers of this country who are looking for employees ignore, in so far as they can, the national employment offices. The big employers in this country did not want the national employment offices. They accepted them partially during the war when there was a shortage of labour, but I know that so far as the steel company is concerned and the coal company, they do not put their requirements through any national employment office. They pick up their own personnel through their own agency.
Now, this Drake-Merritt agency in Moncton, under some arrangement with the Newfoundland government, must take all the unskilled labour they can get from Newfoundland. The skilled labour can be picked up anywhere. I am making this complaint to the minister on behalf of the national employment office in Sydney. There are mechanics, machine tool workers and skilled tradesmen of all kinds registered at this office, and to my knowledge that office has been trying to get the recruiters at Moncton
Supply-Labour
to take some of that skilled labour. They have not been successful so far in getting any co-operation from the recruiters who operate from this agency. I would suggest to the minister that this is a United States agency and it should at least work through the employment offices rather than pick up their personnel wherever they see fit. I would suggest the minister might communicate with this agency from Ottawa, and do something to have this condition rectified.
There is another thing about which the minister can do something. A complaint was made in this house on one or two occasions that there was a possibility that immigrants coming into this country were being used by employers for the purpose of reducing wages. The evidence I heard here in the house was not conclusive proof that that might be taking place. I have accurate information, however, that there was a lumber firm at North River Bridge in Nova Scotia, known as the Mariana timber company, which tried to secure 200 immigrants from Montreal to work in the lumber camp established in that area. This shows that there is a labour supply available in Montreal through immigration circles if the regulations can be circumvented by an employer who wants to pay less than the going wage.
I want to tell the minister again that it was due to the vigilance of one of his offices that the employer did not obtain the personnel through immigration circles in Montreal. I am not saying that the immigration people in Montreal would have co-operated, but the evidence is that there is a source there to which employers can apply for surplus immigrants who are in that area if they can find a way of short-circuiting the regulations. The fact that this employer asked for 200 immigrants to work at wages that would be much below those prevailing in the area proves that there are employers in this country who will make use of immigrants for that purpose unless the labour department is on its toes and makes it compulsory to route all immigrants for employment purposes through the proper channels. If a surplus labour force is built up in this way in some centres, then employers who are interested in the economy of this country can obtain labour at bargain prices. The area into which these labourers would have been moved could be called a depressed area, so there are labourers available in the area. This employer would have brought in 200 more men to dump into the area because he wanted to make a few more cents on the cutting of lumber.
I mention this now to the minister because one of his offices was smart enough to put a sprag in that kind of thing. However, the

Supply-Labour
next area in which that type of thing occurs, the office might not be so vigilant. I feel there should be some definite understanding between the department of immigration and the Department of Labour that immigrants brought into this country cannot be used for that purpose.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that everyone wants to get home, just as I do. I am going to finish by saying this in connection with the matter of vocational training. I have told the minister privately, and I have told him publicly, about the great need all over this country for vocational training, with particular emphasis on the island of Cape Breton. That island is one of the biggest industrial sections east of Montreal, where a third of Canada's basic steel is turned out, as well as about half its coal. And employment conditions are bad. I do not think I need stress to the minister the need for a vocational training school in that area, because he is fully aware of it. But the angle I do want to stress is this, that the reason there is no vocational school in the area is that apparently the provincial government has not been able to raise money to match the grants of the federal government, under the agreements applying to the provinces.
At some time the department is going to have to sit down with the provinces and try to work out some kind of agreement that will enable some vocational training to be carried on in all the provinces across Canada. It is not possible today to get equality in all these fields, because of the differences in provincial income. We have gone into that matter on many occasions. I am sure if the government in Nova Scotia would co-operate with the federal government, something could be done. I know this, that the federal government has leaned over backwards, but the province has just shrugged it off with the statement that it cannot match the grants.
If there is a dominion-provincial conference -and indications are that there may be-this matter should be on the agenda, with a view to getting some equality across the country in the matter of vocational training.
That is all I have to say at the moment. There are some thought-provoking items in the minister's estimates, and no doubt very soon we will be chucking some short questions in his direction.

Mr. Chairman, this group believes it should avail itself of this opportunity to say something on the first item in the estimates of the Department of Labour. Before going into the particular theme I had planned, however, I should like to make one or two observations concerning the speeches of hon. members who have preceded me in the debate.

I am not so much concerned about the little bit of by-play which may have gone on between the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Hamilton West, when the former indicated that the latter was playing on the same team as the minister. I do not know whether or not they are on the same team. I cannot quite reconcile myself to the belief that the Liberal party in Canada is in every particular a free enterprise party. However, this may all be a matter of interpretation.
If anyone were to ask me which side of the game I am playing on I would say that I am not going to be on either side, just so long as the rules continue as they are now. I do not think the game is to be played between the free enterprise side and the socialist side. Surely that is not the problem. As I see it, the problem is not one as to who plays the game, or the plays they make, on whatever side they may be. The problem is that the rules of the game are wrong. No matter how it is played, under the present rules no side will win, and the whole country will lose.
I believe that sometimes we need to redefine the purpose of industry and of government. It appears to me, if I may judge from speeches made in the house, that hon. members appear to think that the purpose of industry is to provide jobs. I do not think that is correct. It is not my belief that industry exists primarily to create jobs. I believe a coal mine exists to produce coal, that an automobile industry is there to produce automobiles, and that an oil well is drilled to produce oil. The purpose of industry is to produce those things which the people of the country enjoy.
Then we hear this attitude: Well, now, the government is supposed to manage industry so that industry can provide jobs. In other words, it is said that indirectly the government exists for the purpose of giving jobs. I do not think that is right, either-that it is the purpose of government to give jobs. If it is, then we might as well have the extreme socialist state and say: Now you are in power; just take over and put everybody to work. If that is what the people want, it can be done-as it is done in certain parts of the world.
The fact of the matter is that industry exists for the purpose of producing the things the nation requires to enjoy a high standard of living. And when industry has done its job-and in this instance it has-the problem that is basic is this: How are we going to distribute among the people the things industry has produced so that the people can have them?

A moment ago I said that at times we must redefine our terms. We say that people need jobs, that they have got to have jobs, that they want jobs. It is all very well to say that; but when the statement is completely analysed we realize that it is not jobs people want. The fact is this, Mr. Chairman, that if it is jobs they want, then all their lives they work as hard as they can to acquire enough income so that they do not need to have jobs.
What people must have is income; and when we think in terms of income another factor enters the economic picture. I said a moment ago the purpose of industry was to produce goods. When industry has done its job of producing goods we should be able to sit back and say: Now we have surely accomplished a great thing in this country; now we can sit back and enjoy ourselves. But that is not the way it works out, at all. When industry has done its job and has produced an abundance of everything we just sit back and, instead of taking out our pipes and smoking them, with the thought that we can take it easy, everyone becomes worried lest they are going to starve in the midst of this abundance that industry has been able to supply.
Even the hon. member for Cape Breton South said that we have an abundance, and that the problem is one of distribution. We have been telling parliament and the country that very thing for the last 18 years. Of course it is a problem of distribution. Let me ask, how can that problem of distribution be met? By putting everybody to work and producing more? The hon. member for Cape Breton South did not answer that. I know a little play went on between him and one af the hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party in respect to defining socialism. The hon. member asked him to define it. I am not so particularly anxious whether be does it or not, but may I tell you what [ should like. I should like some of these socialists to define socialism for us. I should iike to know just exactly how, if there were a socialist government in this country, they svould distribute the abundance by giving everyone what is known as full employment. [ should like to know that. I should like to bear them say how it could be done; I should like them to give us a picture of how ;hey would administer that matter from the rery beginning to the ultimate end. Trace it ill the way through. Say: We would first do ;his; second, we would do this, until we would eventually arrive at this stage. I should ike them to tell us how they would handle hat thing step by step. I should like to enow whether it is worth while plunging
Supply-Labour
this country into a state of extreme socialism. As far as I can diagnose what is happening in the world today-I may be wrong; they can correct me if 1 am wrong-I do not believe that there has been what our C.C.F. friends would term a socialist government in the world that has solved the unemployment problem. The only governments that have actually solved the unemployment problem have been the extreme socialist states, those that are behind the iron curtain, or the national socialists of Germany previous to the war. Those are the only governments I know of that have been able to do it. What I say is, it is not a matter necessarily of solving the unemployment problem. It should not be looked upon as being a problem; it should be looked upon as being an accomplishment that we have been able to reach such a vast stage of production with the least amount of work. It should be an accomplishment to be able to take the sweat and the toil from the backs of our workers. It should be an accomplishment, if we can produce an abundance with five hours' work a day instead of eight hours' a day or a forty-hour week. That should be an accomplishment, but instead it is a problem.
The problem of course is income. We in this group claim that the present functioning of the economic arrangement, such as we have, does not return enough money out of the process of production to buy all the goods produced; therefore incomes must be supplemented. We have been proclaiming that for many years, and that is the thesis upon which we work.
These are some preliminary observations I wanted to make, complementary to the speeches that have already been made; but I rose particularly to present another angle that is not usually referred to in the course of a debate on labour. It may be casually mentioned at times, but I should like to present this for the minister's consideration. I know his department realizes the situation and I am sure they have not been idle in doing what they can in at least trying to diagnose the problem; whether they have the remedy for it or not is another thing.
I should like to put up a plea for the older worker. That is a problem in the present-day functioning of industry in respect to labour. How often do we hear of a man of forty or forty-five or fifty coming home and saying: "Well, I do not know; but I guess I am getting too old". They do not want to employ the older man any more even though he is not particularly old as

Supply-Labour
far as the numerical age is concerned. It is common talk that they do not want to employ older men any more. This is a young man's age. Well, it may be a young man's age to a large extent. I do not wish to discourage the young man at all; it is a young man's age very largely. We live in an age of speed. Our best pilots and aeronautical engineers and so forth are very largely young men. They like adventure; they are able to do it. When a man gets to be thirty-five or so he cannot fly with the same precision as he used to. That is the claim, and there may be something in it. I am not saying it is not very largely a young man's age. But, after all, if you take all the older brains out of our modern civilization I do not think there will be very much left to run it. However, there appears to be that idea abroad. It is largely a mental condition that even management in industry has adopted. They believe that the younger man can do more than the older man. They fear that there are certain obstacles in the way of the full use of our older workers. I think it is largely developed by a mental prejudice rather than anything else.
That mental prejudice can be broken down into three thoughts that I believe will hardly bear investigation. The first one is that the older worker is not readily adaptable to learning new techniques in a rapidly developing age. The second is that absenteeism is a problem and that absenteeism is found largely among older people because accidents are more frequent or perhaps sickness is more frequent. That idea could be exploded. The third is that age brings a sort of slowdown and lessens production. I believe that all these three ideas can be exploded when they are looked into and analysed.
As I said, I do not believe these prejudices are well-founded. The danger of these prejudices remaining in the minds of management is that they prejudge the situation rather than investigate it seriously.
I should like to put on the record some thoughts. One authority has said that a man of sixty may be as young, as vigorous and vital as the average man of forty. I want to quote from a reference to the ageing process by Dr. Edward J. Sheglitz, a leading American geriatrician, who says:
The changes which come are not all decline. 1 think there is a general opinion that it is all downhill. Speed of reaction does diminish; but endurance increases in certain capacities.
[Mr. Hansell.l
It is not without significance that the records for all the sprints are held by youngsters but the marathon records are held by men 38 to 45 and have been for many years. Endurance of a certain type, for the long, slow grind, the continuous type of labour operation, increases. As speed declines, skill declines, judgment increases. The mental changes are not all decline either. There is some depreciation in the ability to learn but it is extraordinarily less than the average person assumes.
Now, Mr. Chairman, here is another quotation from Dr. Nathan W. Shock, chief of the cardiovascular diseases and gerontology section of the United States public health service:
It should be pointed out that no differences in efficiency in the performance of moderate work are observed between the ages of 17 and 71 years. This finding is of considerable importance since most work of an industrial nature falls within the classification of "moderate work".
Now, Mr. Chairman, in taking the matter of the adaptability of age to new techniques I think experience has to a large extent given the lie to that old saying "You cannot teach an old dog new tricks". As somebody said, "You can teach old dogs new tricks if the old dog wants to learn and if the teacher is smarter than the dog."
The psychological research department of Columbia University, which dealt with the mental ability of several hundred test cases of older workers, found that the intellectual power to learn does not change between the ages of 20 and beyond 70, and we are told that in this same investigation by Columbia University which dealt with the efforts of a class of 300 to learn the Russian language, there was no significant difference between the ages with respect to their ability to learn.
Now, let us deal for a moment with the accident frequency and the absenteeism rate as age increases. I do not think I need labour the point by argumentation but I do wish to put on the record a table which was devised by the bureau of labour statistics, a branch of the United States government. This analysis was published three or four years ago and perhaps, Mr. Chairman, in order to save time I might have the consent of the committee to put this table on the record. It covers only about a dozen items and it would save time, and figures are laborious in any event.

For one thing he has experience behind him, steadiness and reliability, and surely when it comes to a question of craftsmanship age is a contributing factor in the quality of such craftsmanship.
