No one would think there was much of a job in slap dabbing a brush over a barn. But I had an experience not so long ago when one of these immigrants came to a neighbour of mine who wanted a paint job done and the immigrant said he would do it in so many hours. He said, "It will take me longer to do it than my competitor but I will guarantee that it will last longer and be a better job." My neighbour thought the matter over. He could have had the job done a little cheaper by another man who was not such an experienced painter, but he decided to pay a little more for the services of the skilled man, and when that job was completed my neighbour said to me, "Well, I did not make any mistake in having that man do the job." Men can become real craftsman only by many long years of applying their hands, minds and tools to the task. I think there should be plenty of places in our industry for our older workers. My plea this afternoon is for the older worker, and when the minister comes to reply I would appreciate it if he would give the committee some idea of what the government is doing to encourage industry to keep the older worker in employment.

Mr. Chairman, I have some questions on the various items but I also have a few general remarks to make, and they can probably be made at this stage. Welch company with the department of immigration and the Department of Transport. Only a couple of days ago I received some correspondence from the general chairman of the brotherhood of maintenance of way employees of the Canadian National Railways with reference to a matter which comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour. The general chairman says this:
As general chairman of the brotherhood of maintenance of way employees on western lines of the Canadian National Railways, I am very much interested in the outcome of questions raised by you...in respect to the R. F. Welch company.
We have attempted to contact the upper brackets in C.N.R. officialdom in an effort to get release from a condition which has given us great concern for years . . .
In November, 1951,-

And I think this is the point that the minister may be interested in and may be able to do something about:
-the labour relations board certified our brotherhood as the bargaining agent for all maintenance of way employees including extra gang labourers. The C.N. has been evading the certification by transferring certain of these men over to R. F. Welch for payroll purposes in spite of the fact that the work performed is in all respects identical with that performed by other extra gangs under complete supervision of the C.N.R.

Will my hon. friend repeat the name of the company?
Mr. Nose worthy: The name is the R. F. Welch company.
I listened with a great deal of attention to everything the minister had to say with regard to the retraining of the unemployed. Like the minister himself, I am keenly interested in any kind of training or education. I believe-as I am sure does the minister-that any man or woman acquires a greater capacity for becoming a better citizen by reason of the fact that he or she acquires training or education in any field. The heartbreaking thing about the present situation is that it is our skilled workers in Canada today who are unemployed. My experience is that, while the unskilled jobs are being taken to a large extent by new Canadians, our own skilled and trained Canadian workers can find no jobs.
I just recall one particular instance as an example of many. It is that of a man about whom I have been writing to the minister, a man who was trained in a skill four years in the services; he drew skilled pay and was trained for that particular vocation. He had five or six years' employment with a specialized branch of the minister's own department. He took six months' specialized training at a well recognized technical institute at the department's expense. Yet he has been three or four months looking for a job and is unable to get any assistance from the minister's employment officers. That is the situation in which we find ourselves today.
While I am all for retraining-as much of it as we can get-I do not think that

retraining alone is going to meet our problem. As long as the government considers that its only responsibility with regard to employment is to create an atmosphere that will be conducive to full employment instead of taking some practical measures to provide employment, we are going to have this problem before us.
There is a great deal of truth in what the hon. member for Cape Breton South said with regard to the capitalist system or the system now better known as the free enterprise system and which the government supports. I challenge the minister or any supporter of the free enterprise system to point out any prolonged period in human history during which that system has been able to maintain full employment during peacetime. We were saved from unemployment in the thirties by the war. We were saved from mounting unemployment again by Korea. Unless we can get some little war started somewhere to replace Korea, we are going to be faced with a situation of increasing unemployment.
I want to deal with something a little bit more specific because I know that, as indicated, it is beyond the minister's power to do anything about changing the system. The best he can hope for, in order to maintain employment, is that the international tension with regard to communism does not ease to the extent where we can lop about $1 billion off our defence budget. The day we cut $1 billion from the defence budget, on that day the minister's headaches will increase as will the unemployment. That is a part of the system.
There is another matter that is a bit of a worry to the unemployed. I know that we have the unemployed with us now and it looks as though we are going to have them with us in increasing numbers when the fall comes again. One thing that is causing a great deal of dissatisfaction among some of those unemployed is that, because of stringent rules with regard to unemployment insurance, many of them are unable to draw the full amount of unemployment insurance which they have built up over the years. Generally they have not been able to get the requisite number of days in the specific years to entitle them to withdraw from that fund all the credits that they have built up. Now, an unemployed man who cannot get a job, who cannot get any help from the government's employment offices, who knows that over the years he has built up a backlog of unemployment insurance and who finds that he cannot draw more than a part of that because he cannot fulfil certain rigid conditions, is not in a very happy frame of mind

about it. I would suggest to the minister that some steps be taken to see if it is not possible to make provision that an unemployed man for whom a job cannot be found and who has unemployment insurance built up to his credit may be able to withdraw at least the full amount of that even though he is not able to comply with the regulations requiring a definite number of days in certain years. I think it would do something to soften the disappointment and disillusionment of some of the unemployed regarding unemployment insurance.
There is one other result of mounting unemployment that I want to bring to the minister's attention. With that, I will leave the rest of my questions for the individual items. That matter is the burden which is already falling upon local municipalities with respect to the support of employable unemployed. We are back now where we were in the 1930's when those who needed municipal relief were passed from the municipality to the provincial government, from the provincial government to the federal and back again and were given the merry-go-round treatment. Today the provincial governments say that provision for these unemployed employables is a federal matter, and generally speaking they are refusing to do anything about it.
A municipality just cannot stand by and see citizens of the municipality starve or families go without food. Consequently local taxpayers are being called upon to bear that burden which certainly should be borne by one or both of the major governments. I have two resolutions here. As a matter of fact they are copies of resolutions that were sent to the minister, and I have no doubt he is familiar with them. They were sent by the municipal council of the township of York which forms the major part of the riding of York South. They both have to do with the question of unemployment relief. The first calls upon the federal and provincial governments to get together with representatives of local governments to see if this problem cannot be ironed out before the situation becomes more desperate than it is at the present time. The resolution reads as follows:
. . . that the provincial and federal governments be requested to arrange for the immediate holding of a further federal and provincial conference at which representatives of local governments will be permitted to be present for the consideration of a broad adjustment in the tax basis between the federal and provincial governments and local municipalities and for the purpose of finding some immediate means of relieving municipal governments from demands for increased unemployment relief, which the municipal taxpayers are unable to bear . . .
Supply-Labour
The other resolution I wish to put on the record is similar and reads as follows:
That whereas the number of employable persons who are unemployed is increasing in number in this and other municipalities, and in most cases such persons have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits and are accordingly forced to appeal to the municipal relief department for assistance in providing food, clothing and shelter;
And whereas the government of the province of Ontario has taken the position that relief for unemployed employables is the responsibility of the dominion government and not of the provincial government;
And whereas the welfare departments of this and other municipalities are unable to assume the responsibility of financing the cost of relief to such unemployed employables which should be the actual responsibility of the federal and provincial governments as recommended in the interim report of the Ontario provincial-municipal relations committee;
And whereas up to date no action has been taken by the federal and provincial governments to meet the present situation and the possibility of more serious unemployment conditions arising;
Therefore be it resolved that the government of the Dominion of Canada be strongly urged to provide directly or through the municipalities a suitable formula to meet such situations as they arise, in order that the municipalities may be better able to cope with the problem without unduly and improperly burdening their ratepayers . . .
These are the only two matters I am going to raise on the general discussion: the question of unexhausted unemployment insurance which the unemployed are unable to draw because of the department's regulations; and the question of who is going to feed, clothe and house the unemployed employables, a matter which is becoming more serious every day to industrial municipalities. If the minister will make some comment on these matters we will appreciate it.

Mr. Chairman, I rise with some apprehension to speak on the estimates of the labour department inasmuch as approximately a week ago a small but determined delegation met with the Minister of Labour and officials of his department and the unemployment insurance commission. May I express to the Minister of Labour and the heads of his department on behalf of the members of the delegation their thanks for and appreciation of the wonderful reception they were given by the minister and his officials, their attentiveness, and the time they spent in listening to the problem that they presented at that time. However, they did not go away with any assurance except that the minister promised, and has followed up his promise, that close contact would be maintained with the Oshawa unemployment insurance commission so that if the unemployment situation there becomes any more serious than it is at the present time some

Supply-Labour
action will be taken by the department in order to meet the situation. This was appreciated.
Nevertheless no definite policy was expressed by the government for the purpose of alleviating unemployment. When I listened some few months ago to the six-day debate on unemployment that took place in the house it struck me that the government was rather uninterested, and at that time seasonal unemployment was given as the reason or excuse for the situation. I am amazed that the government did not take any action at that time to show that they were willing to look for some solution in order to forestall any further increase in unemployment in Canada. I do not wish, Mr. Chairman, to discuss unemployment generally as it affects all of Canada. My prime interest is in the area that I represent, and particularly the area under the jurisdiction of the unemployment insurance commission office located in Oshawa.
In April of this year there were 3,443 unemployed registered in that office, and a month later in May there were 3,961. A year ago at the same time there were 1,519, so from this it can be seen that the increase is close to 160 per cent as compared with a year ago. As of April 15 of this year some 670 unemployed were removed from the list for supplementary benefits. What has happened to those people seems to be a mystery, because they seem to have disappeared. Thank heavens, not too many of them have gone on the relief rolls of the city of Oshawa, but that is no guarantee that they might not do so before too long.
I am saying these things, and repeating what has been presented to the minister by this delegation, simply for the record because the matter is serious enough that it should be emphasized over and over again in order to impress the government with the situation as it is now. During these discussions the question arises as to who is responsible for unemployment. In certain quarters there seems to be some doubt. The responsible labour organizations of this country have stated that unemployment is the problem of the federal government, and with that I concur. However, the government seems to feel that it is a sort of combined provincial and federal responsibility, and that the provincial governments should take the initial step in bringing to the attention of the federal government the seriousness of the problem in a particular province or a particular area in that province.
Neither the municipal nor the provincial governments, Mr. Chairman, can exert control over the causes of unemployment,

which are, of course, economic. Only the federal government is in a position to exert control over these economic and financial policies. Canada has always depended, and will probably continue to depend for many years to come, upon foreign trade to maintain a level of economic activity that will guarantee a high employment scale. Only the federal government is in a position to influence even slightly our position in this respect. Only the federal government can regulate national financial and tariff policies or exert any control over other factors in Canada's economic picture that have a bearing on unemployment.
I maintain, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that the responsibility for measures to offset or relieve unemployment must be laid mainly at the door of the federal administration. Unemployment, because of the complexity of the whole economic structure in the modern world, is a federal and not a local responsibility. It should be recognized as such. It is the federal, and not the provincial or municipal administrations that shape national policy, which is the main factor in determining employment or unemployment.
I should like now to take up the matter of unemployment insurance. Since its inception in 1940, unemployment insurance has been a great help to the working people in Canada. It is quite true that in the early stages of unemployment insurance, the rules and benefits had to be more or less rigid in order to build up the fund sufficiently to maintain its solvency. Since that time, although there have been some inroads into the fund, jobless insurance has stood up very well. We find that on March 31, 1954, the unemployment insurance fund stood at $881,274,000, compared with $851,585,000 for the same day in 1953. This represents a gain of nearly $30 million during that period.
There have been certain amendments made to this act since it was first introduced that have benefited many of the people affected by the act. First of all, there was an increase in the benefits from a maximum of $21 for a person with a dependent to $24. There was also an amendment which allowed a person who was in receipt of benefits from the unemployment insurance fund, and who during that period of time became ill, to continue drawing unemployment insurance benefits. Then, there was a reduction by three in the number of waiting days, and that was also a step in the right direction. Previously the waiting period had been eight days, which meant that there were nine noncompensable days at the beginning of the benefit period, since the first day in any period of unemployment is non-compensatory.

The reduction of the waiting period from eight days to five days meant that the initial non-compensable period was reduced from nine days to six.
Now, these amendments were very welcome additions to the act. The minister told the unemployment delegation which appeared before him a week ago, and myself, that the unemployment insurance commission was reviewing the benefit structure of the act. I am sure he is unable to divulge information in that respect because the review is probably still in progress at this time. May I make some observations and perhaps some recommendations which may be considered in connection with that review of the Unemployment Insurance Act. There have been various submissions made by labour organizations that have appeared before the government this year to the effect that a higher bracket of benefits should be instituted because there are people who are earning over $48 a week. These labour bodies also recommended that the present maximum should be increased from $24 to $40. I believe it could be left to the minister and those associated with him in the review of the act whether it is done in that way or whether it is done on a percentage basis.
I feel, however, that some substantial increase should be made because of the fact that in certain areas in Canada employees are earning wages that enable them to build up commitments in connection with their family life. Certainly the maximum of $24 at the present time is barely sufficient to pay for the board of a family consisting of a man, his wife, and possibly three or four children! Definitely it does not permit the head of the family to carry out the commitments of insurance or the commitments of a mortgage, as well as the few luxuries that we fee] Canadians are proud to possess and should have at their disposal.
To my mind it should be increased on a percentage basis possibly to the extent of two-thirds, in a manner somewhat similar to the way in which the Ontario compensation board establishes its rates when a person meets with an accident in a plant.
Consideration should also be given to a longer minimum period of benefit for which a claimant may qualify. It is considered that the maximum period of approximately a year should be sufficient for the normal occurrence of unemployment. But there is some concern for the worker who is eligible for only the minimum period of six weeks, as he may be facing a period of unemployment of longer duration.
I feel that the waiting period should be eliminated altogether. At the present time it
Supply-Labour
is six days. A person who is laid off one day should, in my opinion, become eligible immediately to draw his benefits as of the following day. As it is at the present time, a person who has been laid off must register at the unemployment insurance office, and the waiting period commences from the day of registration. Let us consider the case of a person laid off one day and who, through some misfortune, is unable to register at the unemployment insurance office on the following day. It may be that he is called out of town on a matter of urgency, and may be away for a week. Upon his return he registers, but can draw insurance only from the date of registration. Because of the misfortune that has befallen someone in his family he has not had time to register, and is forced to lose the time he was away. I repeat that in my view a person should be eligible for unemployment insurance from the day following his lay-off or termination of employment.
Regarding the supplementary benefits, the period of time is set aside from October to March. From the experience of a few years it is felt in all circles who are interested in this matter that this should be extended from October to June, inclusive. I would bring to the attention of the minister the case of a married woman covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act. As an example we will consider the married woman who is employed in one municipality and who, through necessity, must move to another. She is not eligible for the benefits of unemployment insurance until she has worked 90 days in the new location, in order to establish her qualifications. I say this penalty of 90 days should not be imposed, and that such a person should be eligible for unemployment insurance as though she had not moved from the original locality.
Let us consider the case of a single girl who is employed and eligible for unemployment insurance. She gets married and leaves her employment. Under the present act she is unable to draw unemployment insurance unless she obtains employment and works at it for 90 days. I feel that this penalty should be eliminated.
Then there is the person who is employed and is laid off, and who under the present act is eligible for unemployment insurance. But if that person is fired from his job-and there may be various circumstances under which a person is fired, through no fault of his own-under the act he is penalized for a period of six weeks before he can make application for unemployment insurance.
I shall not take up further time of the committee, because within the next few days

Supply-Labour
we are most anxious to get as much done as possible. I did feel however that it would be proper for me to rise at this time and bring these matters, which I feel are important, to the attention of the minister. I would hope that he would give some heed to these recommendations, and that at least a portion of them might be included in the amendments to come before the house at the next session for purposes of review and implementation.

Mr. Chairman, I doubt if the usual benign look on your face would continue at this time in the session were I to respond to the invitation extended to me by the honourable and amiable member from Cape Breton South. I am not disposed to quarrel with him when he describes as a model 1903 Ford the machine the government is attempting to operate, but I fail to recognize the brilliance of the 1954 Cadillac that was supposed to emerge from my hon. friend's criticism of the government.
However, I have risen today to remind the minister of a promise he made. And, incidentally, before I proceed further, I would be delighted to engage in offering a description of socialism at any time. And if the hon. member wants a definition now I could give him one. I must say, though, that it does not entirely suit him.
Perhaps I could give four others to offset it.

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three items I wish to bring to the attention of the minister before this vote carries. On two different occasions when dealing with labour problems I have drawn to the minister's attention what I consider one of the primary problems not only of labour and management but of Canadians generally.
I think that Canadians are a bit worried about the recurrence of industrial strife. Probably this is a case of fools rushing in where angels fear to tread, but it does seem to me that some method must eventually be found to overcome this difficulty. In all other human relations courts are set up to deal with disputes between man and man. It would seem to me that if the proper, wise justices were selected some of this industrial strife would be done away with.
On other occasions I have suggested to the minister that an increasing number of firms throughout Canada and the United States have adopted the profit-sharing plan. I am not going to go into that again. The very fact that more and more firms are turning to that type of arrangement, under which labour in the factory is a partner in the firm, as it were, indicates its popularity. If the company has a successful year, labour also has a successful year. I am just going to take this opportunity to highlight, as it were, one of the most successful plans, namely, that of the Dofasco Company. I am going to read just a little from their report:
For the benefit of non-fund members, the plan is an agreement between the company, the fund members and the trustees under which each member saves 5 per cent of his salary or wage each year up to $5,000 (a total maximum saving of $150 per year) and the company on its part agrees to pay in not less than 10 per cent of its net earnings and not more than four times the fund members' saving. In practice, the share of profits has always exceeded the minimum and for the last two years has come close to the maximum. The plan is open to all full-time Dofasco employees who have been with the company continuously for three or more years and so far no one eligible has refused to join.
The fund has grown from a modest beginning in May of 1938, with about 750 members, to its present size with about 2,500 members and assets of $13 million.
That in itself points out some of the benefits, how production can be increased and how the cost of the product can be decreased to the consumer and at the same time the labourer in that particular industry benefit from his services.

I should now like to quote from a recent issue of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce magazine:
In the recent submission to the ministers of finance and national revenue by the executive council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce prior to the last budget, the executive pointed out that "the present basis of taxing deferred profit sharing plans . . . subjects the employee to tax on the contributions made to the plan by the employer, and also on the earnings of the plan at the time such contributions are made or such earnings accrued, although the employee does not receive such moneys until some later date and in some instances may never receive them. The submission suggested that the beneficiaries, under a deferred profit sharing plan, be taxed when they receive the actual benefits.
That submission is a good one, and one that the minister might recommend to his colleagues as an important incentive to other firms in Canada to consider introducing this type of profit-sharing plan.
Other speakers have said something about the unemployment situation. The latest figures indicate that there are almost twice as many unemployed now as there were a year ago at this time. During the early part of this session considerable emphasis was laid on the fact that it was seasonal. I do not think you can answer the criticisms now by saying that it is seasonal. Other factors are involved. In my estimation one of the biggest factors is that inflation has helped to price Canadian products out of many world markets. There is also the fact that a large number of Canadian people are in receipt of less money. They have less money to spend, especially those who are on short time, and more especially farmers whose incomes have been greatly reduced, regardless of what the Minister of Agriculture may wish to say to the contrary.
Let me go back to the budget. It did not do anything to relieve the situation so far as labour is concerned. There was no reduction in taxation to relieve the low income groups to any great extent, and consequently their purchasing power, as I mentioned before, has not been augmented so far as the budget was concerned.
I should like to mention another matter. I realize it is not a federal matter in a sense. It has to do with the workmen's compensation acts, not only of the province of Ontario but of other provinces. My suggestion is that a three-man medical board should rule on questions of dispute as to whether a man is eligible for assistance under the workmen's compensation act or not. In some cases arbitrary rulings are made. An independent medical board might find differently and would give the labourer the benefit of the doubt, as it were, to improve relations between labour on the one hand and the 83276-420i
Supply-Labour
administration of the workmen's compensation on the other. If this independent board brought in a report it would be respected and it would improve relations. That is all I have to say.

I should like to make a few brief remarks on this first item. First of all, I should like to say I sympathize in every respect with the minister, because he has had a particularly difficult time this year owing to the world economic situation generally. It would be a particularly difficult situation for anyone in the minister's position.
There seems little doubt that unemployment has been on the increase this year over last year. I do not mean to reiterate what has already been said. A certain amount of it has been seasonal, but the facts would indicate that unemployment at this period of the year, as compared with the same period last year, is considerably greater. In this regard I refer to an item on the front page of the London Free Press of Wednesday, June 23, of this year. I quote as follows:
Informants said that at May 27 about 336,000 persons were registered for work with national employment service. This was down from 549,000 at April 15, the last figure made public in the government's monthly labour surveys.
However, it was still more than 60 per cent higher than the 202,000 in late May of 1953. At that time, though, Canada's labour force was smaller.
In this regard I would also like to quote very briefly from a press notice which appeared in the Sentinel Review of Woodstock, Ontario, which indicates certain figures relative to that part of Canada. It states:
In Ingersoll, however, the situation is not as encouraging since April figures showed 210 unemployed compared with 193 at the end of May.
In other words, the number decreased slightly over the period of a month.
Benefit payments were increased from $16,000 in May, 1953, to $32,000 in May 1954.
Generally speaking, and according to what we have heard and what has been indicated in press notices, it appears that unemployment is considerably greater at this time than it was at the same time last year.
I would like to make some remarks with respect to the textile industry. It is an industry which is of considerable importance to the people of my riding as there are a great many textile workers there. The textile industry as we have heard many times in this house this session is sometimes called a depressed industry. It has suffered severely during the last few years and there have been substantial lay-offs which apparently still continue. I would like to read a paragraph from a letter I received from one of the

Supply-Labour
prominent union leaders in the textile industry in the city of Woodstock, Mr. E. B. Tilford, who states:
Harvey Knit laid off 32 people on Friday the 4th of June and 12 more on Friday the 11th so they are not so good.
He then makes further reference to other matters which are not relevant to this discussion, but his letter indicates that the textile industry is still having its difficulties. Undoubtedly the whole answer in this regard lies in the policy the government will adopt with reference to this particular industry. We all know that during the war years we had to have a textile industry for war purposes and after the war the industry was encouraged to continue production because of the great shortage of consumer material. Consequently, the textile industry continued to do fairly well immediately after the war but eventually the heavy demand for clothing, fabrics and draperies and other products of the industry fell off and many of these textile units, sometimes referred to as marginal units, found it difficult to survive in our economy.
I fully realize that raising the tariffs in this matter is not an answer because it only raises the cost, but if we are going to have any kind of textile industry at all, which can successfully compete with similar industries in countries such as Japan and India where they have very low wage rates, we are going to have to keep some sort of tariff barriers to protect the workers in this industry. It must inevitably depend on what policy the government is going to adopt and how much of the textile industry they determine we are going to keep in operation.
I think all hon. members will agree that a certain proportion of the textile industry must be retained for national defence and other purposes which are uneconomic in themselves, and indeed it may very well be that at the present time some portions of the textile industry are marginal or uneconomic, though I do not think that as yet we have the proper figures in this regard. However, the government must decide to what extent various portions of the primary and secondary textile industry can be let go, so to speak, and since this matter concerns trade and commerce as well as labour I think that before any decision is reached by the government in this regard the matter should be thoroughly examined.
There are two suggestions I would like to make to the minister. The first is with respect to unemployment generally. It seems to me that during this last winter we had a particularly unpleasant picture in Canada with a large number of persons becoming

unemployed, and indeed in much larger number than we have had for many years. This, of course, was referred to as seasonal unemployment and undoubtedly it was to a large extent. However when large groups of people become unemployed it is fairly axiomatic that their purchasing power goes down and we then begin to start that long downward spiral of deflation which has the accumulative effect, like a snowball, and generally wrecks the economy.
I have heard this suggestion by a number of persons and I certainly hope the minister will look into it if he has not already done so. The suggestion is as follows: When unemployment in the country reaches a certain figure, which would have to be decided upon, and let us say for the purposes of example, 300,000 or 250,000, the amount of benefit paid for unemployment insurance be increased. The figure involved of course would have to be decided after careful study. However, this plan would have a much quicker effect in stopping this downward spiral than would the suggestion of instituting a program of public works. That plan would more quickly scotch and stop the downward spiral of so-called added deflation.
Since the geographic and climatic conditions of Canada make it almost inevitable that Canada suffer permanently from this problem of seasonal unemployment, my suggestion would be that, in order to stabilize the economy and eliminate so to speak the crest and trough of unemployment between the seasons, everyone in Canada contribute to a certain extent in overcoming this situation. Because of the climatic and seasonal conditions under which we live I do not think it is unreasonable to suggest that these fluctuations in unemployment be moderated a little possibly by some form of extra taxation. I think we will all generally agree that the economy of our country would be much better if we did not have these seasonal dips in the unemployment situation, and if the purchasing power of those temporarily out of work on a seasonal basis could be kept up so that the economic effects all the way down the line would be considerably lessened.
With respect to the textile industry generally there is a brief suggestion I would like to make. If a large industry employing large numbers of persons such as the textile industry is to be dislocated as a matter of national policy on a permanent basis then it hardly seems fair that all those persons employed in that industry be thrown out of work at once. In other words, if the government takes the view that in our trading relations with other countries such as Japan we will have to buy something from them in return

for their buying our agricultural products- and that is the line of reasoning I have often heard expressed-and that in the national interest they should dislocate an industry such as the textile industry, which was encouraged and built up during the war in some cases on an artificial basis, then large numbers will be thrown out of work.
I think that will be unfair for two reasons. First of all it is very unfair to those people from a personal point of view so far as their families are concerned and because it will cause great hardship. From a broader economic point of view, it naturally tends to dislocate the economy of the country if a large number of people are thrown out of work all at once. I think there will be little argument about that statement.
If it is found necessary not to protect the textile industry or any other industry that might get into a similar situation by additional tariffs or something of that nature, and if it seems necessary to allow a portion or even a large part of this industry to go by the boards, so to speak, and to go out of business, then in the interests of the persons employed in the industry, I think something should be done for them. If an industry is allowed to go by the board, to coin a phrase, in the national interest I think everyone in the country should share a proportion of that burden and that it should not fall just on those who are employed in that particular industry.
It might mean some sort of small tax levy, but until these people who are out of a job because of national economic policy can find other employment I think that under these circumstances the benefits to these people should be raised. The situation is no fault of their own. It is a matter of national policy in a particular industry. I know that the minister will probably say, "In a broad sense, that might apply to any industry", and that the national policy might occasionally hit one industry from time to time. That is true. I would not make that suggestion in a general way. But when you get one industry that has been built up to a large size and is a large employer of persons, and when as a permanent policy some portion of that industry is going to be put out of commission, so to speak, in my opinion those persons who are out of a job because of this policy should be given, until they can be re-absorbed, a higher rate of unemployment benefit. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I should like also to suggest in this regard something to which I know the minister is himself sympathetic. When an industry is dislocated, as the textile industry is, quite possibly a scheme such as that which I have heard has been started in Marysville-which I believe is in the minister's constituency; it is a scheme of retraining people who have been in this industry

might be implemented. I think that is an excellent suggestion. But while these people are being retrained, I think they should draw these somewhat increased benefits I have suggested because it is a question of reallocating these particular persons from one job to another.
Also, as my colleague the hon. member for Hamilton West pointed out earlier today, this question of moving large groups of the population from one part of the country causes great expense and hardship. The textile industry, or the parts of it that are apparently marginal and are going out of business, are often located in communities in which there is only one industry. I suppose that is the situation in the towns in the Ottawa valley, one in the minister's constituency and many others. The textile industry often seems to be located in small villages and towns. If the people of these places are going to be permanently out of work, and even if they are paid some unemployment benefits or something along that line at a rate higher than that at which they are now paid, and even if they are retrained, the job of moving those people from one centre of population to another where they can get future employment is going to be an expensive one.
If people are forced to move because of this national policy, I feel that possibly some percentage of their expenses ought to be contributed to by the government which, of course, is the people of Canada. As I said before, if things of this nature are done for the benefit in the long run of the people of Canada, everybody should contribute his small share and we should not just make a certain percentage of the population suffer.
I know the minister will likely say that it is not the intention of the government to try to create ghost towns out of some of these textile towns that may have to go and that they hope that the people can be retrained and find new jobs in those communities. Nevertheless, there will be a large number of persons who, as a result of the present textile situation, will have to move in the long run; and, as I have said, I feel that those persons should have a part of their moving expenses contributed to.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I should like to acknowledge the tolerant and helpful tone in which the speakers this afternoon have presented their views on the general item of my estimates. With very few exceptions, all of those who have spoken so far have mentioned one item. If the hon. member for Hamilton West will not consider me discourteous, I should like to deal with that item first. I may say that she also mentioned it. I refer to the responsibility, as it has been called, for the welfare of the unemployed employables. Much has been said about that matter.
However, I think there are several things that should be said again. One of them is this. The so-called offer or the agreement, as it has been called in some cases, of 1945 was never in reality crystallized into an agreement. I think all hon. members will agree with that statement. That being so, there have been many things that have happened since. One of those things has been the setting up of the federal-provincial tax arrangements. Those arrangements have been made in the light of the fact that there was no agreement on the offers and counteroffers that were put forward and were left in the air in 1945. I think that situation should be made clear because I am quite certain-as some hon. members have indicated this afternoon-that those representing some municipalities in this country have felt quite sincerely that there was a crystallization of responsibility at that time when, in reality, there was not.
That being true, a great many other things have happened since that time. It was on the basis that no responsibility had been assumed there by the federal government definitely for the unemployed employables-except for unemployment insurance which I will go into in a moment-that the federal taxpayers, through the federal government, assumed some responsibility for the costs of what we used to call the unemployed unemployables, namely, older people over 70. As a second step this year the unemployed unemployables came partly within the scope of the federal field through the bill brought in by my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
There is one other statement that should also be made. I think it will be agreed by all hon. members here that the federal government should not go out to the municipalities and make individual arrangements with those municipalities on these matters without the knowledge, or without the request or the concurrence of the province in which those municipalities exist. I think every one of our provinces has a minister of municipal affairs. Certainly this province has one, and
LMr. Nesbitt.]
my own province has one. I believe the minister of municipal affairs for this province represents a constituency not so far from here. As has been mentioned this afternoon, during the past winter when representatives of municipal governments and trade unions came here and interviewed members of the cabinet, the Minister of Labour and his officials and presented their briefs, it was found that practically all of them came from the province of Ontario. I can state this afternoon that as far as I know no representations were made during this past winter or spring by the province of Ontario to the federal government on behalf of those municipalities that have presented their case.
In his remarks the hon. member for St. Paul's kindly reminded me of a promise which I had made. Following what I have just said, I should like to tell him that I did not forget the promise. I will not say that the notes I made afterwards would answer his question fully, but nevertheless I should like to refer to it, and in so doing perhaps I might be considered as having referred to all the questions that have been put forward this afternoon on the subject of the responsibility of municipal, provincial and federal governments in respect of unemployment assistance.
My colleagues, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance and others, have said on earlier occasions in this session and others that since the passage of the Unemployment Insurance Act in 1940 the federal government has accepted the responsibility for developing and administering that act for the protection of the welfare of the fit workers of Canada. As part of that responsibility the coverage of the act has been gradually extended from time to time. The effort to extend the coverage is continuing, and at the present time an attempt is being made to bring in other groups. It was also said this afternoon that the financial cost involved when workers of Canada are unemployed should devolve upon the federal treasury. I contend that that is true at the present time because in addition to contributing $32 million during the calendar year 1953, or one-sixth of the total paid into the unemployment insurance fund, the federal government has assumed full responsibility for the administration of the unemployment insurance program and the national employment service at a cost of $25 million a year.
In other words, during the last fiscal year federal taxpayers paid a total of $57 million for the purpose of protecting the fit workers of Canada against hardship when they are unemployed. So far as I know, during recent

years the contribution of most of the provincial governments and municipalities toward assistance of the unemployed employables has been relatively light. In some cases provincial governments have decided to turn over this responsibility to the municipalities, and in those instances no provincial expenditures have been incurred during recent years.
In addition to unemployment insurance, the federal government has increased substantially assistance extended through other social security and related measures in the last ten years. I am not going to deal with them in detail this afternoon because members of the committee know what has been done through the federal treasury. When I spoke at the beginning of the unemployment debate in February I indicated then that no representations had been made by provincial governments that they were unable to cope with the situation in their provinces, and the same holds true today. We have received no such request, and I should like to repeat that we regard unemployment as a matter of concern to all levels of government. It is not the exclusive worry of any one level, and we feel it can only be dealt with satisfactorily by cooperative action by all concerned.
Several other matters were referred to by other members. One of them concerned the retraining of unemployed persons under an agreement known by the department as schedule M for the training of unemployed persons. The hon. member for Hamilton West rather implied that the only place the Minister of Labour had put that into effect was in his own province. I can tell her that it was put into effect quickly in my own province to help to relieve the difficulty in the textile industry because the provincial government was on the mark and was ready with a plan to propose to the Minister of Labour who was happy to put it into effect under schedule M, for which he already had received authority.
There again I can say to her, without wanting to be insistent, without wanting to be impertinent, that because of the large number of representations we have had from the province of Ontario this year we have suggested to the government of Ontario that we would be willing to co-operate under schedule M within the province, but up to this time they have not entered into an agreement.

Is it not so that there is an entirely different arrangement in the province of Ontario entered into by the Ontario industrial and educational council and the Canadian Manufacturers Association, and that a new ten-year agreement was drawn up this year?

Between the provincial government and the federal government?
Yes.
No, there has been no agreement drawn up under schedule M.

No, but this does away with the necessity for operating under schedule M, does it not? It is a complicated agreement, and I understand it expired this year and that a new ten-year agreement was drawn up.

We have had no application from the government of Ontario for matching dollars for the training of fit unemployed workers. As I indicated in my opening remarks, the estimates envisage extending that field if the provinces are prepared to do so and if it is felt that assistance can be given in the provision of greater skills for the individual, thus assisting in helping to solve unemployment to that extent in the particular vicinity as well as adding to the sum total of skilled personnel in Canada.
I agree with everything the hon. member for Hamilton West said regarding apprenticeship training. The total number registered as of March 31 this year was 12,900, but that is not nearly enough. It is a field of training which is of the utmost importance, but I am sure that the hon. member will agree that it is again a field where the federal government cannot impose its will. We have a very capable, active and aggressive voluntary committee working on the matter, and I believe management and organized labour are coming to realize more and more the importance of apprenticeship training.
With all that has been said this afternoon regarding older workers, I agree. I should like to reassure the committee that not only in the Department of Labour but elsewhere we are doing everything we can to encourage the employment of older workers. The government itself through the civil service commission has set an example this year, I believe, in the retention of older workers for a longer period than formerly, and through the civil service commission has perhaps cast a slightly more friendly eye on applicants who are no longer young.
The hon. member for Macleod referred to the suggestion that is made that older workers are unable to learn new techniques. I can assure him that is a prejudice that has been proved to be wrong. As to absenteeism, the attendance to their work of older workers has proved to be much higher than that of younger workers. The charge has also been made that the use of older workers means a lessening of production, but that is not true.

In connection with this matter some of the members of the committee may have noted that the Canadian Manufacturers Association has conducted a very broad based survey during the last few months, the results of which were incorporated in a recent issue of their magazine. The subject of older workers and the matter of seasonal unemployment were brought forward at their convention, and are the top items on their agenda not only for study but for carrying on experiments within certain parts of Canada.
My hon. friend referred to the Government Employees Compensation Act. This act, as she said, is a co-ordinating act and the benefits arising out of it to federal employees come under the province in which the federal employee happens to be. The amendments to it were pretty well administrative and routine. There was some difference of opinion as to whether the amount accruing to a federal employee who, for instance, was injured in British Columbia when his place of employment was in Ottawa should receive payment through Ontario or British Columbia. I can tell her it is my intention to bring this forward as soon as these kinks are ironed out. I made a reference to the women's bureau in my opening remarks.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said there were going to be tough years ahead. I hope they are not going to be as tough as he indicated. He also stated that the hon. member for Hamilton West and I were on the same team. For my part, I am quite satisfied with that.
The minister noticed that I disclaimed that.

I noticed my hon. friend did not brag about it.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South brought up two points, one of which was specifically related to Cape Breton and concerned a very important group of men. I am going to tell him here and now, without taking up the time of the committee, that following the end of this session, which I hope will be very soon, we will investigate that matter once more.
I might say the section of the act to which I referred could apply in that way in any part of Canada in which similar circumstances arose.

As the hon. member knows, under the act we have not only the commission but umpires and other bodies, so we will have the appropriate people take a new look at the situation before the new holiday period rolls around. The same

remarks apply to his second point with regard to the Moncton office recruiting workers for the north. I believe the same remarks apply to the third point as well.
In so far as the hon. member's last point is concerned, I could not agree with him more. Perhaps I should not say so, but I feel that since the greater portion of Nova Scotia is now to be tied together at last by the Canso causeway I would hope before too long there might be a vocational school located there.
The hon. member for Macleod asked what the government was doing in connection with the older worker. If I may I am going to send him along a copy, not of a speech I made but of a report that was made to me on that subject. I am sure it will answer the questions he had in mind. We are really doing something worth while in that connection. The value that is being brought about lies in the fact that employers and trade unions are more and more recognizing the facts that the hon. member for Macleod brought forth, that is the problems arising out of the longer life expectancy today and people who have nothing to do getting fed up with life. Therein lies the hope for providing more useful employment for the older people and thus adding to the productivity of the country.
The hon. member for York South referred to the matter concerning the R. F. Welch company. I will look into that. I should like to refute completely the remark which my hon. friend made when he said that unless we get a little war we are going to have terrible times. I do not think my hon. friend really believed that. In spite of the sympathy that was passed on to the Minister of Labour this afternoon, I would rather see success at Geneva and a peaceful world established by some means or other than have whatever value there may be from the superficial employment that comes from expenditure of money to be blasted away in the air.
The hon. member for Ontario, as well as others, proposed some amendments to the act. It was suggested that there could be a rearrangement of the benefits that might be of value during another serious period. I can tell the committee that even though the session is nearly over and even though we are approaching summer, my department is taking a very serious and continuous look at this act in the light of experience gained during the past winter. I believe that we will all agree that this last winter is the first time anything approaching a severe test of the effectiveness of the Unemployment Insurance Act has occurred.

I shall admit at once that the total number of unemployed has been large. I can admit, too, that the government has been greatly concerned and I can assure the committee that steps are being taken to guard against hardships in the future, just as I hope the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act has softened the really heavy sting of hardship during the seasonal unemployment of this past winter.

Before the committee
takes recess, may I say that I would not want the minister to get the impression that I advocated another little war, nor would I want him to give the impression on the record that I did so. My statement was that wars have saved us from unemployment in the past and that unquestionably a little war would save us from unemployment now as long as the capitalist system remains in vogue.

I admit at once that I knew my hon. friend was not advocating war. I believe he knew that I did not understand him as saying that. I should like to say again, with regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Middlesex East, that that is a really constructive suggestion. He has made it before. This afternoon he said that everything possible should be done to encourage the profit sharing plan in industry as a method of working towards industrial peace. However, the federal government cannot impose such a plan.

There is one subject with which I wish to deal in connection with this item, Mr. Chairman. It will take me less than five minutes. If there is not going to be further discussion, then perhaps we could deal with this item if that is satisfactory to the committee.

I wish to deal with the statement made by the minister growing out of the remarks in regard to responsibility for unemployment in the municipalities. The minister in seeking to correct impressions that have been conveyed made statements that are directly contrary to the record.
He was referring to a statement that had been made about the problems of the municipalities. He in some measure brushed aside the seriousness of that situation. But I would point out that as recently as June 9 representatives of 900 municipalities meeting in Windsor were agreed that unemployment now is serious, and that the question of unemployment relief for the municipalities is 83276-421

critical in many cases. They urged that the government recognize this fact and that it do something about it.
The minister explained that the difficulty arose out of certain discussions in 1945. Without attempting to quote his exact words he said there were certain proposals put forward and that the proposals put forward and the conditions submitted were not agreed to, and that therefore the discussions ended. They did not end in 1945. Those discussions began on August 6, 1945, and they continued on different occasions until the adjournment on May 6, 1946. There was no refusal at any time, as the record shows, of the proposals put forward by the federal government nor was there on the other hand a refusal of the proposals put forward alternatively by the provincial governments.
If the record is examined-and there is a Hansard record-it will be seen that it was expected that the meeting was only adjourning and that a meeting would be called again at the instance of the federal government. The agreements that later emerged were not agreements resulting from negotiations arising from this discussion. They resulted from a statement by the minister of finance at that time, Mr. Ilsley, that the money arrangements would be made by the federal government. It was not a question of negotiation; it was a statement that this would be done. And certain provinces entered into an agreement on that basis.
The minister has said that there are substantial payments going back to the municipalities. That is true. But, Mr. Chairman, I mention this to put on record the fact that there is only one reason this conference did not continue and that was the failure of the dominion government to reconvene the conference which adjourned on May 6, 1946. It is difficult to imagine how much greater concentration of taxation is needed before the federal government will deal with the problem.
It now is getting the major proportion of all taxes in Canada. How much farther does it have to go before it can deal with this matter of employable unemployed or unemployable unemployed which today gives so much concern to the municipalities, as is indicated by the resolution passed at Windsor early this month?
I leave that subject now. Referring back to certain statements I have made before, if the minister thinks-and I hope he does- that it would be advisable to have some discussions as to the way in which this could be dealt with, and so as to meet the argu-

ments I have put forward in asking lor a conference between the federal and provincial governments, and to meet the conditions that the mayors and reeves from 900 municipalities in Ontario have placed on record, then I say the way to do it, the way to lay the foundation for the solution of this problem is to have a conference right away between the federal and provincial governments, not merely to discuss constitutional problems but to discuss this extremely important problem which today is particularly unfair in its application to municipalities right across Canada.

180. Fair wages, conciliation, industrial relations, industrial disputes investigations including the administration of legislation relating thereto, and for activities re promotion of co-operation in industry between labour and management, $468,714.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Item 180 has to do, amongst other things, with the conciliation of industrial disputes. Has the Minister of Labour any comments he would care to make regarding the dispute between the railway companies and the non-operating employees?

Mr. Chairman, the representatives of management and of the unions met last Thursday, and then adjourned and met again on Tuesday afternoon. Before the meeting adjourned on Tuesday afternoon I understand that they made an arrangement that they would not at that time make any public pronouncements as to the negotiations up to that point. They having done that, consequently I cannot make any comment regarding it. All that I can say is that the ending of the meeting on Tuesday afternoon was left open to reassemble on the invitation of either of the two parties.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I appreciate the position the minister takes in view of the meetings of last Thursday and this Tuesday between the two sides to the dispute. However, there are a few words that I should like to say. The first thing I want to say-perhaps it is unnecessary for me to say it in view of the situation but I shall say it anyway

is that I trust that the Minister of Labour will put his best brains and everything he has got into the effort to avoid this dispute resulting in a strike. I am sure it is the desire of everyone, including the employees, that there not be a strike.
And the employers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The only reason I neglected to say that was that could be taken for granted. But it so happens that the employees are voting on the question as to whether or not to back up their demands by going to the length of a strike, and it is possible that they may cast an affirmative vote on that matter. . That was my reason for referring to the employees, for even though they may vote for a strike they would rather not see one.
There can be no doubt that it would be disturbing to the economy of the country as a whole and disturbing to the people of Canada if there were another railway tie-up such as we had in 1950. I must say, however, that what disturbs me most about this

situation is that I do not feel there is sufficient understanding of the position of the men. I refer to the non-operating employees who have presented certain demands to their employers. "Demands" happens to be the word that is used, but in my view it is of the nature of things that, with technological progress and other improvements in industry and in our economy, the workers have a right to share in that progress and in those improvements. I cannot see the logic of those who would contend that there arrives a time when workers such as our railway employees should be satisfied with what they are getting and should ask for nothing more.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Nobody in this house has said that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No, no one in this house has said that, but there are people in the country-

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
-who express that view. I should be very glad if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration would give us the benefit of his comments on this important matter. I say I feel that the workers in this instance have been most responsible in what they have requested. As everyone knows, they have not asked for any increase in their hourly rates of pay. They have asked for a series of what are known as fringe benefits. They have asked for an increase in the number of annual holidays with pay to be granted to the workers; they have asked for a certain number of statutory holidays throughout the year; they have asked for certain sick benefits and also for certain overtime rates of pay for Sunday work.
As hon. members will recognize, in all cases these are what are known as fringe benefits. We do not know what went on at the meetings in Montreal last Thursday or the earlier part of this week, but it is a matter of public record what happened as a result of the deliberations of the board over which Mr. Justice Kellock presided a while ago.
As hon. members are aware, in addition to Mr. Justice Kellock, there were two other members of the board, one representing the railway companies and the other representing the railway employees. Nevertheless that board did not produce what might be called a proper report. It was not possible apparently for any two of them to get together on a set of conclusions. What happened was that three reports were made. That is not without significance. To me this is the disturbing feature of this whole situation, that 83276-42IJ
Supply-Labour
the member of that board representing the railway companies and apparently speaking for them refused to give a single inch. His report was an uncompromising recommendation that nothing that the men were requesting be granted. On the other hand, the representative of the employees did make a report which represented a scaling down to some extent of the requests or the demands of the employees.
One does not know just what relationship exists in a situation like that, although I have been a member of such boards myself and I know a little about it. But one can assume that when the representatives of the employees suggested a settlement on the basis of a slight scaling down of those demands that that indicates a willingness on the part of the employees to enter into something of a compromise. That seems to be the situation as it stands at the moment. The companies are not prepared to move an inch, but the men are prepared to compromise.
It is because of that situation that there is a great deal of feeling about this issue amongst the employees affected, and I share their feeling. I have been in pretty close contact with these employees across the years and indeed there are a great many of them in my own constituency. I was home for a couple of days a week or so ago and I made contact with some of them while I was there, and I can say that the feeling about this situation is very high. The reason it is high is because of that uncompromising stand taken by the employers even in the face of the willingness of the employees to enter into some sort of compromise. One reason I say this in this House of Commons is because I hope that it may contribute to what I feel is necessary, namely, an understanding by the public of the position of the men. They do not want to suffer the loss of time and pay which will result from a strike, but they also feel, because of a situation such as that which now faces them, that they have no alternative but to back up their just and reasonable demands by the use of the only weapon that is in their hands.
When I say I hope the minister will give this matter his best attention I imagine it is already on the top of his priority list and that I do not need to say that to him. Indeed, with all the other matters that have been thrown into his lap this afternoon I do not see how he is going to have much of a holiday this summer. But I hope, if necessary, he will call in any of his colleagues who may be able to help him so that they may join with him in trying to solve this problem by

Supply-Labour
giving whatever publicity is necessary to the issues in the case, I urge him to do his level best to see to it that a strike is avoided if it possibly can be, but also to see to it that justice is done to these men.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there are those who will say, "Well, why should they not withdraw their demands; why should the company be asked to move in view of the financial position which they say is theirs at the present time?" Well, it is the same old story, Mr. Chairman, as I indicated a moment ago. The fact of the matter is that as time goes on we do make progress with regard to technological improvements, and the amount of wealth that can be produced with a certain amount of labour power keeps growing. The tendency is for labour always to have to put up a struggle to get its just share of that increased production of wealth in which our workers participate to such a great extent. I know there are arguments that will be put forth on the other side, but I must say that I feel very strongly for the position of the men. I think they are making very just and reasonable demands and I hope that a solution will be found that will make it unnecessary for them to go out on strike, but which at the same time will do justice to the men and will give them a larger share of the wealth they are producing, which they are asking for not in any increase in hourly rates of pay but in these other social benefits which in my view they thoroughly deserve.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had to say and with some of his remarks I concur. However, I must say, having taken part myself in labour negotiations, that I realize full well there is a time when it becomes a matter of saving face on both sides of the fence. The negotiator who can produce a formula by which the two factions can come together and from which each of them can be content with the report which they take back to their individual factions is going to be the person who saves the day.
But it looks very much as though we are headed for an impasse in this particular matter. I do not think so myself, I think we are probably remote from the time when we will reach that stage. But nevertheless I think that all of us should realize the weaknesses of human nature. After all, all of those people on both sides, whether on the side of management or labour, are human and they want to save face. They hate to give in to the other side and yet they realize over their better judgment that certain elements emerge that are probably unforeseen.
tMr. Knowles.]
I know, Mr. Chairman, that this is a slim house tonight. I know that we should be considering very seriously the implications of a problem which, if it is allowed to develop, might blow up in our faces and affect all of our people in the entire Dominion of Canada. I think those of us who are here should very seriously consider what our responsibility is in that regard, and so accordingly I urge the Minister of Labour to use his influence to see to it that a conciliatory attitude is adopted by both factions in this dispute.
I have a great deal of sympathy for those people who realize the time is not ripe for a demand for an increase in wages. They know that their only hope is to get some concession in the way of fringe benefits. An absolutely adamant stand on the side of the employer is going to achieve nothing. It is only going to stiffen the backs of those who have been instructed by their union membership to make demands which have come up perhaps through the ranks, or possibly have been suggested to the rank and file of employees as reasonable demands to be made upon the employing agency.
Whatever the situation may be it boils down to a matter of conciliation, a word which has become common in our everyday life. I urge the minister to use his best offices to stop this before it goes so far that neither side can give in and still save face. I would urge him to stop it now by means of conciliation before we are forced into a position where even members of this house will have to take a stand, as they did once before, for or against an arbitrary decision. I ask the minister to do that. I think that is what every member of the committee has in mind.

I give to the committee and to the hon. members who have spoken my complete promise that nothing will be left undone by my department or by the government to accomplish a mutually equitable solution to the problem.
