Department of Citizenship and Immigration has done so, but I went through the estimates today and I found a great many instances in which the amount was exactly the same as it had been in former years.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Let us take that matter up with those departments.

Either it is an over-all policy or it is not an over-all policy. As a matter of fact, I personally think that it would be a good thing if every department was charged for its postage and that amount was credited to the Post Office Department. I think it would give a clearer picture of postal revenue and expenses. But I notice that, all the way through the labour estimates, this matter of postage is quite an item, with increases in some places as I have just mentioned from $15,000 to $25,000 and in other cases increases of lesser amounts. But I notice other departments also in which there is no increase whatever. If that is the explanation, I wonder whether it is government policy or whether it is not government policy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No. I should like to have an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Since I perhaps started this argument, I might say this. I must apologize for doing so. I do not want to hold up the committee. I have not the time to go through the various estimates. I have just looked at the Department of Agriculture and I notice that it has been done there. I know my own department is now charging postage whereas it has not done so before. I daresay that if I have time I can unearth some figures that might satisfy my hon. friend. But it is the policy, as I understand it, that has been decided upon.
It may be, Mr. Chairman, that some of the departments had already inaugurated this service.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It may be so.

However I open my book of estimates at random and I look at defence production and at page 154 I find they had $30,000 last year and that they have $30,000 this year. I turn over the pages and I see

Supply-Labour
national health and welfare; I find that under the heading of immigration medical services they had $2,600 last year and they have $2,600 this year. Everyone knows the volume of material that goes out from the Department of National Health and Welfare. I turn over quickly to the laboratory of hygiene of the Department of National Health and Welfare and I see an item of $100 for last year and $100 for this year. Then I turn to-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would come back to the Department of Labour, if she would.

Mr. Chairman, I have only brought this matter in because the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has said that it is the policy of the government. Apparently it is not the policy of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I say, I cannot keep up with my hon. friend who is very quick-witted and has read from the pages she has looked at. I have looked at the Department of National Health and Welfare-she mentioned that department-and at page 327 there is an increase in the postal charges shown there.
How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is $1,000. As I say, I do not want to continue this argument because we are considering the estimates of the Department of Labour. If my hon. friend will take my word for it, I will go through the whole of the estimates before the evening is out and see if I cannot convince her that there have been increases.
An increase of $1,000, from $6,500 to $7,500 is not a great deal of difference, is it?

Mr. Chairman, last night when I was going through my appropriations for the Department of National Revenue, I myself was rather surprised that the postage for national revenue cost $725,000 a year. Of course, we are dealing with 4,500,000 people who make income tax returns. That is $125,000 in excess of the amount we paid last year. I enter into this discussion because of the fact that for the last eight or ten years I have presided, I would think, at 99 per cent of the meetings of treasury board. As a matter of good accounting we expect that each department should pay its postage account to the Post Office Department. Therefore I think the increase in postage expenditure in the labour department is quite justified.

I do not object to it at all. I think it is the adoption of a realistic attitude. The Minister of National Revenue

has cited one instance, but on page 361 I find there is an increase from $200 to $8,000 in the customs and excise division. Then I see that the inspection, investigation and audit services branch decided to leave their postage at exactly the same amount. So it goes down the line. Some departments have done it and some have not. It just brings us right back to the contention which I made on the post office estimates, that if the departments would pay their own postage we would not have needed an increase in postage rates.

Item agreed to.
186.	To provide for expenses of a women's bureau, $24,090.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has the director of this bureau been appointed yet?

No, Mr. Chairman. In my opening remarks this afternoon I made an apology, on behalf of the civil service commission, for taking such a long time to provide a woman for this post, but I have hopes that they will have a recommendation to make in the very near future. I would make one comment on what the hon. member for Hamilton West said. She criticized mildly the fact that we had not established the junior positions during the past year. We refrained from doing that deliberately. I have felt from the beginning of this plan that the whole form of a women's bureau in relation to my department and the unemployment insurance commission, where the greatest scope lies so far as the country generally is concerned, would depend upon the character and capacity of the woman chosen to head the branch, and that it would be unfair to her to build up something and hand it to her when we were starting on this work. I am hoping to have a more complete report when I have occasion to talk about this subject again.
I hope the minister will have something by the time we next come together.

Item agreed to.
187.	To provide for payments to implement a program for the rehabilitation of disabled persons, in accordance with terms and conditions approved by the governor in council, and administrative expenses connected therewith, $197,513.

I see that the amount voted last year was $195,000 and that the amount actually expended was $101,000. Yet the appropriation requested for this year is $197,000, very close to twice the amount actually expended last year. I should like the minister to tell us why they need twice the amount expended last year. Will he also tell us what program is anticipated which

necessitates an increase from $15,000 to $25,000 in the amount for radio, film and other publicity.

In response to the first question, the past year has been a period of organization, as I pointed out in my opening remarks. It has been a year of discussion on the part of the two officials, one from my department and one from the Department of National Health and Welfare. They have taken up this matter with all the provinces in the utmost detail for the purpose of working out a co-operative plan. As in so many things, the initiative has to be taken by the province and we assist financially. We assist financially in a special way here in that we assist the provinces in the provision of a provincial co-ordinator. Therefore the first year of organization is not an indication at all of the amount of money that we will need. I am sure we will need that amount of money during the coming year.
The other point has to do with the amount set out for publicity and information. In the early stages of getting into action on this plan we believe that a good deal of its success will depend upon co-operating with the provinces in making the plan known, in assisting in the placement of disabled persons after they have been medically rehabilitated and trained and in encouraging employers to employ a larger number of rehabilitated disabled people.

I am sure no one objects to any amounts which are expended for this purpose, but it is a little confusing to find these things in two different departments and to try to bring them together and form a clear picture. That is the sole reason I asked the question.

I am very glad my hon. friend mentioned that because I should like to take a moment to say that the reason why we in Canada have been so long in getting the plan under way is that it is a matter that comes within the scope of municipal, provincial and federal governments, a vast array of national organizations both specialized and miscellaneous, and a great array of provincial and municipal organizations and voluntary agencies which have been doing magnificent work in this field. But after three or four years of patient and loyal effort on the part of a great many people throughout the country we have worked out what I believe is a unified plan that is going to work well towards the objective we have in mind.

I cannot help but comment on that because it has been my very happy experience to work closely with some of the people who are doing this community
Supply-Labour
work. I am sure the minister will agree with me that it would be impossible to do this work if it were not for the voluntary services of people throughout this country from Halifax to Victoria in the rehabilitation of disabled persons, not only the rehabilitation of those of mature years but the training of young people too. I realize that the training of young people probably comes under the Department of National Health and Welfare, but they eventually come under the minister's department. I cannot speak too strongly of the great contribution which is made by people who have their own responsibilities but who give greatly of their time and effort in order to supplement whatever contributions are made by the various levels of government towards the rehabilitation of these people.

I would venture to make an appeal to the minister by reason of what has just been said by the hon. member for Hamilton West, and I think agreed to by him. I want to ask the minister if he will make a very special appeal to the Minister of National Health and Welfare emphasizing the great importance of the voluntary organization. I sought to do that on the minister's estimates but I am not at all sure I made a very good job of it and I would be very pleased if the Minister of Labour would assist.	-

I am sure it will not be needed but I will be very glad to do that. It is quite true that in this effort the voluntary agencies are in the front line and governments are there as allies, financially and otherwise, to help in the effective work which has been carried on.
I suggest that the minister might use that phrase "front line" to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I doubt if he has that conception at the moment.

Item agreed to.
Vocational training co-ordination-
189. Training payments to the provinces, $4,290,000.
Would the minister tell us which provinces, if any, failed to take advantage of the federal grant last year, and how much was involved.

There are, as my hon. friend knows, a number of agreements with the provinces. We have one, for instance, which my hon. friend mentioned this afternoon, under schedule M. We have one for youth training, one for apprenticeship training, and so on. Did my hon. friend have any particular type of training grant in mind? My hon. friend meant capital grants, was that it?

Supply-Labour

I asked lor training
grants, Mr. Chairman.

Well, I have, for instance,
apprenticeship training; did my hon. friend want that?
Has the minister not a recapitulation of the amounts available for each province and the amount of the total that was taken up by each province?

I can give my hon. friend the figures for the youth training, for the apprenticeship training and for the vocational training. Then, we have, of course, the armed services personnel training which is carried 100 per cent by the federal government. The figures for youth training are as follows: Newfoundland, allotment, $30,500; at the end of March, 1954, the actual was $8,000; Nova Scotia, allotment, $43,740; actual, $19,398.49; Prince Edward Island, allotment, $7,000; actual, $3,957; New Brunswick, allotment, $43,450; actual, $22,884; Quebec, allotment, $175,000; actual, $132,157; Ontario, allotment, $100,000; actual, $40,000; Manitoba, allotment, $17,500; actual, $8,278; Saskatchewan, allotment, $45,000; actual, $39,145; Alberta, allotment, $32,500; actual, $16,506; British Columbia, allotment, $52,000; actual, $44,825.

I should like to say that the figures the minister has put on the record just now clearly indicate the reason we have not the vocational training that we should have. It is not the fault of the federal government.
Hear, hear.

The allotment for Nova Scotia was $43,000, and they took up only $19,000. The only province that did take up their quota fairly well was Saskatchewan. Ontario had an allotment of $100,000 and took up only $40,000. We ought to get some organization back in the provinces that is going to co-operate, and at least try to take advantage of the money that is available for carrying on this program.
That is all very well, but as long as the federal government takes the major share of taxes of the country I do not know how they can expect the provinces to match them dollar for dollar.
It is not very often I have to defend the federal government, but the shoe is on the other foot.
You have been doing it all along, brother.
The shoe is on the other foot.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He is not on your team, so you should hardly call him "brother".
The heck he is not; he has been defending the federal government ever since I came here this session.

Any time I get up in this house, I know the difference between the labour estimates and the post office estimates, and any time I say something in this house I generally try to have all the facts and put them honestly. The "crack" the hon. member just made clearly indicates she is not very well acquainted with the facts, because according to those figures the provinces definitely are not co-operating with the federal government in taking advantage of the funds made available for vocational training.
Those figures were for youth training.
I should make it clear-
I understood they were for one schedule. We are not dealing with schedule M or with rehabilitation, we are dealing with the youth training program.

These figures were for one schedule only, the youth training program. There are others that refer to the apprenticeship training program, the vocational training program, the armed services personnel training, defence industries and so on. The main one, or the large one, is for federal assistance grants to vocational training schools.

That is right, but if the minister went into the whole picture it would be much worse. I am talking about the schedule to which the minister referred, and I resent the observation by the hon. member for Hamilton West that I defend the government. I am merely trying to be honest about this thing. I am not concerned about making political propaganda out of the situation in the provinces which needs correcting. The only way to correct it is to understand where the trouble lies, and so far as I can see the trouble lies with the provinces.
The excuse that the government is taking most of the taxes is not a valid one, because most of the provinces that are under the dominion-provincial taxing agreements are better off financially than if they were not under them. I have taken a look at my own province, and I am interested in it. I want to get some vocational training in that province. If the fault is with the province, then that is where I am going to place the responsibility and that is not defending the federal government. It is trying to get something done in a field where the provinces are

not measuring up. It they cannot match the federal government dollar for dollar, then it is up to the provinces to say so. It is not good government to allow hundreds of boys and girls to come out of school, largely because of economic circumstances, when they are still untrained for anything and when there is this amount of money available to help train them. If any province is not able to take up the money that is available, then it is nearly time the government of that province was replaced by somebody else.

I notice, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Cape Breton South frequently defends the government on something that is of a federal nature only, like post offices, which he has introduced into this discussion, but nevertheless-
You introduced it; you have been talking post office rates all night.
Oh, I have not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

The hon. member must have a peculiar echo in his brain, but in any event, Mr. Chairman, he does defend the government on everything that affects federal policies. When it comes to provincial policies, he defends the only one province that is governed by the party to which he gives loyalty.
It is not any provincial policy at all.

I feel I should like to know a little more about this item. I want to read the item, and perhaps the minister would say a word of explanation. There is the sum of $513,000 for youth training and $931,500 for apprenticeship training. Would the minister explain exactly how that works? And then I find a further amount for vocational school assistance; one for foremanship and supervisory training, and then the following:
Training of persons to fit them for gainful employment or for defence industries including vocational training for the physically disabled.
And then there is a further sum of $100,000 for the training of persons to fit them for the armed forces. There must be a wide variety of objects and purposes. Would the minister give us the position with respect to those?

To take first the apprenticeship training, to which we have just referred in passing. That is carried out on a fifty-fifty basis between the provinces and the federal government. Does the hon. member want details as to figures?
Supply-Labour

No, but would the
minister explain how this is done. I remember being in a plant and seeing some youths apprenticed there. Would they come under this scheme? Is this done in co-operation with industry?

It is done in co-operation with industry, and in some cases assists in bearing some of the cost. But whatever costs there may be in those provinces which industry does not bear, then they are shared equally between the provinces and the federal government. But every encouragement is given industry to do as much of this work as it possibly can, not only because of the cost but because we feel it is more effective if industry does it rather than by establishing apprenticeship schools.

It would seem to me that if industry would do it it would be more realistic and effective. But when industry does not do it, what is the relationship of those apprentices which are in industry? Are they like visitors who are in there, just looking on, or are they an integral part of the work going forward?

While we are on this point let me say that I hold no more brief for the Liberal government in Ottawa than I do for the Conservative government in Ontario. But I do suggest that school boards should be made cognizant of the amount of the grants made by the federal government. I know of school boards in Ontario where federal grants have been given through the provincial government, and the school boards have been given to understand that the entire grant was paid by the provincial government.

Concerning this item which has to do with trade training, and the training of persons to fit them for the armed forces, as set out at page 238, I notice that the amount listed is $100,000. In the report of the Department of Labour at page 87 there is a table showing the federal allotment as $138,542. And then in the same table, breaking down the people enrolled under training and the like, it indicates that for those training for the army in New Brunswick there is a payment of $12,585.50, and the total days training is shown as 5,668.
Then if one follows it down you see the Quebec army plan, the Manitoba army plan and the Alberta army plan. You find there is a difference in the cost of a day's training in each one of those provinces. It varies from something over $2 in New Brunswick to more than $3 in Manitoba.

Supply-Labour
Then, at page 76 of the report of the Department of Labour it speaks of this trade training for the armed services, and says in the last paragraph:
During the year 62 instructors were hired by Canadian vocational training tor this purpose, the money being provided by the Department of National Defence.
The question I would ask based upon those figures is this: What is the nature of this training, and why is not the cost of it the same from province to province? In what way is the money allotted for this purpose expended? Is it expended for the payment of other instructors rather than those who are provided by the Department of National Defence, or is it for some other purpose?

I shall come back in a moment to the question asked by the hon. member for Greenwood. My hon. friend knows that this training is done by the provinces, through the federal government, where 100 per cent of the cost is paid, because it is being done on behalf of the armed forces. In the Department of Labour we are acting merely as a sort of honest broker between the Department of National Defence, the provinces and the schools.
The other question asked was as to the variation in costs, as to why it is much cheaper in New Brunswick than in Manitoba. Well, the obvious answer is that we are a poorer people than you are in Manitoba. But I think it is due to the fact that there are bound to be variations in the schools, and the number of students under training. Consequently this would govern the cost per head in training.
Then to answer the other question concerning apprenticeship training, I shall refer to my memorandum. This is a renewed apprenticeship training agreement. As I said a moment ago, this schedule was the basis of training under separate agreements between the federal government and the provincial governments. So that apprenticeship training is an agreement all by itself. The renewed apprenticeship training agreement is in operation in all provinces except Quebec and Prince Edward Island. The Northwest Territories have also entered into an agreement recently. The agreements which cover a ten-year period expire on March 31, 1964. The purpose of the apprenticeship agreement is to promote and develop training programs for indentured apprentices registered under various provincial laws and regulations, and to encourage the training of more skilled workers in all types of industrial employment where apprenticeship is applicable.

Subject to the amount voted annually by parliament the federal government shares equally with the provincial governments in the cost of organizing and operating special training classes, and maintaining adequate field supervision of provincially controlled apprenticeship programs. Apprentices registered March 31, 1954 totalled 12,902. The apprenticeship program of Quebec differs from that in the other provinces, as it is controlled by special committees operating in designated zones, and is financed by assessment.
How many are there under agreement?
As at March 31, 1954 there were registered for training, all told, 12,902.
Under the apprenticeship scheme?
Yes, under the apprenticeship scheme.
And the amount appropriated for it is $900,000. Will the minister just tell us what the relationship is? We will say that there is an apprentice working in a factory; is that correct.
Yes.

How much does he
receive from public funds and how much from his employer?
When he is at school we pay an allowance, and the tuition fee at the school. When he is taking his training with private industry, then private industry absorbs all the cost.

Item agreed to.
190. Payments to the provinces for capital expenditures for vocational schools, buildings and equipment, $300,000.

I am rather surprised that these items are so small for past capital expenditures. Can the minister tell us in what provinces that $400,000 was spent last year, and just what the conditions are on which those grants are made?

The reason the amount is so small is that we had cleared up prior to this year practically all the payments that were owing by the federal government on schools that had been constructed during the post-war period. The amount last year was to provide for commitments only in Newfoundland, Ontario and Manitoba.
What are the conditions under which this money is available?

The conditions are that the vocational school or the technical school must

be up to certain general standards that are satisfactory to the kind of training that our department feels should be done, and following that the cost is matched on a fifty-fifty basis with the provinces.
Will the minister give the provinces which have participated?
Newfoundland, Ontario and Manitoba.

These are grants, of course, and every province will take them all up. There is no matching in this. The minister indicated that only Newfoundland, Ontario and Manitoba received anything by way of grant last year. Under what circumstances does the minister start negotiations for the establishment of a vocational school or high school? Am I right in assuming that the province must first decide to build a school in some section of the province, determine the cost and the federal government will then offer a grant in aid of a certain amount of money. Suppose you are putting up a school that costs $2 million. The grant made by the federal government is a small fraction of that, is it not?
Fifty per cent, if within the allotment.

Fifty per cent of the total cost of the erection of the school. Once the school is in operation, its maintenance is in the hands of the municipality in the province? There is no grant by the federal government for maintenance?
We pay 50 per cent up to a maximum annually.

After it is in operation, who maintains it? What I am interested in now is this. How do you get started on this application for a school? Does the provincial government make application to the federal government, or do they build a school and determine the cost and bill the federal government for it?

The normal way is for the provincial officials to discuss it with our officials at the planning stage. This will include the size, the cost, et cetera, and we pay 50 per cent of the cost within their allotment.
What I am thinking of now is this: Newfoundland gets $300,000 of these estimates by way of capital assistance.

May I make an explanation, because I think it is important? We were working on a ten-year period from 1945 to 1955. This of course is another outgrowth of the war. The ten years are ending this
Supply-Labour
fiscal year. We shall now be going on, I hope, to another period in the future. During the ten-year period certain amounts were allotted federally to each province. The amounts were not all spent in one year. They may be spent as the schools proceed.
It might be of assistance if I just put on the record how much these allotments were in that ten-year period and how much was spent, because it would be unfair to say that because that small amount of money was paid to those three provinces this year that is all they received. It might give a distorted picture. I will give this in round figures: Newfoundland, allotment $219,000. No claim has yet been made in Newfoundland. I am going to give the whole thing.
Prince Edward Island, federal allotment $61,500 for buildings: paid, $61,500; allotment for equipment, $20,500; claims paid, $20,500.
Nova Scotia, allotment for buildings, $378,000; claims paid, $378,000; for equipment, allotment, $126,000; claims paid, $68,000.
New Brunswick, allotment for buildings, $324,750; paid, $324,750; for equipment, $108,000; paid, $108,000.
Quebec, allotment for buildings, $2,354,000; paid, $2,354,000; for equipment, $784,000 allotted; $784,000 paid.
Ontario, $2,272,000 allotted for buildings; paid, $2,273,000; for equipment, allotted $757,800; paid, $534,060.
Manitoba, allotted for buildings, $492,000; paid, $373,000; for equipment, $164,000; paid, $74,000.
Saskatchewan, allotted for buildings, $643,000; for equipment, $214,000; paid, $214,000.
Alberta, allotted for buildings, $525,000; paid, $525,000; allotted for equipment, $175,000; paid, $175,000.
British Columbia, allotted for buildings, $446,000; paid, $446,000; allotted for equipment and paid $148,000.
Northwest Territories, allotted, $12,700; it has not yet been paid.
These were ten-year agreements? Does the minister renew these agreements this year?
They may be renewed after March 31, 1955.

I thought I knew something about this, but between the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the answers given I am all mixed up, and I think I shall have to ask the minister a question or two. These are not grants, are they? Is this money not paid more or less under what we call arrears? Does the municipality or

Supply-Labour
the school board not decide on the buildings, with the approval of the department of education of the province, and then the building is erected? The federal government deals with the provinces after the building has been erected and has been approved by the department of education? In other words, there is no particular grant given to a province and they get it whether they use it or not? It is paid in arrears, is it not?
I do not think I said that, Mr. Chairman.
No, it was the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

The provinces knew what they could expect if they were able to provide the kind of buildings for the purpose, and then went ahead, consulting along the line. When the construction was ended, 50 per cent was paid by the provinces and 50 per cent by the federal government up to the amount of the allotment for each province. Some provinces have spent additional amounts over the allotments.
Is the minister in a position yet to indicate what is likely to be the nature of the next ten-year agreement? Will that be more or less left for the future?
No, Mr. Chairman, I am not in a position at the present time to say that, as my hon. friend will understand.

Item agreed to.
Terminable services-
192. To provide for expenditures incurred in implementing recommendations of the national advisory council on manpower, and for the administrative costs of the council, $11,700.

Would the minister say what has happened on these terminable services. This item provides for expenditures incurred in implementing recommendations of the national advisory council on manpower, and for the administrative costs of the council. Last year the item was $66,780 and this year it is $11,700. According to the details there was one item last year covering office stationery and supplies amounting to $55,000, which is a sizeable amount, and this year it is reduced to $500. Would the minister say whether this means that the activities of this council have been, I might say, curtailed, though that is a very mild word. Has it been wiped out or what has happened to it?

No, the council has been doing very good work. We have only had one meeting and I hope we will not have to have meetings of the full council more often than that. On some other occasion I would be glad to give a full report of the activities of

the council and indeed I explained them fully to the hon. member for Broadview last year. The reason the vote is so much smaller this year is that last year under the advice of the council a certain amount of material was stockpiled against the day when it might be needed in case of an emergency. This is a non-recurring item.
Carried.

No, do not get excited. The total expenditure last year was $4,231 and the amount appropriated last year was $66,780. That seems to be a magnificent piece of budgeting. This year, in spite of the fact that $4,231 were expended for last year, we have an estimate of $11,700. How does the minister explain that this particular item will cover almost three times the expenditure last year despite the curtailment of the activities of the council?
If my hon. friend will look at page 29 she will see that under item 192 for 1953-54 there was an estimate of $66,780, and for 1954-55, that is this year, the estimate is $11,700.

But that is not a very good comparison because although they estimated to the extent of $66,780 last year they spent only $4,000 and now the estimate of expenditure amounts to $11,700, which is three times as much.
What about the $55,000?
In reply to the hon. member for Hamilton West I might say that this is due to the fact that we expect to have one more meeting of the council this year.
Will that one meeting cost $7,000?

I would like to know what this council does. The minister has told us they have had a laudably small number of meetings. I think that is desirable. But I would like to know just what they do. The item reads, "implementing recommendations of the national advisory council." I think it would be reasonable for us to know what we are implementing.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not think my hon. friend would want me to go into a full report tonight. I did that on one or two other occasions. In 1950 there was an apparent need for an organization through which the employers, workers, farmers, women, and other groups could bring their views bearing on manpower problems to the attention of the minister and the Department of Labour, and this very excellent council was organized to carry out this work.

The minister has not
answered the basic question which I put in regard to the sharp cut in the appropriation for this department amounting to about one-sixth. The minister has just made a statement about the tremendous amount of work done by this council last year and yet they did it on $4,000. Does the minister say that $11,000 is going to produce three times the result? Or does he say that in view of the appropriation of $66,000 for last year this council is practically going out of existence?

I shall not admit the latter point at all. All I will say to my hon. friend is that this council is not in the same category as a branch or sub-branch of the department which has a stabilized expenditure that can be figured exactly. Certain plans are under way which vary from year to year.

The minister said a few minutes ago that it cost almost $7,000 to call a meeting of this council. But they spent only $4,000 last year and they are calling for $11,000 this year. They had an appropriation of $66,000 last year and 1 think the committee should have an explanation.
The normal expenditure for calling a meeting together is $1,114.
Is the personnel of this council more or less permanent?
Yes.

Like the hon. member for Hamilton West I am a bit confused by these figures and I think we should get them straight. Let me read what these figures say. The item on page 29 asks for $11,700 for 1954-55 and indicates that this is a decrease of $55,000 from last year when the item was $66,780. So far so good. Now, on page 240 I confess I become confused because first of all we have a reiteration of the figures on page 29, namely the request for $11,700-and I still feel the hon. member for Hamilton West has not been answered very well on that point-and then there is the figure of $66,000 for last year. But following that we have another figure which does not seem to tie up with anything because it says "fiscal year, 1952-53, expenditure $106,099; fiscal year 1953-54: estimated total $4,231." I must admit I am completely confused.

I do not think there is anything confusing about it. When we prepared the estimates last November we felt and still feel that there are certain projects during this fiscal year that the council could well undertake and carry through and it was known at that time that an amount in the estimates would be required to do it.
Supply-Labour

I am not at all satisfied with this. In the first instance the amount for office stationery and supplies has been reduced from $55,000 to $500. Everyone who ever ran an office knows that the measure of your activity is, to some extent, the amount of supplies and so on that you use in your office. But to cut the thing right down to 1 per cent is a ridiculous item. Then you turn around, on the other hand, and you have "allowances and expenses of council members and others" raised from $9,000 to $10,000. I think this committee is entitled to some explanation of this item. Travelling expenses have gone down from $1,500 to $1,000. Terminable allowances have been wiped out completely. Office stationery and supplies have been reduced, as I said, from $55,000 to $500. Yet the allowances and expenses of council members and others have gone up from $9,000 to $10,000. What is the answer?

Mr. Chairman, I hope that my hon. friend will not think that there is anything deep and devious here at all. I tried to explain the matter of the office expenditure. Office expenditure is the wrong word there. It was a special kind of paper that was required for a special kind of use to have ready in case of need. That happened only once and it will not happen this year. Consequently we did not put the amount in the estimates.

You mean to say the
inventories on hand will last for how many years?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
The minister does not know.

Item agreed to.
194. To provide for expenses that may be incurred in the arranging for and the movement of workers from outside Canada to work on farms and other essential industry in Canada when Canadian labour is not available to meet the need, including costs connected with the supervision and welfare of persons already immigrated to Canada; administrative expenses connected therewith and to provide for expenditures under agreements with the provinces authorized by the governor in council, $878,258.

Will the minister please explain the procedure under this estimate which is to provide for expenses that may be incurred in the arranging for and the movement of workers from outside Canada to work on farms. From what country do they come? What citizens of which country get assistance under this vote? How is it applied?

Supply-Labour

Where firms require workers the Department of Labour, in co-operation with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, if it has not those workers available in Canada, co-operates to bring over groups of workers. They come from any country in which the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is operating.

Under this item there is a decrease of $115,574. In the supplementary estimates there is-wait a minute, maybe I have the wrong amount-no, in the supplementary estimates it is under unemployment insurance commission. It is to provide for the transfer of labour to and from-
That is a different item.

I know, but it is for the
same thing, is it not?
No. It is a different thing.

It is a case of robbing Peter to pay Paul, I would think, because it says in the one instance, in item 194:
To provide for expenses that may be incurred in the arranging for and the movement of workers from outside Canada-
In the other case it says:
To provide for the transfer of labour to and from places where employment is available-
And so on. It is still juggling with labour.
One has to do with workers coming into Canada and their getting work; the other has to do with moving workers from one part of Canada to another.
Just a minute. It is still a case of juggling workers around, is it not?

I should like to have some information as to the number of people involved. The item reads:
To provide for expenses that may be incurred in the arranging for and the movement of workers from outside Canada

And so on. I think we should have quite a little bit of information as to just what is involved. We are trying to get through these estimates, Mr. Chairman, but we are not trying to pass everything in a rush, only to be asked questions afterwards which make us look like ninnies for not having asked them.
I am glad to give all the information that is required.
The minister is very good about it, but there are certain signs of impatience in the committee which makes it a little bit difficult for us to continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Summer heat.
[Mr. Herridge.l

The technique of group movements was developed in 1946 when 2,876 Polish soldiers who had served with the British in General Anders' army were brought to Canada for employment on farms. I mention that only to indicate its inception. I am not going to trace down the history of it from there. During the fiscal year 1953-54 there have been 9,952 immigrants brought forward in group movements, including 3,543 domestics, British, German and Greek; 5,003 farm workers and sugar beet workers; 1,142 track maintenance workers and 264 general labourers from the island of Malta.
In previous years substantial numbers of immigrant workers were brought forward in group movements for employment in woods work and mining but there was no demand for this type of worker during the fiscal year 1953-54.
Displaced persons who came forward in previous years were provided with free ocean transportation by the international refugee organization. Since IRO ceased operations on December 31, 1951, there is no provision for free transportation to immigrants coming to Canada. The cost of ocean transportation for immigrants coming to Canada in group movements is now provided by way of assisted passage loans granted by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in some instances and in other instances the immigrants themselves pay their ocean passage.
The Department of Labour pays the cost of inland transportation for domestic workers and farm workers, provided they are placed in employment by the national employment service or the federal-provincial farm labour committees, and provided that such workers remain in the employment to which they are assigned for a period of one year. I should of course add there that they do not always all do that. If there is any other information my hon. friend would like to have, I shall try to give it to him.

This seems to be like a piece carved out of what one would expect to be the functions of the department of immigration. What is the relationship between the two departments? Why, for example, is this particular activity assumed by the Department of Labour? Is there any other feature or factor of immigration which is assumed by the Department of Labour and not by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration?

The main reason is that the requirements for those workers come to the

attention of the national employment service and the Department of Labour in the first instance and they are subject-

May I interject a question there? Are they different from all other immigrants in that respect and are all those that are included in the description the minister has just given covered under this grant?
Only those that I mentioned. Those categories that I mentioned are included in this move of the Department of Labour.
Do these groups come out for farm labour or are they employed in any kind of labour that is needed?

I will give my hon. friend the groups for this last year. That will give him an idea. For the last year the figures are as follows: General labourers, 264; farm workers, single males, 2,448; farm couples, 478; farm families, 166; sugar beet families, 1,506; special church groups-that is in cooperation with church organizations and agricultural organizations-405;	then on
construction, 1,142; domestics 3,318, domestic couples, 224. Those are the only categories, namely, construction and farming.
What denominations were they? What church denominations?

Lutheran, Baptist, Roman
Catholic, Methodist and Mennonites.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No Anglicans?

Are any of these expenses returned? It was our understanding that money was advanced by the immigration department to pay the way of certain people coming out here to work as farm and other types of labourers, and that there was a revolving fund set-up under which the money was repaid. I understand this has nothing to do with that type of immigrant. If not, are these people expected to refund to the department the money advanced? For instance, there is an item here of $30,000 for travelling expenses and then an item for food and other supplies. I suppose the purpose of these items is to look after these immigrants until they are settled.
In these cases their transportation to this country is paid.
And it is not refunded?
It is not refunded.

With respect to the details on page 241, what is the explanation for the reduction in the amount for professional and
Supply-Labour
special services from $162,000 to $15,000 and for the reduction from $55,000 to nothing in the case of rental of buildings?

When these groups came over here, particularly in the winter months, it was necessary for them to have a stopping place until they were moved out to their places of work. Consequently some of the buildings at Ajax were utilized during that period, but last year we closed that out.
That still does not explain the reduction in professional and special services from $162,000 to $15,000.
The catering there was defined as a special service.

I am also a bit puzzled about this item. It is not only farm labour that is involved. The amount of money provided is quite large and the item states that it is to be used for the movement of workers from outside Canada to essential industry and so forth when Canadian labour is not available. There is a lot of Canadian labour available in this country at the present time. When you look at the details on page 241 it makes you wonder what kind of services are provided. The amount for housing, board and maintenance is dropping. The amount for professional and special services has gone up.
No.
There was $90,000 last year and this year there is $125,000.
That is food and other supplies. You are on the wrong line.

The rest of the items appear to be about the same, and it would seem to be more or less a permanent organization. The amount for rental of buildings has gone down but the amounts for repairs and upkeep of equipment, electricity, heat, water rates and other municipal services, sundries and hospitalization expenses appear to be about the same. Is this vote, the details of which are set out on page 241, for the purpose of maintaining some centre to house immigrants coming into the country as farm or industrial labourers until such time as employment is found for them? Is money provided to move them from one section of the country to the other? Is it for the purpose of maintaining a centre for immigrants? That is what it looks like.

That is correct. As I said a moment ago we have cut down radically on that kind of stopping place. There were two, one at St. Paul l'Ermite outside Montreal and one at Ajax in Ontario. We have closed down the one at Ajax but we still maintain the one hostel near Montreal. As to the

Supply-Labour
emergency professional and medical services, they are provided for the people who are there from time to time.

Are similar services available to the scores of unemployed people who are and have been permanent residents of this country? I know that in Ontario, the mari-times and all the provinces you will find pockets where there is unemployment. Are such services available to our own unemployed? Can they get transportation from one section of the country to the other to a job? Is there some centre to which they can report where they will be fed, clothed and provided with hospitalization in case of illness? Could these centres be utilized for the purpose of moving our own people around the country?
The minister will remember that in April of this year there were 56,000 Canadians receiving supplementary unemployment insurance benefits who went off the rolls completely at the 15th of April. We know there were 56,000, and we also know there were many more. Are there no services available under this department that would provide the same kind of protection for these people? That is pretty full protection. I am not objecting but I do think that people who have lived in Canada for a good many years and have paid their taxes and are now out of work through no fault of their own and are off the unemployment relief rolls are at least entitled to the same consideration as people we may bring into the country. The least we should do is to equalize the situation so that people who have been here will have the same kind of privileges if they are out of work as are being provided at this place in Montreal.

I think the hon. member will recognize that these were emergency cases of a temporary nature. These people were brought in, taken to the hospital and were only there for a very short time until they went to their work. I am glad to say that it has been possible to lessen the amount of that kind of accommodation. I might also say that under a later item some provision is made for co-operating in helping to move Canadians who are unemployed to other places where employment may be found, although it does not fill all the requirements.
I am not quite clear on this item. Is this the only item under any department of government providing assistance to farm workers in Canada?
We passed that one. That was item 185.
We are on item 194. Is that the only item that makes provision-
Item 185 on page 28.

This item also makes provision for farm workers. I was wondering whether this included them all or only a percentage of them. There is a great deal of complaint about many of these people coming to this country under the pretext of going on a farm and then "doing a bunk". There is no question about it. I want to read a short extract from the Saskatchewan News published by the government of Saskatchewan. It is headed, "Few Immigrants for Farm Work", and reads as follows:
The federal-provincial farm labour committee has recommended that no more than 100 German farm immigrants be confirmed for placement in Saskatchewan this year. L. J. Hutchison, secretary of the committee, said the recommendation was based on the realization that German farm immigrants had not assisted materially in reducing the farm labour shortage.
He explained that a reason for this is the movement of labour from agriculture to industry which is evident across Canada and which is particularly true with respect to German farm immigrants placed on Saskatchewan farms.
I do not know about Saskatchewan conditions but I have heard general complaints that these people who get assistance to come to Canada to work on farms have no more idea of working on farms than I have at the present time. They stay for a while and then disappear into industry. I do not think it is good enough that this government should assist people to come here to work on farms under those conditions. I think the same amount of money could be better used to help some Nova Scotia people get to employment in western Canada.

I understood the minister to say that these grants for hospitalization and medical services are of a temporary nature for immigrants coming into this country who become ill and have to go to hospitals. There is a $150,000 grant there. Any experience that I have had with the department of immigration would indicate that anyone coming to this country is given a thorough medical checkup before he comes here. It would seem that these people who, as the minister indicated, are brought here by employers may get in without any such medical checkup as ordinary immigrants receive. I believe that requires some explanation.
Before the minister answers there is just one other question I should like to ask. The minister told us that this grant is for payments, in co-operation or conjunction with the department of immigration, for workers

who are brought in by employers. Has the minister any record there of the names of some of the larger employers who are bringing in these people?

No, I have not the names of the employers, Mr. Chairman, because there would be a long list. Most of them are farmers who are employing farm workers. I should have added to my remarks, so as to allay the fears of my hon. friends, that this comes about as a result of close liaison between the officials of the Department of Labour and the farm labour committee as well as representatives of each of the departments of agriculture in the provinces. These people meet, and I recall I was present at the meeting when Saskatchewan representatives were here. They stated how many and what kinds they wanted. They discussed the question of the difficulty of keeping the new Canadians on the farm as well as the difficulty of keeping domestic help for the housewife. I can assure my hon. friend that they are not brought in if there are Canadian workers available to do that work.
The other question raised was as to how could we make sure these immigrants fulfil their year's obligation. This is a very difficult question with which the farm labour committee has wrestled for two or three years. They have not got the complete answer as yet but they feel they are making some improvement. As I said in my opening remarks, the operations under this vote will be less this year than they have been in the last few years.

I have just one other
question, Mr. Chairman. I notice that there is $125,000 in this item for professional and special services. What is the nature of the professional services receiving the bulk of the $125,000?
If my hon. friend looks at page 242 he will see that $30,000 is for professional services and hospitalization expenses.
No, the item to which I am referring is on page 241, the second item, professional services and special services, $125,000.
No, that is for food and supply.

On page 241 to which my hon. friend refers, at the bottom of the page there is an item for housing, board and maintenance; then, there is a subhead, professional and special services, $15,000. It that right?

Yes, the next item.
Supply-Labour
The next item is for food and other supplies, $125,000. As I said, that will go to take care of accommodation at the hospital.

I want to ask a question or two about the organization we have that is involved in this operation consisting of the provinces, the Department of Labour, and at some point the department of immigration. First of all, what offices has the Department of Labour in Europe?
We have no offices except personnel attached to the office of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
In other words, the department uses the offices of the department of immigration in Europe, with personnel from the Department of Labour attached?
You mean on the continent of Europe?

On the continent of
Europe.
There is very little on the continent of Europe; it is mainly in London.

Perhaps the minister
would be able to say whether this item we are discussing now applies chiefly in the United Kingdom? Do the people concerned in this thing come chiefly from the United Kingdom and can this be regarded as a United Kingdom operation?

No, Mr. Chairman, these are officials that the Department of Labour has in London mainly, I think with one or two others on the continent. They are not specifically for these groups of people, but on behalf of the Department of Labour with regard to all immigrants. These officials are able to advise immigrants with certain skills as to the working opportunities in Canada, and when applicants come in to be interviewed they would be available for that purpose. They are there for that purpose.
The minister says available to all immigrants; do I understand then that the Department of Labour concerns itself, to some extent, with all immigrants?
Only at the request of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration officials at that point where interviews may be required with respect to certain qualifications.
Who is responsible for selecting, screening and passing on immigrants?

Our people are on the selection team at that point.

Supply-Labour
Will the minister expand that a little by saying who is on the selection team? My question is; who seeks out and passes on the immigrants? I take it the minister says it is a team.
The department of immigration.
The department of immigration?
Yes.
And they are responsible until when, until the immigrant arrives in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What difference does it make?
They are responsible until they arrive in Canada and, in some cases, until the new Canadian is placed. Our national employment offices co-operate in that placement at all times.

The Minister of Finance says, "What difference does it make?" I think I am justified in saying that it may make quite a lot of difference. I believe that sometimes there is a good deal of difficulty and even of confusion as between the two departments. I wish to be perfectly frank and to ask at what point there is a division of responsibility as between the two departments. There is every chance of a difficulty arising. It would be a great surprise if it did not arise, and I would like to know exactly what the division of responsibility is.

I can assure my hon. friend there is no difficulty between the two departments. The responsibility for immigration rests with the immigration branch. The Department of Labour, the national employment service and the unemployment insurance commission in these various activities act in all respects as an agent of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in co-operation toward achieving a common purpose of getting immigrants over.

I understand the minister is speaking about activities in Europe at the moment. What happens when they arrive here? Who is responsible for these people we are talking about when they arrive here? Under which department do they come, then?

These we are talking about under this special vote, because of the fact that they have been demanded or required through our machinery in the employment office-the federal-provincial farm labour committee-are moved from the point of landing in Canada and go perhaps to a hostel, but often go to their employers, and are there turned over and placed. Is that an answer to my hon. friend's question?
[Mr. Gregg.l
Let me be clear. Up to arrival in Canada they are under the immigration department, and when they reach Canada they come under the Department of Labour, which then governs their movements?
That is right.

May I ask a further question. When the immigrant comes out and is placed on the farm, he seems to be under the supervision of the immigration officer. Can the minister explain how it is that he comes under that officer? That is what is confusing us. Immigrants who have arrived on farms in communities we know are supervised by immigration officials. The man representing the department seems to be an immigration officer. It may be that we are all wrong, and that it is the Department of Labour. I would like to know that.
Naturally it is the desire that a representative of the department of immigration in the area keep supervision over the progress of new Canadians during their early period in the country.

He places him on the
farm?
Yes.

As I understand the picture these people are brought in under a joint arrangement between the immigration department and the Department of Labour. I understand the minister to say that once they arrive in Canada the Department of Labour accepts some responsibility after they have landed. My question is this: During the year in which they are working under the arrangement under which they came to Canada, do they come under the supervision of the federal Department of Labour or of the various provincial departments of labour in respect to their hours of work, the sort of wages paid, and other working conditions? Does the Department of Labour accept responsibility for that during the first year?

To go back again; the request for them is made with the concurrence of the representative of the provincial department of agriculture-in connection with agricultural workers. In that province the minimum amount that those new Canadians will be paid when they arrive at the farms is already decided each year at the annual meeting of the committee. So that that is settled, and the information is conveyed to these men going on the farms when they arrive in Saskatchewan or Alberta. And it is then the responsibility of this department in conjunction with the provincial department of agriculture to see that that agreement is carried into effect.
Has the figure been given as to how many were brought in under the aegis of this activity of the Department of Labour?
I gave that earlier in the evening.
And how many it is anticipated will be brought in this year?
I gave that information earlier in the evening.
Does the minister recall it offhand?
And it is anticipated that how many will be brought in this year?
It is estimated there will be about 8,000.

There is one thing that
interests me considerably, and that is the amount for hospitalization and medical aid. This year it is $155,000. What has been the experience in that regard? Has it been necessary to provide that amount of hospitalization and medical aid for these people brought in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Order for return.
If my hon. friend would agree, I would prefer to make that an order for return. I would like to give him a more complete explanation of it.

Mr. Chairman, it begins to look as though probably I have been labouring under a misapprehension. All along I have thought that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was probably responsible for some of the reports which come to me from abroad, and from some of the people who come to this country from abroad. Now I am inclined to think that, after all, he is innocent, and that the particular misdemeanour may lie with the Department of Labour.
I have people come to my office telling me that in various places in Europe, as well as in London, England, they were painted glowing pictures of what was available for them in Canada. Then they come here and find out there is no work at all for them. It is difficult to nail these things down, but I must say that I have always blamed the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. But after what has developed here I am beginning to wonder just who is to blame; and I would like to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All very confusing.
Supply-Labour

I would like to know, if I can, so that I can nail it down. Someone overseas is definitely giving a very glowing picture of what conditions are in Canada; but when these people come out here they find there is no work available for them. I think there should be some explanation. Someone should be able to tie this right down to an individual, somewhere.
Oh, oh.

You do it, if you are so
smart.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-
I was not referring to the minister. I meant one of the members in the back row.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will be glad to explain the responsibility and the chain of command in connection with immigration when we come to my estimates.
When will that be?
The minister will say it is the Department of Labour when he comes to his estimates.
There is an item of $325,000 for transportation costs. Can the minister tell me how much of that is recovered?

None.
Mr. Pallet!: To what travel particularly has it reference? Is that paid for bringing immigrants to jobs in this country?
From the time they arrive at the port to their place of work.

Item agreed to.
Unemployment insurance commission-
195. Administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, including expenditures incurred in connection with the activities of the national employment service as delegated by the Minister of Labour in accordance with section 97 of the act. $23,122,859.
Is the minister in a position to make any further statement in respect to unemployment insurance to fishermen or wage earners or any scheme that may benefit small self-employed operators?

A group of officials are working at the present time and looking into the position of workers in agriculture and in the fishing industry in relation to unemployment insurance. I should add perhaps that as far as fishermen are concerned, the officials are considering the position not only of wage earners but also of sharemen and own-account fishermen. Hon. members will appreciate that this is not a simple problem, and there are a good many matters which have

Supply-Labour
to be taken into account before any decision is made as to whether it would be possible to extend coverage to them. Until a report is made and considered by the government it is not possible for me to say whether coverage can be broadened to include all these workers.
Mr. Nose worthy: I have two questions on this item, Mr. Chairman. The first one I asked at the beginning. Can the minister tell us whether there is any likelihood or possibility of the department making it possible for unemployed, who have accumulated an unemployment insurance backlog, to draw on that fund, although the present restrictions regarding the number of days per month are not complied with? It is pretty difficult for unemployed who are in desperate circumstances and who over the past years have built up a sizeable sum of unemployment insurance to find that they can only draw a part of it because of the department's regulations.

I am sure the hon. member will agree that the unemployment insurance plan must be kept actuarially sound, but I will take his remarks of the early part of the evening as well as those now and have them reviewed by those who are at present studying the act.

This is my second question. I notice in the details that we have a few well-paid personnel in the unemployment insurance commission and the administrative offices. A few of them are in the $7,000, $8,000, $10,000 and one in the $12,000 class. I notice that there are about 165 office managers who apparently never get out of the $3,000 class. They may get up to something over $3,000, but they never get up to $4,000 or in the $4,000 class. I know a considerable number of those managers. They have to be bankers, accountants, public relations men, public welfare officers; they have to combine a dozen different vocations in one to manage some of these large unemployment insurance offices. Is the department giving any consideration to stepping up the salaries of these 165 managers, all of whom are still either in the lower $3,000 or middle $3,000 brackets?

These have all been considered during the past year and of course the civil service commission has taken into consideration the work load of the office and all the factors that my hon. friend is concerned with.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is the unemployment insurance commission, or any other section or officials under the jurisdiction of the minister, giving any seriour or detailed study

to the question of a guaranteed annual wage? The minister knows that that is now a major question in the field of labour-management relations.

No, not any more than I am sure my officials in the department and the commission give study to anything that affects labour, but certainly are not giving any study to it as something that should be sponsored by my department.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I shall just make one remark. I suggest that in this department where a great deal of study is made of many matters, where a great deal of serious research is carried out, a very serious study should be made of this question. I suggest it is the coming issue, indeed it is here now, this feeling on the part of labour and on the part of workers. My hon. friend, the Secretary of State, can mutter if he wishes, but he is on a guaranteed annual wage, as are many professional and salaried people. Industrial workers feel that they too are entitled to a guaranteed annual wage. I urge that this matter be considered.

Can the minister tell the committee how many people who once paid unemployment insurance are now no longer paying it? By that I mean students, single girls who got married and people who went from the salary classification which required them to pay unemployment insurance and thus graduated from that classification. Can the minister give me that figure? Can he also indicate to the committee how much money is represented by the amounts that they have paid in which they are not now entitled to draw on by reason of their having discontinued paying in?

I do not think it answers my hon. friend's question, but the percentage of Canada's working force now under the act is about 75 per cent. It would be impossible for me to say how many of the other 25 per cent is or would like to be. All I know is that some of them would be, but I do not think that answers the whole of my hon. friend's question.
Mr. Pallet!: Did I understand the minister to imply that no records are kept of people who have paid into this unemployment insurance fund and now are no longer paying into it? That was the question.
No, they may have left the country. We have no means of keeping track of them after they disappear from our records.

I should like very much to make some extended remarks on the question of the unemployment insurance commission.

However, I have on one or two previous occasions expressed some of my views as to in what direction I feel the present act should be extended. I do not propose to take the time of the committee at any length at this time. While I am on my feet I should like to say a word in support of the remarks expressed by the hon. member for York South in regard to the heavy load which many of the local unemployment insurance office managers are carrying today, with their manifold responsibilities, and to suggest that I too feel serious consideration should be given to the possibility of making that office one which does lead to something of a higher level of income than at present applies to them. I feel that in large measure the whole success of the operation of the Unemployment Insurance Act, particularly in the matter of personal relationships and the general feeling toward it in the communities scattered across the country, depends so much upon the personality and efficiency of the person who holds that office.
