speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I propose at this time to make a resume of the operations of the coal board and to try to give as clear a picture as I can of the state of the coal industry as it exists at the present time. Canada is still a young nation and is at an early stage in the development of its resources. To some it may seem rather unfortunate at this time that our resources of fuel are so far removed from the main markets. But, as Canada develops industrially, and with the spread of industry from central Canada, the distribution problem with regard to fuel supplies will lessen.
However, for those of us who are living today in the present formative era, effective distribution presents a serious problem. The federal government during the past 26 years has assisted coal movements in Canada by freight subventions. The rate and the variety of these subventions have varied from time to time to meet changing conditions. Through two world wars the contribution made by the Canadian coal industry to the national defence effort has at least partly justified these expenditures of public funds.
Since 1948 with the discovery of oil and gas in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, and with the increased supplies of oil from other parts of the world, severe competition has been experienced by the coal industry in Canada and for that matter in the United States and other parts of the world.
In western Canada, the Canadian National Railways passes through oil fields; and heavy oil suitable for locomotive use is available in large quantities at low cost. As a result the Canadian National Railways has converted the greater part of its remaining steam locomotives to oil and within a year the system will be burning very little coal on its lines west of the great lakes. The main line of the Canadian National Railways between Edmonton and the Pacific coast is now completely converted to oil locomotives and diesels. Many of the mines in central Alberta were almost entirely dependent on sales to the railway company and, as a result of this recent development, these mines are now nearly all closed.
[The Deputy Chairman.]

In southern Alberta and British Columbia, where the main producing area is in the Crowsnest pass, the Canadian Pacific Railway has followed a different policy. In the first place, the Canadian Pacific Railway is further removed from the sources of oil and it would therefore find it less profitable to convert to oil. The C.P.R. still continues to buy over 1-J million tons of coal for locomotive use per year. I understand the Canadian Pacific is not buying any United States coal for use on its lines west of the great lakes, and it is even hauling Canadian coal eastward from its coaling point at the head of the lakes. As a result the coal mines of the Crowsnest pass, although facing stiff competition from oil and gas in the domestic and commercial fields, have still a basic market in the C.P.R. requirements. A steady decline in the purchase of coal by both railways can be expected.
Recently there was a mine casualty at Coleman, Alberta. The Coleman collieries international mine is now closed, presumably on account of the lack of markets. Another factor in this situation is the existence of a second mine operated by the same company but which has a very short life expectancy. By closing the Coleman international mine at this time and concentrating on the mine with the short life the company will be able to recover a maximum amount of coal. This they could not expect to do effectively by a less concentrated effort. Meanwhile the international mine is being kept in repair and when the mine being operated at the present time is exhausted the working force will be transferred back to the international mine.
Once coal is extracted it cannot be replaced, and inevitably the time comes when a mine is depleted. People engaged in mining operations always face the hazards of disruptions and of making adjustments when a mine is closed. Recently the Alberta government passed a coal marketing act. I understand that the coal mining operators were consulted in this connection and assisted the provincial government in working out and drafting the provisions of the act. This legislation provides for classification of the various types of coal produced in the province. It also requires that coal offered for sale must be labelled as to grade and analysis. This year the federal government is relating its subvention policy to the provisions of the Alberta coal sales act.
Generally speaking the coals of the prairie section of Alberta have a high moisture content, are friable and have a relatively low b.t.u. value. Most coal mining on the prairies is now carried on by stripping

methods involving the use of power machinery and a relatively small working force.
Coals in grade 5, Alberta standards, have been completely removed from eligibility for subvention aid. Strip mining operations in grade 4, which includes coal produced in the Drumheller valley, have also been declared ineligible for subvention assistance. Briefly, coals eligible at the present time for subvention aid are produced by underground mines in the Drumheller and Lethbridge areas and from the foothills and mountain mines.
Coal operators have estimated there is a market for western steam coal in northwestern Ontario to the extent of about 100,000 tons a year. The subvention rate last year was insufficient to permit western coal to compete in that market with United States coal. The subvention rate was raised by a recent order in council to the extent of 65 cents per ton additional to enable Canadian mines to meet this competition. The rate in that area is now $3.50 per ton.
The domestic market for Alberta coal in Ontario has always been restricted by the fact that much of the western coal shipped east was of comparatively low quality and would not store in the open without disintegration and danger of spontaneous combustion. The change in regulations, eliminating the lower quality coals from subvention assistance, should take care of that factor.
Another handicap to efficient marketing of western coal in central Canada is that up to the present time there has been no central selling agency. I was pleased to learn that coal operators in the west are now in the process of setting up such a selling agency. This agency would have the responsibility of marketing the bulk of western coal shipped to central Canada. By this arrangement coal will be sold on grade, possibly under trademarks, and customers will be able to buy with confidence.
Another encouraging feature of the marketing problem is that Alberta and British Columbia coal mining companies have been successful in negotiating a five year stabilized freight rate with both railways. Another stabilizing factor is indicated, I believe, by a news item which I saw the other day that the unions have agreed to forgo any increase in wages for the coming year. This will enable the mines to proceed with marketing arrangements with a degree of stability and confidence that has been lacking heretofore. In the west the production per man day is relatively high, production per man day in Alberta and British Columbia mines being approximately 4-79 tons per man day.
Turning now to the maritimes, in which the hon. member for Cape Breton South is 83276-422
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys particularly interested. The major part of the coal mining industry is in Nova Scotia with a relatively small portion in New Brunswick. The main problem as I see it is the high cost of production. The production per man day in the maritimes is very low, being two tons per man day or less. In that area a great many of the mines extend out under the ocean for several miles with resulting high transportation costs and loss of time between the pithead and the working face.
Following the war the Carroll commission studied the problems of the Canadian coal industry, and one of the recommendations of that commission was that the federal government should assist in the mechanization of the maritime coal industry. A fund of $10 million was established to be lent for that purpose. Immediately following the war the American coal industry, which is the chief supplier of coal requirements of central Canada, embarked on an intensive mechanization program which was completed in a comparatively short time.
The mechanization program in Nova Scotia has been delayed for various reasons until it is now at least two and a half years behind schedule. One result is that American coal is now competitive even in the home market in the maritimes. While American coal has decreased in price since the war, the price of Nova Scotia coal has continued to increase. During the period from 1948, when the mechanization program was started, to 1953 the actual cost of producing a ton of coal by the major company in the area increased approximately $2.25 a ton.
The mechanization program by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, although considerably behind schedule, has made progress. One of the main efforts was the production of a mechanical miner. This miner was developed in the machine shops of Trenton Industries and is now at the production stage. Some fourteen of the machines are in actual operation and it is anticipated that within a very short time there will be a total of twenty-seven. I had the privilege of seeing this machine in operation and it literally throws out a river of coal. I am told that it can produce as much as 500 tons in an eight hour shift. This machine is a credit to the ingenuity and resourcefulness of Nova Scotia engineers and workmen.
I believe that some very noteworthy progress has been made in coal preparation and cleaning, especially at Old Sydney mines. I am told that the cost of production has levelled off and is showing signs of a decline this year. At the present time the Dominion Coal Company is making a careful study and
6680	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys reassessment of the original mechanization program with a view to modifying it, if necessary, to meet changed conditions. As yet the coal board has not received the final report from the company.
Several of the smaller independent companies have taken advantage of the mechanization loan and have installed machinery with very satisfactory results. In any discussion of the over-all problem in Nova Scotia we should keep in mind that the Dominion Coal Company and its subsidiaries produce about 90 per cent of the total output of coal and employ about 81 per cent of the labour. In considering the problems of this company's operation, therefore, we are dealing with the major problems of the Nova Scotia coal industry.
As I said before, the main problem of the industry is the high cost of production. Although the subvention assistance administered by the dominion coal board is providing a market for coal produced in that area, nevertheless the industry is vulnerable because of the high cost of production. This is true, even in the maritimes, where markets are being lost to other types of fuel. It is estimated that there are 90,000 oil burning installations in Nova Scotia.
I spent about a week in the coal fields of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick last November. My observation at that time was that the people of the area were not supporting the coal mining industry as they should, because it is by far the largest single industry in that area. I was very surprised to see oil and propane gas tanks serving residences, business premises and industrial establishments. It is estimated that oil has displaced at least half a million tons of coal per year in that area.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this is a free country and one cannot blame anyone for burning oil or more convenient types of fuel if he can afford to do so. However by burning coal in their homes, offices and factories the people of Nova Scotia can help to stabilize this important industry on which their basic prosperity depends. The development of modern coal stoking and burning equipment has gone a long way towards making coal just as convenient to use as the liquid or gas fuels. Consumers, coal dealers, furnace equipment companies and chambers of commerce can do much to promote the use of coal. They must realize that if the coal industry is lost, the whole economy of the maritimes will suffer.
Further, I believe that the management of industries should consider very carefully the risk of converting from coal to oil, because I believe they would probably reach the
[Mr. Prudham.l

conclusion to stay with coal. In the event of a war or an international emergency, supplies of oil would be endangered and quite possibly cut off. I know that some major industries have already decided to continue to use coal just for that reason. Recently a large delegation, including the ministers of mines for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and their advisers, Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation officials, representatives of two unions and two independent operators associations, came to Ottawa to discuss ways and means of solving the problems of the industry. One of the main results of that meeting was the establishment of a committee with representatives of the unions, companies, provincial governments, various boards of trade and similar organizations through the area to promote the more efficient and extensive use of coal.
On May 20 I attended a gathering in Halifax sponsored by the provincial government for the purpose of initiating a provincewide campaign to enlist the support of the community for the greater and more efficient use of coal. The meeting was well attended and it was quite evident that the people of the area were beginning to realize that the future of the industry depends largely on its own efforts, and the continued support of the community.
Employment in the Nova Scotia coal industry has been relatively high, as compared with the United States or other parts of the world. The subvention policy, administered by the dominion coal board, has provided a market for all the quality coal produced in that area since the war, and that condition obtains for this year as well. But, as I told the meeting in Halifax, if the industry is not supported in its home market it becomes increasingly difficult to justify continued aid from the taxpayers of Canada. I believe that if the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick meet the challenge of lowering the cost of production and supporting the industry in the home market, they will soon put the industry on a sounder basis.
There is a long history in the maritime coal industry, according to rumours I have heard, of difficult labour-management relations. But I am convinced, from personal observation and regardless of the past, that there is presently a good relationship between management and labour and a growing sense of responsibility. I am convinced that both management and the executive of the unions are very sincere and are doing their best to work out the salvation of the industry. If the present campaign to enlist the support of consumers is successful, it will help, not only to preserve the home market but to

provide much needed encouragement for those who are struggling directly with the problem.
The dominion coal board has engaged the services of Dr. A. G. Christie, professor emeritus of the Johns Hopkins University, who is an outstanding expert on thermal power development, to make a survey of the power establishment and potential of the maritime provinces with a view to promoting the greater use of coal in the production of cheaper power. He is presently engaged in that survey and the report will be made available to provincial governments and private industry. This is being done on the theory that the production of power will consume more coal, and cheaper power will attract more industry which will also enlarge the market for coal. We are hopeful that Dr. Christie's report will lead to beneficial results.
The Mordell project to develop a coal-fired gas turbine is in its third year. The results to date have been satisfactory. The machine is presently in operation for testing purposes. The results are being carefully studied with a view to the next step which will be practical application. The results are being carefully watched by the railroads and other industrialists. Similar experiments are being carried on in Great Britain and the United States and their results are being carefully checked with experience gained at McGill.
Our laboratories at the fuels division of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys are continually experimenting with coal combustion problems, relating to the Mordell experiment and other enterprises, and also new uses for coal. The experiment carried on in the fuels division are closely co-ordinated with other efforts throughout the world, and with other efforts throughout Canada by provincial governments and others. The experiments in this field require large capital investments in equipment, and in planning the work of the department an effort is made not to duplicate work done by the provinces or by other agencies in the United States and Great Britain. At the present time the fuels division is carrying on an experiment which was initiated by the United States bureau of mines and discontinued at the time of the last change of administration.
Although there have been no recent spectacular results to report, the field of research is not being neglected. Two-thirds of the funds available to the fuels division of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys are being spent on coal research. There is now a staff of approximately 50 engaged in this work. The annual cost of coal research to this department is $332,750 for this year, including the Mordell project.

I believe that the provincial government of Nova Scotia and others in the industry are giving careful study to the possibility of heating by electricity. This would indirectly promote greater use of coal, and would perhaps provide the answer to oil competition for domestic heating. Our country is expanding rapidly. If Canada reaches a population of 22 million by 1975, we will require for all purposes at least 2-5 times more fuel than we now use. Although the coal industry is now fighting for its life, I am sure that within a few years coal will play an increasingly important role in the supply of energy and fuel. We believe that it is in the national interest to extend support to this industry for the year 1954.
Before resuming my seat I should like to pay tribute to the dominion coal board, and also to the permanent staff of the coal board. The members of the dominion coal board serve without pay and come here several times a year to assist the government in the problem of administering the subventions, the problems of research and the over-all problems of the industry.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the statement the minister has given dealing with the problems of the coal industry. Certainly I am not in a position to comment on the suggested program he has brought forward-or possibly failed to bring forward, I am not sure which-with respect to the Alberta and western coal industry. That is a matter in connection with which I am sure hon. members from western Canada can make comment, when they see fit to do so.
But I must say, so far as his proposals for the coal industry of the east are concerned, that we have not been furnished with a particularly sumptuous fare tonight. After all, these discussions were delayed from March until now so that the minister could give us an announcement of government policy. And having heard that announcement we find that Dr. Christie has been retained to make further research studies in the use of coal. We appreciate any research that is to be conducted; but that is not very much to offer an industry upon which the whole life of the maritime provinces depends.
The minister has also commented on the fact that Nova Scotians must support the coal industry, and has also said that he was down there recently attending a dinner given in Halifax. I shall comment upon that dinner in a few moments. I think possibly the sumptuous fare he received that night was on a more generous scale than he is proposing to offer to the industry at the present time. Because apparently he was impressed by the argument which was advanced that night,
G682	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys that Nova Scotians must burn more coal if the industry is to survive. And we realize that in that province there is a responsibility on everyone to support an industry which means a great deal to the province. But that, in itself, is not a solution. If I recall his figures correctly, the minister said a moment ago that about 500,000 tons has been supplanted by the installation of oil burners in the maritime provinces, and 500,000 tons is no mean amount. I grant that. But that, in itself, is no answer to the problem.
One would hesitate at this late hour of the night and late date in the session to take the time of the committee to deal with this problem, were it not for the fact that this is of vital interest to the people of the maritime provinces. Not only is it of vital interest to the people represented by my hon. friend from Cape Breton South, and other constituencies in that area, but it is also vital to all of us in the maritime provinces. It is vital to the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, and to the hon. member for Charlotte, in the extreme southwest corner of New Brunswick. It is of vital interest to the Annapolis valley; for the economy of the maritime provinces, to a greater or lesser extent, is reflected in the prosperity of the industrial area of Cape Breton. And if that area goes down, or is prejudiced to any material extent, then we are all prejudiced. And that is why I do not apologize for speaking at this time.
The minister has referred to a dinner he attended. I read a press report concerning it and, if I recall correctly, the minister of mines in Nova Scotia said at that dinner that the coal industry brought directly to Nova Scotia more money than is received in that province for family allowances, old age pensions, and all the cash payments made by the dominion treasury to the provincial treasury of Nova Scotia, which is a very substantial amount of money. One can easily see what that means in the purchase of agricultural products and everything else in the maritime provinces.
There is no doubt that the coal industry as a whole is in a bad way. One does not have to reinforce that statement with figures. I have some figures which are published by the minister's department and which show a reduction in the consumption of coal-a reduction not only in Nova Scotia. The minister has said that Nova Scotians must save the coal industry. Well, look at the consumption of Canadian coal as a whole and you will find, using round figures, that in 1949-50 the nation consumed 19,726,000 tons, that in 1951 that amount had fallen to
18,400,000	tons and that by 1953-54 it is


estimated that it is going to fall to 15,500,000 tons. In other words there is a fall of 4 million tons in the last two years in the consumption of Canadian coal by the nation. And a substantial part of that reduction comes of course from the use of American coal. There are various explanations offered. The minister has suggested that one reason has been the installation of oil burners. I know people are inclined to blame the railways for the installation of diesel engines. Indeed, sometimes I have indulged in some such criticism, myself.
I noticed the other day, in reading the evidence of Mr. Donald Gordon before the committee of this house, that he gave figures to show-and I shall not repeat the figures at this time-what the dieselization had meant in a reduction in the consumption of coal in Canada. And, although it is substantial, it is not such an impressive figure. He made this positive statement, that the Canadian National Railways could and would buy every ton of coal produced by the maritime mines, of adequate quality, if the price was right. In other words he indicated that it was not a matter of coal being supplanted by dieselization, but that to a certain extent at any rate it was a matter of government policy, as to whether the government-owned railway was prepared to buy coal from our mines at this time.
That is something I would impress upon the minister, as well as the fact that Nova Scotians must burn more coal. We have to consider how many government institutions have supplanted coal-burning installations with oil-burning, and how much coal is being burned by the railways today, or could be burned.
I say again it is not a matter of dieselization so much as it is one of government policy as to how much coal will be used. And this is not the first time that the coal industry has faced a disastrous situation. My memory goes back, as I am sure the memory of the hon. member for Cape Breton South does, to earlier days in Nova Scotia when the mines in that province, as it was then said, were facing disaster. And whatever one may say of a company which today is operating 90 per cent of those mines, certainly one can say at least that the labour situation is vastly improved over what it was in the twenties. I recall a time when special mounted police were requested by the Nova Scotia government to ride down miners on the streets because they were protesting against unemployment, and the virtual starvation which was in existence at that time.
The consumption of Nova Scotia coal at that time was down to a matter of a few

hundred thousand tons, and I think it is only right to say that it was due to the energy, the courage and the imagination of two men, and those who were associated with them at that time-the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, who was then prime minister of Canada, and Gordon Harrington, then premier of Nova Scotia, and the minister of mines-that that situation was solved.
We find, for instance, that in 1931 and 1932 only 413,000 tons of maritime coal moved outside for consumption. In face of that disaster the Bennett government, at the request of the Nova Scotia government, increased subventions materially, and as a result the consumption of Nova Scotia coal jumped in the next year or two years later to 1,600,000 tons, an increase of over 400 per cent, and went on from there to over 2 million tons. Even today it is still at the level of 1,600,000 tons. That shows what can be done by, as I say, imagination, energy and courage directed toward the solution of the problem.
I am not suggesting for one moment, Mr. Chairman, that increased subventions are going to solve this problem, except to a minor degree; but it was used as a solution at that time, and it proved successful. It gave to the industry what one might call a shot in the arm, which pulled it out of the slough into which it had fallen. We had a reorganization of the company; we had better labour relations, and as a result we went on until we came to the situation with which we are confronted today. I believe that again something can be done to improve this situation if you have imagination and if you face the situation realistically.
In its report the coal board set forth what it believes must be the solution of this problem. I will not read it. At page 13 we find the following:
That the Canadian coal mining industry is vital to our national economy is axiomatic. The best approach to these problems appears to be by way of concerted courses of action by the federal government, the provinces and components of the trade itself.
What is the future? Is there a future for this industry? I think the minister, by his own departmental officials, establishes definitely that there is. The other day we listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce speaking in this house. He was dealing with atomic energy. He outlined the demands for increased electrical energy in this country which were to follow if Canada pursued the normal course of development. Without checking on his figures, as I recall them, he stated that by 1975, if Canada had developed every bit of hydroelectric energy which would be available, including the proposed
24. 1954	6683
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys development of the St. Lawrence seaway, we would still be 10 million horsepower short of full requirements of the development of industry, and he suggested that some of that would come, he hoped, from atomic energy. I hope he is right. But why concentrate on the development of atomic energy for this purpose? I think that a large amount of that power could come from a further utilization of coal.
The minister paid tribute to the officers and members of the dominion coal board. I join in that. I hold in my hand a speech which was delivered to the mining institute by Mr. O'Brien, who was assistant to the chairman of the dominion coal board. He deals exhaustively with the situation as it is today, and points out that the total consumption of Canadian coal this year has dropped down to 15,500,000 tons. He says it is going to drop still further. He fears it may take a substantial drop. Do not forget that the total, including United States imports, was 32 million tons. He goes on to say that on the basis of any reasonable estimate, and I think his estimates are reasonable, it would appear that by 1965, and that is not very far away as time goes, we are going to use 45 million tons of coal in this country. That is going to tax the coal-producing facilities which we have today. Therefore I say this is a matter of national economy, not only from the standpoint of saving the economic framework of the mari-times but also from the standpoint of the nation as a whole; it is essential that we safeguard this mining industry.
I do not have to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that a mine is not like a restaurant. You cannot close it up today, put a padlock on the door, go away and come back ten years from now, clean out the spiders and cobwebs, put in a new stove and start operations. You have to maintain those facilities.
The minister has told us about our mines being expensive. We realize they are based under the sea; we realize that the seams go down under the sea. We realize also there are problems of flooding, and the rest of it, which once allowed to get away from us would be almost insuperable to deal with in the future. Therefore I say that the figures definitely establish there will be a need for Canadian coal, a great deal of Canadian coal, over the next few years. The minister says that his department realizes the importance of it. I say that if that is the case, then certainly there must be a greater degree of co-operation than we have had heretofore in the development and the maintenance of that industry.
6684	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
There are many ways in which it could be done of course. There is the steel industry of the maritimes, one of the great potential markets for coal. It should be further extended and developed. One can feel a little bit unhappy about threats which one sees today in the export of ores to other parts of Canada rather than to Cape Breton where, if we had them, and under co-operation with management, a greater steel industry could be established and far more coal could be used.
The minister referred to the development of electric energy from the use of coal. He said that a survey is being made of the use of coal for that purpose. Well, power demands for energy are expanding, Mr. Chairman, but the answer to that is to provide more industrialization. If we have more industries in the maritime provinces we will need more energy, and therefore we will be able to use more coal.
I want to pay tribute to the Nova Scotia Light and Power Company for the way in which that company is burning Nova Scotia coal today and is offering a greater market for that coal in the future. I am told by engineers that oil is almost competitive with coal today. When speaking about oil potentials we must remember this. Almost half of our time in this house is directed toward international affairs and the possibility of crises; in other words, the possibility of war. Do not ever forget, Mr. Chairman, that all of the oil that comes into the eastern seaboard is brought in by ship. We have no pipe lines in the east, and we will not have them, as far as one can see, in any possible foreseeable future. We therefore cannot allow a situation to develop where our industrial life, our domestic economy, is dependent upon the importation of oil, because it might be cut off at any moment of time.
The minister referred to research. That has been discussed before. The minister has mentioned also the possibility of the turbine engine. He says that research has gone on for three years, and is going to go on further. I think it should go on, Mr. Chairman, much more rapidly. Possibly there lies the solution to a major problem of the coal industry. If they could solve the problem of avoiding the ash, the engineers say that the engine is just about ready for commercial use. That is quite possible. I have seen the engines and the engineers before the railway committee, and we read of them in other places. Once a few more kinks are ironed out, the turbine engine can produce power more economically than any other instrument known to man. If that happens you will

Mr. Chairman, I am disappointed that this item had to remain in the blue book until this stage of the session. I anticipated there would be a discussion on this subject much sooner than this, otherwise I would have raised it on a motion to go into supply because it is a question of great urgency and importance and I do not give the minister very much credit for the way in which he handled it.
But I am not going to criticize the minister because he is relatively new to his present position. This industry faces a very serious crisis. There was a meeting held on March 12 in this city at which representatives of the mine workers union, the coal companies, and members of the provincial government were present and the recommendations made at that meeting, so I understand, went to the cabinet. The main reason why we delayed this discussion was to give the minister an opportunity of finding out exactly what the government policy was so he could announce it in the house and lay the basis for discussion. But that announcement was never
made in this house until tonight, and as far as I am concerned I am disappointed with it.
However during the period when we were waiting for the minister to issue a statement arising out of the deliberations of the cabinet the minister issued a statement to the press and I would suggest to him that in future it would be good policy for any minister in this house to make his announcements in the House of Commons before making them through the public press.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege. The hon. member is wrong. I am quite sure I did not make any statement to the press. What the hon. member may be referring to are the orders in council approving the extension of subventions at the same rate as last year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I am not going to argue that point with the minister. I have half a dozen clippings here from newspapers in which he is reported to have stated that the government had increased the subventions and made a sort of packaged deal with Westville, Nova Scotia, and so on. These are matters which arose out of the cabinet deliberations based on that meeting. This announcement was never made in the house. However, I guess we all make mistakes.
I want to assure the chairman and members of the committee in this house that as far as I am concerned I am not fighting for the maintenance of the coal mining industry because it provides good jobs. It is the last job I would recommend anyone to undertake as a means of obtaining a livelihood. I have done a lot of it myself and I hope that I live to see the day when it will not be necessary for men to go underground and sweat and go through the misery I have gone through in operations of that kind in order to obtain a bite to eat, and that is about what it amounts to. Therefore, I do not want anyone to think that I am pleading for the maintenance of that industry because it is a good means of obtaining a livelihood for those who are obliged to go underground and dig coal.
I am not including those who operate these coal mines and those who have investments. It is a relatively good position to be on the board of directors or in the higher echelon of officials, but as a means of livelihood for a man who has to dig coal, and I do not care whether he gets it with modern means or with the old-time shovel, it is still a long, hard, backbreaking job in which you become prematurely old at the age of 35 or 40, when your back begins to break, and then you are seeking a cure for arthritis for the rest of your life.
6686	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
Another thing I am not doing is asking for charity for the people of Cape Breton island. They are pioneers. They are the stock that came to this country when there was very little in it and they chopped down the trees and built whatever there is in the way of industry and civilization in that part of the country and in other stretches of this country.
They are not the kind of people who want charity. If they have to get out, they will do so and they will not do much squawking about it. But in order to get an intelligent discussion of this problem there are two or three things that we must think about. The first one is this. We must make an assessment of the value of this industry in the Canadian economy. If it is not of any value, it should not be maintained. But if it is of some value in the economy of the country, it should be maintained just as we have to maintain wheat and other essentials.
I am first going to point out what the coal industry means to that community. The minister knows that about 30,000 people are employed there. There are another couple of thousand in Newfoundland in the iron industry. Let it not be forgotten that coal is the basis of the iron and steel industries. All of that set-up is dependent upon the maintenance of a basic coal industry. The corporation produces half of the bituminous coal mined in Canada. Its steel plant at Trenton and so on is based on coal. Coal is the main prop of the whole economy of Nova Scotia. What does it mean to Canada as a whole?
I assume that the minister and every other responsible member of this committee think that we are going to build up and to expand the steel industry in this country. Any nation that asserts that it is an industrial nation but does not develop a basic steel industry is only trying to fool someone. It is necessary to have a basic steel industry in a country like Canada. You cannot have a basic steel industry without bituminous coal. That is something that must be remembered. When there is talk about letting the basic bituminous coal industry go in Canada, it means that you are going to let your steel industry go also because you have no other fuel which will take the place of coal, whether it is oil, natural gas, atomic energy or anything else. You must have bituminous coal and you must coke it in order to turn out basic steel. So if for no other reason than for the sake of the national economy of a country that in the future will be a great industrial section of North America, in my judgment it is necessary to have a coal industry. The basis of the economy of an industrial nation is steel. The basis for steel


is the bituminous coal industry. For these reasons this industry is important to this country.
The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is a good witness to call on the subject of the importance of the industry. In the Ottawa Citizen of February 4, 1954, the minister makes a very good statement. This article was written by Austin Cross, and the minister is likely to remember it. In that article written by Mr. Cross the minister points out the importance of the coal industry in the event of another war; the possibility of an increase in the coal needs of Canada; the fact that you cannot measure the oil deposits accurately; that you do not know how much you have; that there is not any assurance that it is going to last forever; that with the development of air transport and ships the use of oil is so great today that the drain on it is going to be terrific in the future; that to think about letting the coal industry go, as I mentioned a few moments ago, considering the factors I mentioned is not to be considered. The minister builds the thing up to a much greater extent. I do not want to read his own statement back to him but it is a good statement with regard to assessing the value of the coal industry in Canada's future.
There is another analysis made here just recently. Quoting the dominion coal board, this writer points out as follows:
"Final analysis of Canada's future energy requirements," reports the dominion coal board, "indicates that the demand for coal will substantially increase over the present level from about the year 1S65 onwards. A major problem facing the Canadian coal industry is how to bridge the gap between today's lowered consumption and the expected augmented demand of the future."
That is a realistic position for the coal board to take. However, there is quite a large gap there between 1954 and 1965. It is too long to keep coal miners on unemployment insurance; and if they are not on unemployment insurance, it is a long time to be hungry. The coal board is there definitely warning, as did the minister, that by the year 1965 we are going to need a coal industry. As the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings-Hants pointed out-

speechtext: The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Yes; the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I always get that holy trinity mixed up. As I say, he indicated that closing up a coal mine is not just like closing up a restaurant or a beer parlour. If you close a coal mine-particularly one of those submarine mines-and leave it shut down for three or four months, that is the end of it. It takes in water very fast; it

fills with gas; the roof will cave in; and the first thing you know you have no mine to come back to.
Another thing that needs to be remembered is this. If you get your trained coal miners out of that industry and into something else, you will not get them back into it. A great many people proceed on the assumption that you can take anybody and put him down in a coal mine and he can dig coal. That is a wrong assumption. The Americans found that out in 1920 when they thought they could dig coal with bayonets in Colorado. Fairly soon they did not have any bayonets, they did not have any soldiers going to dig coal and they did not have any coal mine.
To become a coal miner, in a submarine mine in Nova Scotia at least, there is a certain procedure that must be followed. You are not even permitted to go to the coal face and be recognized as a coal miner or to engage in that work until you have had three years of apprenticeship. After you have had three years of apprenticeship you must write an examination and be qualified before you get a certificate. That is just the ordinary Joe who digs coal. It takes him at least 3J years before he is allowed by law to go to the coal face in any mine in Nova Scotia. Of course when you get into your managers and your overmen and those categories, the mathematics required is equivalent to a university education. You just cannot get that kind of people overnight. It takes time to get them.
In that industry in Nova Scotia at the present time you have a well-trained staff. If they were displaced and got away from there, you would not be able to replace them in this generation. If by 1965 the requirements of the country are as forecast by the coal board, someone in this country must take some responsibility for the maintenance of the industry. I think that is all I need to say as to the value of the industry, not only in the economy of Nova Scotia but in the future development of Canada.
There is another question we shall have to ask ourselves, and I hope someone in the opposition will not accuse me of looking for a seat in the Senate or of always defending the government. I like to call the shots as I see them. That industry is in bad shape. Who is responsible? The answer to that question is obvious. The coal resources of any province are in the hands of the province. The government of the province is the custodian of the resources for the people of the province. That is the first point to remember.
The second thing to remember is that the provincial government leases that resource to the corporation. Under the terms of the 83276-423
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys lease the corporation has the right to manage it. During the last twenty-five or thirty years the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation has had a complete monopoly in the province as far as coal is concerned. Under the present scheme of things nobody has a right to dictate to the provincial government or the company as to how they should manage the industry. So they go along and they get into difficulties. I want hon. members to remember that the federal government has no authority to give orders either to the province or to the corporation as to the management of the industry.
There was no authority at all until the outbreak of the war. Then it was made a national industry under the War Measures Act and the federal government had some say. But after the war was over the authority reverted to the province. Therefore whatever is wrong about the condition of the industry from the standpoint of marketing and salesmanship, the responsibility for that rests squarely on the shoulders of the provincial government and the corporation. After a lot of discussion in the house from year to year the government finally appointed a royal commission which brought in a report analysing the industry from coast to coast and saying what they thought should be done. The minority report contained a recommendation to set up a dominion coal board.
On June 17, 1947 a bill was passed by the house establishing the dominion coal board. If members will look at that legislation they will see that it gives the board very little authority. The explanatory note merely stated that the bill provided for the setting up of the dominion coal board, that the board would have advisory functions under section 6 and administrative functions under section 8, and that its regular officers, clerks, employees and so on would be civil servants. The board merely had an advisory function. But that was one thing at least that was done to bring about some regulation on a national scale. An effort was made to see what could be done about developing the mechanics to make it work.
After a lot of deliberation and consideration legislation was passed by the house to assist the producers of coal in the Atlantic maritime provinces. I heard arguments advanced before the passage of the bill that production was down and costs were high, and the reason that was given was absenteeism, that the men were not working. That was the swan song of the corporation for several years. You do not hear that any more. However that was said to be the trouble. The industry was in bad shape but it was said that the company was not responsible. Therefore this legislation was introduced to
6688	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys lend them some money for the purpose of carrying out a program of mechanization.
I am not going to repeat my opinions. I said a good many times in the house long before that legislation was passed that that kind of program would not be of very much value. Of course I only worked in these mines for twenty-six years. I did not know anything about them, but someone with a little book knowledge comes in as general manager and he knows all about it. An appropriation of $10 million was made and a mechanization program was started. The minister told us tonight in his policy statement that the program is two and a half years behind. That is pretty good engineering, two and a half years behind with a mechanization program that was going to increase production tremendously.
It did not increase production. Just on the eve of the federal election the company closed one of their largest collieries, the one in which they installed their first heavy electrical equipment. Of course this business of mechanization is a misnomer so far as these collieries are concerned. These mines were always mechanized. The coal was cut and bored by machinery, but the machinery was operated by compressed air. The change-over could be more properly termed an electrification program because they put in electrical equipment to replace air-driven machines.
That mine was closed affecting some 1,600 men. It was done overnight with no notice except a radio announcement that they were not working any more. So far as the company was concerned, that was all the notice the men got, although there was talk about the closing for a year before. At that time the men made an offer to the provincial government and the company. They said: "There is no need to close the mine. It is faulty engineering that is the trouble. Give us that mine for one month and we will increase production by 40 per cent. Let us have a try at it and get these engineers out of the way for a while". But the mine closed. It is now back in operation.
The company is hollering today because in the maritime provinces there are 90,000 domestic units using oil or propane gas. Whose fault is that? Is that the fault of the people? If you are operating a business, have a commodity to sell and do not sell it, it is not the fault of the customer who may turn to some other commodity. The fact that oil and propane gas installations have been made to that extent in the maritime provinces adds up to a faulty sales policy on the part of the company, and nothing else.

The minister did not say this but I said it to a board of trade meeting in Sydney at which the general manager of the company was present. I said that I was prepared to argue that the Canadian National Railways had carried out their dieselization program too fast. I said that in the house and in the railway committee to Mr. Gordon before any diesels were used on the C.N.R. I told Mr. Gordon that he should make haste slowly with that program and give the coal industry a chance to adapt itself. But while we can criticize the C.N.R., and rightly so, for carrying out dieselization east of Montreal too rapidly, I should like to ask the minister if he knows that at the steel plant in Sydney, operated by the same corporation that operates the coal mines only thirteen miles away, there are thirteen diesel engines doing the shunting in the general yard which has meant that some 1,200 tons of coal per month are no longer used.
That is the company that is operating the coal mines. I should also like to ask the minister if he knows that in a recent swing-over in their open hearth operations the company installed electric equipment that displaced the use of another few thousand tons of coal. They changed to electricity. They can argue of course that it was done because they have to cut costs and so on. That is fine, but if we are going to sell that coal-and I have told them this-to people in eastern and western Canada, including the Canadian National Railways, the company should lead the way by using their own product in their own business in and around the steel plant.
Now, the responsibility rests with the provinces. There is where the first responsibility lies, with the company and with the provincial government. I go over these disabilities and try to place them where they belong, but that is not the cure for this situation. In my judgment, there is an answer. The coal industry today cannot be looked at by itself. It has to be looked at as one section of the whole fuel industry because they all tie in together. We are spending a lot of money in the development of hydroelectric power in Ontario, in the state of New York and so forth; we are rushing at it in just such a manner as the Canadian National rushed to put in these diesels. At the same time we are building pipe lines from coast to coast. The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce clearly indicated that there was too much haste in building a certain pipe line to the west coast on the assumption they were going to supply the area with oil. It is more economic to


bring in oil by a different method, and people are buying the oil brought in in that way. We are going to pipe natural gas from Alberta all the way down to the east. The coal industry is making a bid to come back.
Does that not tell the minister that in a country like Canada the first requirement before you are going to get anywhere is to try to develop in the centre of the country a body like the coal board. This board would have to have more personnel, a couple of fuel engineers, a few economists and some accountants, who could sit down and examine the country and ascertain the most economic use of oil, gas, electricity or coal in the different zones across this country. Let us stop for a moment and think about the newspaper reports we have seen for the past several months. We are being told that atomic energy is about ready. A few days ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us quite definitely that atomic energy would be used in the foreseeable future for the generation of power and at a cost at the switchboard which would be equivalent to coal selling for $8 per ton.
The minister indicated there is a survey being made in the maritimes of the possible uses of thermal power. If the use of atomic energy is so close, do you not think we are being very foolish in the rush there is today across the country to pipe this oil and gas to various centres? Atomic energy might make these things obsolete next year. I know there is a huge experiment being conducted in Britain. I believe the minister has a committee investigating this question today. What we need is a competent body with some authority because there are certain people in this country who, if they see they can make a dollar in the stock market, will go out and build a pipe line. There are other people who do not realize what the future fuel will be, who will put money into a particular development of a fuel that will perhaps be obsolete next year.
If we are going to be sensible, and if there is a dominion-provincial conference, I believe the proposition should be put to the provincial governments concerning the establishment of a national fuel policy. We can call each other names all we like; we can blame this fellow, that fellow and the other fellow, but in the final analysis if we do not get authority in the hands of some central organization that has the power to analyse the problem and correlate all the fuels that are in their embryo stages today, I am fairly sure that within the next four or five years we are going to wind up with a mess on 83276-423J>

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys our hands in the fuel field. This is a field with which we cannot afford to fool because it is at the root of our whole economy.
In so far as this turbine engine is concerned, I know that everyone who expresses an opinion on it is only making a good guess, but I think the statements in the press during the last several months to the effect that the turbine engine will be the saviour of the coal industry is bad psychology. I have looked at it, and I know the minister has been down to look at it, as has the chairman of the coal board. I do not believe that engine as it is today will ever be in service in a locomotive. Of course that is not yet determined, and the only way it can be determined is for the Canadian National to get a large appropriation of money, put their engineers in there to see what kind of locomotive it would need. Then they would have to build a locomotive to accommodate it, and that would take a long time. I do not believe that is a solution of the present difficulties of the coal industry.
As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings said a moment ago, it might perhaps be the best method for the generation of power in small power plants using coal. However, I still do not believe that that engine will be ready for any commercial use within at least the next ten years; that is my own opinion. It is only a guess, but that is all anyone can make at the present time.
I am sorry that at this stage in the session I had to get up and say this, Mr. Chairman. I want to seriously suggest to the minister that so far as I can see there is no other solution for this whole fuel problem in Canada except getting a competent body, and making arrangements with the provincial governments to make this industry a national industry. Then you could take all the fuels, have them examined realistically by competent people and determine what use you are going to make of them in relation to the possibility of atomic energy in the foreseeable future for industrial purposes.

I did not use the term. I never used the word at all because there are too many people who do not understand it and it has too many bad connotations. The minister will recall what was done during the
6693	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys war. It is peculiar that we can work so effectively in a crisis. One of the first things that was done was that the coal industry was made a national industry. People were put in to handle it who had authority; wages went up; standards were raised and we got vacations with pay for the first time in the history of the industry. Everything went along fine. As soon as the war was over the machinery was unscrambled. I should like to see you take authority for the whole fuel industry across this country as you did during the war. If a war broke out now you would do it overnight; you would have to do it in order to avoid a lot of overlapping, extra costs, competition and mix-up in the fuel industry-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Perhaps shut off the oil into Nova Scotia?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
What was that? No, I do not say cut it off at all. The minister cannot say that because he does not know any more about it than most people who talk about it. We are all feeling our way, but we are honestly trying to get rid of a bad mess. The minister knows this very well. The mess the coal industry is in today is due to the fact that you have been working on the same mechanics for the last 75 or 80 years. It has always been in trouble; this is not the first time. As far back as I can remember it has been in trouble because of faulty mechanics. And it always will be in trouble the way it is today.
Then so far as that business of nationalization is concerned, I seem to have more confidence in the federal government than most of the ministers have because I am quite prepared to hand over the organization and direction of the fuel industry of this country to the federal government, as the elected representatives of the people of Canada. I would rather take a chance on the attitude of the minister of the government, to whom I can talk in the House of Commons, than take a chance on some president of a board of directors living down on mount Royal in Montreal, whom I never have a chance to talk to. If the minister wants to call that nationalization, all right. The only thing is that I am a little bit sorry he is afraid of himself.

speechtext: Ten o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I am prepared to go on, if the
committee agrees. Perhaps after I have concluded my remarks the item might pass- I do not know.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South is a very good friend of mine. In our speeches on coal we always seem to be able to hit it off pretty well. He, of course, has


some practical knowledge. My knowledge is gained from studies I have been able to make, and conferences I have been able to have with those in the coal mining industry. But I will say this, that while the hon. member is a very good friend of mine I do not think he answered the minister's question with respect to nationalization.
We listened this evening to what has come to be known as the minister's policy speech, upon the introduction of the departmental estimates. I should like to make only one or two comments on what he said. He mentioned the fact that the government had been interested in the coal mining industry for the last 28 years, and lauded the work of the coal board, and in that I agree with him. Perhaps the coal board has not had all the authority it may have desired, but so far as the responsibilities placed upon it are concerned I do not think anyone would criticize that board.
The minister mentioned subventions. I am quite willing to give the government all the credit necessary for the introduction of its subventions policy. Because I am quite certain that the coal mining industry of Canada, particularly that of western Canada, would have folded up many years ago had it not been for the subventions paid on the movement of coal. I will give the government all credit for that.
Nevertheless I do maintain, and have maintained over the years, that the government has never really had an adequate national coal policy. The minister was quite apologetic in his speech when he referred to the present situation in the coal mining industry of Canada. He made special mention of the problem in the Crowsnest pass where recently a very substantial coal mine was closed down. He said that these mines in the Crowsnest pass will have a reasonable chance, but in the very next breath he pointed out to us that one of the largest coal mines in the Crowsnest pass area, the International Coal and Coke Company, had closed down. How they can have a reasonable chance when at the same time they are closing down, I do not know.
To my mind the minister's speech painted a rather gloomy picture. He did say he was hopeful, and it is a good thing to be hopeful. But we also hear it said that hope deferred maketh the heart sick. While he said he was hopeful, he said also that the coal mining industry is fighting for its life. That is the expression he used, that it is fighting for its life. And then he proceeded to say, "But I am confident". Now it is a very nice thing to be hopeful, and it is also a nice thing to be confident. When I go back to my constituency and have to meet the coal miners

and the coal mine operators-those who are operating mines about to fold up-I will have to tell them, "Well, the minister has confidence." I am afraid the coal miners are apt to turn to me and say, "That is all right, Hansell, but confidence does not put any pork chops on our tables, nor does it buy the baby any shoes. You can't run the coal mining industry on hope and confidence."
Of course the picture is not all one-sided. While the minister painted a gloomy picture, he said he was facing the facts. The situation is becoming desperate. Some months ago I received telegrams from various parts of my constituency in the Crowsnest pass calling my attention to the fact that these mines were closing down. I have one resolution here from a meeting held at Natal in British Columbia, also in the Crowsnest pass. This community is not in my constituency, but is bordering it. I am sure other hon. members may have received a similar resolution. It was passed at a meeting attended by residents of the Crowsnest pass area in Alberta and British Columbia, and reads as follows:
Resolved that we press upon both the provincial and federal governments to implement a Canadian policy which will enable Canadian coal to supply the Canadian market, which will bring the establishment of the industries to process coal for its by-products: which will increase unemployment insurance benefits and make them continuous until steady work is available; which will recognize that the welfare of the mines and the mining industry is a government responsibility, and it is their duty to provide either work or full maintenance.
The other telegram comes from a public meeting held in the town of Blairmore. I have another telegram from a member of the local legislature. I shall not read these, but they show the seriousness of the situation, because these were sent pursuant to the announcement that these coal mines were closing down. I brought the matter up in the house at that time and, if I may, I shall read the minister's answer. I asked my question when the orders of the day were called on March 24. My question was as follows:
Has the government any knowledge of the report appearing in the Calgary Albertan that the coal mines in Coleman, Alberta, are to close down operations on March 31, and that other mines in the Crowsnest pass are likely to follow with shutdowns? If so, does the government contemplate any remedial action?
And I want hon. members to take note of the answer the minister gave. It is quite lengthy, but the part I wish to call to the attention of the committee is this:-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Read it all.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
All right, I shall, but I did not want to take the time.
Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the report to which tny hon. friend refers. I am sure all hon. members
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys know that the coal industry in both eastern and western Canada is experiencing difficulty at the present time. In western Canada the industry's difficulties have been brought about largely through competition from oil and gas. I need not remind hon. members that the natural resources belong to the provinces. The province of Alberta has prospered enormously from the sale of natural gas and oil rights; only recently I saw a report of one sale amounting to over $30 million for two comparatively small areas of land.
This is the part that I was going to quote, without the other, for the sake of brevity:
The province of Alberta is prospering from these recent developments. The coal industry is suffering from these developments. What I would like to know is, what is the Alberta government going to do about it?
I do not like to be mean in my expressions, but I am going to tell the minister that I regard that as nothing but a cheap political answer. What has the Alberta government done about it? In his speech tonight the minister had something to say about what the Alberta government had been doing in respect to the coal mining industry there. Perhaps I can read a passage from Premier Manning's budget speech of a few months ago. This budget speech was given on March 5. I asked the minister the question on March 24. As I say, the budget speech was delivered on March 5; therefore the minister should have known what the Alberta government had been doing about it. On page 10 of Mr. Manning's budget speech, published by the queen's printer, we find the following:
Alberta's important coal industry has, in recent years, suffered from loss of markets to competitive fuels. Replacement of railway locomotives by diesel units and the conversion of coal burning locomotives to oil burners has greatly reduced what formerly was a substantial market for bituminous coal. Oil and gas progressively have eliminated coal from local domestic and industrial markets, while excessive transportation costs have made the capture and retention of eastern Canadian markets extremely difficult. Production in 1953 totalled 5,917,423 tons, a decrease of 1,277,049 tons from the previous year.
The government has assured the industry of its full co-operation in a renewed effort to increase the sale of Alberta coal in eastern markets and in this endeavour the government of the province of Ontario and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys of the government of Canada have indicated active support. The government is convinced that a long-range solution to the problems facing our coal mining industry must be sought in fields other than the utilization of coal in its natural state. With this in mind, the legislature at this session will be asked to approve a substantial appropriation to provide a research laboratory for the^ Alberta research council with special pilot plant facilities for coal research. The government of Canada has agreed to assist in staffing this research laboratory with qualified personnel to carry out this important program from which it is hoped beneficial results will be obtained.
The minister knew that when he asked what the Alberta government was doing. That is why I say it was a cheap political
6692	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys answer. I am quite sure the minister will not deny that the Alberta government have co-operated in every way possible with his own department in order to bring about a better day for the coal mining industry. I never heard Mr. Manning or anyone in the Alberta government criticize the minister's department. I believe there is the best of co-operation between the two departments. Why? Because they both have something to gain, the country has something to gain, and I am not going to say that the minister's department is not anxious to care for the welfare of the country or of the coal mining industry or whatever comes under that department. The fact is I do not think they know where they are going in respect to a national coal policy.
The situation is serious, Mr. Chairman. Might I say this: Not only has the Alberta government done that, they have done something further, and this is something the minister did not mention in his speech tonight. At the recent legislative session the Alberta government appropriated $100,000 for the rehabilitation of unemployed coal miners so that they could be taken somewhere else and be re-established. That is a magnanimous thing because the situation is serious, without very much hope for the future. Therefore it is a matter of what are these men going to do? They have built their homes there; they have raised their families there; they have worked in the mines all their lives; they are competent coal miners. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said, it takes a lifetime to develop a coal miner, and when they grow older or are thrown out of work there is nothing much else they can do. They have to be put somewhere or rehabilitated, and encouraged to establish some place else if possible. The Alberta government recognized that and appropriated $100,000 for the purpose. When I was home a few weeks ago one of the ministers of the Alberta government was down in the Crowsnest pass looking over the situation and taking applications. In one day they had about 300 applications. That is what the Alberta government is doing, Mr. Chairman, if the minister wants to know. It is not the first time of course that the coal mining industry has had to face a serious situation.
We in this group have brought these things to the attention of the government many times. For the last two years, year in and year out, the hon. member for Red Deer has urged the government to take further steps to make something of this coal mining industry by bringing into existence a real coal policy. The hon. member for Bow River has the Drumheller coal mining industry in


his constituency. I referred to the hon. member for Red Deer. He has the coal mining industry in the community of Nordegg, and I have a coal mining industry in the Crowsnest pass. The hon. member for Lethbridge has a coal mining industry there.
We are interested in this because in Alberta there are countless millions and millions of tons of coal in those hills. I said it was serious, Mr. Chairman, and it is. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Calgary Herald that the hon. member for Red Deer handed to me. It indicates something of the seriousness of the situation. It appeared in the Calgary Herald on March 1, 1954. I will not read the whole article. It states that statistics show that the coal production in Alberta alone-these are not national figures -dropped 1,277,049 tons in 1953. The output in 1952 was 7,194,472 tons; in 1953 it was 5,917,423 tons. The highest production in Alberta was in 1946 when it ran to about 9 million tons. At that time 200 mines were operating. Now there are just 150 mines. In 1946, 9,153 people were employed in those mines; now the employment is less than
7,000	and since this was written several mines have closed down. Another article appeared in the Calgary Herald of May 26, 1954 and it states according to a Canadian Press dispatch:
Supplies of coal available for consumption In Canada reached a 13-year-old low total of 38,163,000 tons In 1953.
These are the figures for the Dominion of Canada now.
The bureau of statistics announced today in a preliminary report that the total was 8 per cent lower than the 41,620,000 tons available in 1952.
In other words, an 8 per cent drop.
Domestic production of coal fell to 15,896,000 tons in 1953 from 17,579,000 tons the year before.
Here is a drop in one year of nearly two million tons. I say the situation in the coal mining industry in Canada, not only in Alberta, is serious. This department of government must have some responsibility. Otherwise this part of the minister's department would not exist. They must recognize some responsibility otherwise they would not have a coal board. But what have they done? What are they doing?
I said a little while ago that we should compliment them on their subvention policy throughout the years, but in reality if you look at it that is not something that the coal board or the minister's own department necessarily worked out. This is a financial arrangement, and all they had to do was simply to go to the Minister of Finance or the treasury board and say, "We can do this

if we can subvent the railways for the movement of coal. Have you got the money?" And when the treasury board answers, "yes, we will pay that sum of money," then that part is taken care of. It is a solution from a financial angle rather than a solution with respect to a coal policy.
But I wish to say that there is no question in my mind that the government have failed in some of their announced objectives. I have here a copy of Hansard for May 13, 1953 and at page 5284 the minister is reported as saying in answer to a question put to him from this corner of the house:
The dominion coal board was created by legislation and brought into being by proclamation on October 21, 1947. The board at an early stage in its deliberations adopted, with the concurrence of the minister, a series of principles that in effect may be recognized as a coal policy. These principles are:
Now let me read them, they are five in number. This is the minister's statement as he continued:
(1)	The maintenance of an adequate supply of coal for our national requirements;
(2)	The support of a sound and healthy coal producing industry in Canada;
(3)	The development of steady and adequate markets for the output from Canadian mines;
(4)	The provision at fair wages of reasonably full employment for Canadian miners;
(5)	The possible extensions of the market for Canadian coals, with the resultant savings of foreign exchange.
Now, let us see how far they have succeeded in that coal policy:
(1)	The maintenance of an adequate supply of coal for our national requirements;
Well, we will say that they have succeeded in that. I do not know that the credit necessarily goes to the government. The coal mining industry is able to supply our national requirements, but we will give credit to the government for success No. 1.
(2)	The support of a sound and healthy coal producing industry in Canada;
They have failed, the industry is not healthy.
(3)	The development of steady and adequate markets for the output from Canadian mines;
The verdict: failed.
(4)	The provision at fair wages of reasonably full employment for Canadian miners;
Verdict: failed.
(5)	The possible extensions of the market for Canadian coals, with the resultant savings of foreign exchange.
What verdict shall we write on the tombstone? Failed! There you have it.
Now, then, Mr. Chairman, that is not all. The thing is becoming a bit of a joke. That was what the minister said on May 13, 1953.
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys But almost a year after that, as late as February, 1954, the minister comes out and says the same thing, knowing that four parts of his declaration of policy had been a failure.
I have here the report of an interview the minister gave. The clipping does not say to whom he gave that interview, but the minister will know. Here is a report from the Montreal Gazette dated February 19, 1954. It is a Canadian Press dispatch. The heading is "Canada Needs All Her Fuel- Prudham". The article states:
Canada should not neglect any of her sources of fuel-she will need them all, mines minister Prudham said today.
I will not read all of this article but this is the thought I wish to emphasize:
On coal policy, the minister said the government favours: maintenance of an adequate coal supply for Canada's national requirements.
What he said a year ago.
A sound and healthy coal industry;
What he said a year ago.
-finding of steady markets for Canadian coal;
Just what he said a year ago.
-reasonably full employment and fair wages for miners and possible development of new equipment and methods which would lower production and transportation costs.
He said it all a year ago and yet he continued to say it then, even though he knew as late as February, 1954, that the coal mining industry of the Crowsnest pass and other parts of Canada was about to fold up. It seems to me such an accurate repetition that the minister must simply have recited it. Whether he knew he was reciting I do not know. Perhaps he was like me when I was a boy at school and I used to labour through these literary gems-
